derivations.claim: Put $X:=\omega(a^*b)$ and $Y:=\omega(b^*a)$. Positivity makes both $q(a+b)=q(a)+X+Y+q(b)$ and $q(a+ib)=q(a)+iX-iY+q(b)$ real; their imaginary parts give $\operatorname{Im}(X+Y)=0$ and $\operatorname{Re}(X-Y)=0$, hence $Y=\overline X$. Thus $(a,b)_\omega=\omega(b^*a)$ is Hermitian.

Suppose $q(b)>0$. For every $z\in\mathbb C$, positivity and the star-algebra laws give $0\le q(a+zb)=q(a)+zX+\overline z\,\overline X+|z|^2q(b)$. Taking $z=-\overline X/q(b)$ yields $0\le q(a)-|X|^2/q(b)$, so $|\omega(b^*a)|^2=|Y|^2=|X|^2\le q(a)q(b)$.

Suppose $q(b)=0$. If $X\ne0$, taking $z=-t\overline X$ for real $t>q(a)/(2|X|^2)$ makes $q(a+zb)=q(a)-2t|X|^2<0$, contradicting positivity. Hence $X=Y=0$, so the same Cauchy–Schwarz inequality holds when $q(b)=0$; if instead $q(a)=0$ and $q(b)>0$, step 2.1 forces $Y=0$ as well.

If $a\in N_\omega$, steps 2.1 and 3.1 give $(a,b)_\omega=0$ for every $b\in A$; conversely $(a,a)_\omega=0$ means $a\in N_\omega$. Thus $N_\omega$ is exactly the radical and is a linear subspace. For $c\in A$, set $d:=c^*ca$. Applying Cauchy–Schwarz to $a,d$ gives $|\omega(d^*a)|^2\le q(a)q(d)=0$, while $d^*a=a^*c^*ca=(ca)^*(ca)$; therefore $ca\in N_\omega$.

Definition of Unital star algebra and positive normalized state: A **unital complex star algebra** is a complex vector space $A$ with a complex-bilinear associative product $(a,b)\mapsto ab$, a specified unit $1_A$, and a conjugate-linear map $a\mapsto a^*$ such that, for all $a,b\in A$, $$ (ab)^*=b^*a^*,\qquad (a^*)^*=a,\qquad 1_A^*=1_A. $$ A **positive normalized state** on $A$ is a complex-linear functional $\omega:A\to\mathbb C$ such that $\omega(1_A)=1$ and $\omega(a^*a)$ is a real nonnegative number for every $a\in A$. This is an algebraic definition: no norm, topology, boundedness condition, or completion is part of the data. derivations.claim: By [F1], $N_\omega$ is a subspace and every element of it pairs to zero with every element of $A$. Thus $([a],[b])_\omega=\omega(b^*a)$ is independent of both representatives; it is Hermitian and nonnegative, and $([a],[a])_\omega=0$ holds exactly when $a\in N_\omega$, so the quotient pairing is positive definite.

For $a,b\in A$, replacing $b$ by $b+n$ with $n\in N_\omega$ changes $ab$ by $an\in N_\omega$ because $N_\omega$ is a left ideal by [F1]; hence $\pi_\omega(a)[b]=[ab]$ is well defined. Bilinearity, associativity and $1_A$ give $\pi_\omega(a+b)=\pi_\omega(a)+\pi_\omega(b)$, $\pi_\omega(\lambda a)=\lambda\pi_\omega(a)$, $\pi_\omega(ab)=\pi_\omega(a)\pi_\omega(b)$ and $\pi_\omega(1_A)=I_{\mathcal D_\omega}$, and left multiplication keeps $\mathcal D_\omega$ invariant.

Apply [F2] to the quotient inner-product space $\mathcal D_\omega$; under the stated Countable Choice assumption this gives the Hilbert completion $H_\omega$ and a dense isometric embedding of $\mathcal D_\omega$, which we identify with its image. This is the only completion invoked.

For $a,b,c\in A$, the quotient form gives $(\pi_\omega(a)[b],[c])_\omega=\omega(c^*ab)=([b],\pi_\omega(a^*)[c])_\omega$. By the definition of the Hilbert-space adjoint, this identity for all $[b]\in\mathcal D_\omega$ shows $[c]\in D(\pi_\omega(a)^*)$ and $\pi_\omega(a)^*[c]=\pi_\omega(a^*)[c]$.

Since $([1_A],[1_A])_\omega=\omega(1_A)=1$, $\Omega_\omega$ is a unit vector. Also $\pi_\omega(a)\Omega_\omega=[a]$ for every $a\in A$, so its algebraic orbit is exactly $\mathcal D_\omega$ and is dense. Finally $(\pi_\omega(a)\Omega_\omega,\Omega_\omega)_\omega=([a],[1_A])_\omega=\omega(a)$, recovering the state.

Let $(H',\mathcal D',\rho,\Omega')$ be another algebraically cyclic *-representation of $A$ with common invariant dense domain $\mathcal D'=\rho(A)\Omega'$, $\rho(a^*)=\rho(a)^*|_{\mathcal D'}$, and $\omega(a)=(\rho(a)\Omega',\Omega')$. Define $U[a]:=\rho(a)\Omega'$. If $[a]=[0]$, then $\|\rho(a)\Omega'\|^2=\omega(a^*a)=0$, so $U$ is well defined; and for $a,b\in A$, $(U[a],U[b])=\omega(b^*a)=([a],[b])_\omega$ by the representation's adjoint identity. Thus $U$ is an isometry from $\mathcal D_\omega$ onto the dense subspace $\mathcal D'$.

Suppose $x_n\in\mathcal D_\omega$, $x_n\to0$ in $H_\omega$, and $\pi_\omega(a)x_n\to y$ in $H_\omega$. For each $z\in\mathcal D_\omega$, step 2.2 gives $(y,z)_\omega=\lim_n(\pi_\omega(a)x_n,z)_\omega=\lim_n(x_n,\pi_\omega(a^*)z)_\omega=0$. Density forces $y=0$. Therefore the closed graph relation of $\pi_\omega(a)$ contains no two distinct outputs over one input: their difference would be a nonzero pair $(0,y)$. The graph closure is a graph, so $\pi_\omega(a)$ is closable. In particular, if $a=a^*$ then $\pi_\omega(a)$ is symmetric on $\mathcal D_\omega$; this does not prove essential self-adjointness.

The isometry extends uniquely from the dense domain to a unitary $\overline U:H_\omega\to H'$ because its range $\mathcal D'$ is dense. It sends $\Omega_\omega$ to $\Omega'$ and, for $[b]\in\mathcal D_\omega$, $\overline U\pi_\omega(a)[b]=\rho(ab)\Omega'=\rho(a)\overline U[b]$; hence it intertwines the representations on the common domains. Uniqueness follows because every vector of $\mathcal D_\omega$ has the form $\pi_\omega(a)\Omega_\omega$.

derivations.claim: For bosons, the ladder formulas [F1] give $a(e)a^\dagger(e)|n\rangle=(n+1)|n\rangle$ and $a^\dagger(e)a(e)|n\rangle=n|n\rangle$ for every $n\ge0$, where the second identity at $n=0$ uses $a(e)\Omega=0$. Their difference is $|n\rangle$; linear extension proves $[a(e),a^\dagger(e)]=I$ on the finite-particle core. For fermions, $c(e)\Omega=0$, $c^\dagger(e)\Omega=|1\rangle$, $c(e)|1\rangle=\Omega$, and $c^\dagger(e)|1\rangle=0$. Hence $\{c(e),c^\dagger(e)\}$ fixes both basis vectors, while $c(e)^2=(c^\dagger(e))^2=0$; these identities hold on the whole two-dimensional fermionic Fock space.

The squared norm of $\Psi$ is $\sum_{n\ge0}(n+1)^{-3}$, which is finite: on each block $2^k\le n+1<2^{k+1}$ there are $2^k$ terms, each at most $2^{-3k}$, so the block sum is at most $2^{-2k}$ and the geometric series of these bounds converges. By [F3], $\Psi\in D(N)$ would require $\sum_{n\ge1}n^2/(n+1)^3<\infty$. Since $n+1\le2n$ for $n\ge1$, $n^2/(n+1)^3\ge1/(8n)$. The harmonic series diverges because each block $2^k\le n<2^{k+1}$ has $2^k$ terms at least $2^{-(k+1)}$, so every block sum is at least $1/2$. Therefore $\Psi\notin D(N)$.

By [F2], the annihilation-domain sum for $\Psi$ is $\sum_{n\ge1}n/(n+1)^3\le\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-2}$, and the creation-domain sum is $\sum_{n\ge0}(n+1)^{-2}$. Each is finite: the $k$th dyadic block of $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-2}$ has at most $2^k$ terms each at most $2^{-2k}$, so its block sum is at most $2^{-k}$; the shifted series has the same convergence. Thus $\Psi\in D(a(e))\cap D(a^\dagger(e))$ while step 1.2 proves $\Psi\notin D(N)$. This is a domain distinction for the stated operators, not a physical or empirical claim.

derivations.claim: Each sector $H_s^{(n)}$ or $H_a^{(n)}$ is a closed subspace of its Hilbert tensor power, being the range of the corresponding orthogonal projection [F2]. The square-summable direct sum of these sectors is complete: for a Cauchy sequence, each coordinate converges in its complete sector; finite partial sums of squared coordinate norms are bounded by the common sequence bound, so the coordinate limits are square-summable; taking coordinate limits in the Cauchy estimate over each finite set of coordinates and then the supremum proves convergence in the direct-sum norm. Truncating a square-summable sequence after sector $N$ converges in norm, so $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is dense.

On sector $n$, creation and contraction have norms at most $\sqrt{n+1}\|h\|$ and $\sqrt n\|h\|$, respectively: the contraction has norm at most $\|h\|$ on its first factor by Cauchy–Schwarz and extends to the tensor product with the same bound [F4]; each symmetrizer or antisymmetrizer has norm at most one [F2]. For $\Phi\in H_s^{(n)}$ and $\Psi\in H_s^{(n+1)}$, use $P_{s,n+1}\Psi=\Psi$ and self-adjointness of $P_{s,n+1}$ to compute $\langle a_n^\dagger(h)\Phi,\Psi\rangle_2 =\sqrt{n+1}\langle h\otimes\Phi,\Psi\rangle_2 =\sqrt{n+1}\langle\Phi,(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes n})\Psi\rangle_2 =\langle\Phi,a_{n+1}(h)\Psi\rangle_2$; the tensor product pairing gives the middle equality because $C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$. The same calculation with $P_{a,n+1}$ proves the fermionic relation.

The maximal bosonic direct-sum maps are closed. For example, if $\Phi^{(j)}\to\Phi$ and $a(h)\Phi^{(j)}\to\Theta$ in Fock norm, boundedness of each sector map gives coordinatewise $\Theta_{n-1}=a_n(h)\Phi_n$; since $\Theta$ is square-summable, the defining sum for $D(a(h))$ is finite and $a(h)\Phi=\Theta$. The same coordinate argument applies to $a^\dagger(h)$. Truncating a vector and its image after sector $N$ shows $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is a graph core for each. For the adjoint, testing against vectors supported in input sector $n$ forces the output coordinate in sector $n+1$ to be $a_{n+1}^\dagger(h)\Phi_n$; square-summability of these coordinates is exactly the displayed domain of $a^\dagger(h)$. Conversely, if that sum is finite, the sector pairing of step 1.2 and Cauchy–Schwarz in the direct sum give the adjoint identity for every vector in $D(a(h))$. Thus $a(h)^*=a^\dagger(h)$ with the displayed maximal domains.

Measurable representatives may be chosen for $f,f',g,g'$. Replacing a
representative on a null set changes its product only on a product-null set:
cover the other sigma-finite factor by countably many finite-measure sets and
apply the rectangle formula [F1] on each. Thus the product rule is well
defined on $L^2$ classes. By [F7], $f\overline{f'}$ and $g\overline{g'}$
are integrable; Fubini [F2] gives the product norm
$\|f(x)g(y)\|_2^2=\|f\|_2^2\|g\|_2^2$, so each elementary product belongs
to the target space. It also gives
$$\langle f(x)g(y),f'(x)g'(y)\rangle_{L^2(X\times Y)} =\langle f,f'\rangle_{H_X}\langle g,g'\rangle_{H_Y}.$$
By sesquilinearity, the rule $\sum_j\alpha_j f_j\otimes g_j\mapsto
\sum_j\alpha_j f_j(x)g_j(y)$ preserves inner products on finite sums. If two
tensor presentations define the same algebraic tensor, their difference has
zero tensor norm by [F5], hence its product function has zero $L^2$ norm; the
rule is well-defined on the algebraic tensor product and extends uniquely as
an isometry $T$ to the completion.

Choose sigma-finite exhaustions $X_k\uparrow X$ and $Y_k\uparrow Y$ with finite measure, and put $Z_k=X_k\times Y_k$. By the rectangle formula [F1], $(\mu\times\nu)(Z_k)<\infty$, and $Z_k\uparrow X\times Y$. For fixed $k$, let $\mathcal C_k$ be the family of product-measurable $E\subseteq Z_k$ such that $\mathbf1_E$ belongs to the closed range of $T$. It contains $Z_k$, since $\mathbf1_{Z_k}=T(\mathbf1_{X_k}\otimes\mathbf1_{Y_k})$. If $E\subseteq F$ are in $\mathcal C_k$, then $\mathbf1_{F\setminus E}=\mathbf1_F-\mathbf1_E$ is in that closed range. If $E_j\uparrow E$ in $Z_k$, then $\|\mathbf1_E-\mathbf1_{E_j}\|_2^2=(\mu\times\nu)(E\setminus E_j)\to0$ by [F6], so $E\in\mathcal C_k$. Thus $\mathcal C_k$ is a lambda-system on $Z_k$. For every measurable rectangle $A\times B$, its restriction to $Z_k$ is $(A\cap X_k)\times(B\cap Y_k)$, whose indicator is the image of $\mathbf1_{A\cap X_k}\otimes\mathbf1_{B\cap Y_k}$; these restricted rectangles are a generating pi-system by [F4]. Dynkin's theorem [F4] gives $\mathbf1_E\in\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$ for every product-measurable $E\subseteq Z_k$.

Let $E$ be any completed-product-measurable set with finite product measure. By the completion definition [F1], it differs from a product-measurable set $E_0$ by a subset of a product-null set, so $\mathbf1_E=\mathbf1_{E_0}$ as $L^2$ classes. Since $Z_k\uparrow X\times Y$, [F6] gives $(\mu\times\nu)(E_0\setminus Z_k)\to0$, so $\mathbf1_{E_0}=\lim_k\mathbf1_{E_0\cap Z_k}$ in $L^2$; step 2.1 puts each truncated indicator in the closed range of $T$. Its norm equals $\|f\|_Q$ on $D(Q)$. Suppose $f\in\mathcal G$ is orthogonal to every $g_n$ in this weighted inner product. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Here
$\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ is the Schwartz space of smooth complex functions
whose coordinate-weighted derivatives are all bounded, as defined in
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]].
Fix an oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski space and an inertial coordinate
chart as in [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use coordinates
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ and metric $\eta=\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, matching the
$(-+++)$ convention of the SR suppliers. Some QFT sources use its negative
$(+---)$; the Lorentz group is unchanged, and the phase is fixed explicitly
below.
Coordinates $x$ have length units, momenta have inverse-length units, and the
Fourier phase below is dimensionless. A parameter $\mu\ge0$ has inverse-length
units and is only a mathematical shell parameter; it is not identified with a
physical rest mass. For $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, set
$$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2},\qquad p_\mu(\mathbf k)=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k).$$
The future mass shell is
$$H_\mu^+=\{(p^0,\mathbf p): (p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=\mu^2,\ p^0>0\}.$$
When $\mu=0$, its apex is omitted; thus $\mathbf k\ne0$ in the massless
parameterization. The scalar shell pairing is
$$p\circ x:=p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$
Define the measure and one-particle Hilbert space by
$$d\nu_\mu(p_\mu(\mathbf k))= \frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)},\qquad H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C),$$
where the omitted massless apex has measure zero. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb
R^4)$ define its pointwise shell Fourier restriction by
$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{ip\circ x}\,d^4x.$$
The Fourier convention is exactly the displayed integral, with no prefactor.
If $\widehat f(\xi^0,\boldsymbol\xi)=
\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i(x^0\xi^0+\mathbf x\cdot\boldsymbol\xi)}\,d^4x$ denotes
the standard transform in
[[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]],
then
$$\mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p):=\int f(x)e^{i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)}\,d^4x =\widehat f\!\left(-\frac{p^0}{2\pi},\frac{\mathbf p}{2\pi}\right).$$
Its inverse is
$$f(x)=(2\pi)^{-4}\int_{\mathbb R^4} \mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p)e^{-i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)} \,dp^0\,d^3\mathbf p.$$
Thus this convention is a time reflection and rescaling of the cited
Schwartz automorphism and has the stated reciprocal normalization.
The proper orthochronous Lorentz group consists of linear maps preserving
$\eta$, orientation and the chosen future cone. A Poincare map is
$x\mapsto a+\Lambda x$ with $a\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\Lambda$ in that group.

This is a mathematical free scalar one-particle construction. It adopts the
chosen coordinates, measure and Fourier convention; it asserts no experimental
observation, physical mass identification or measurement outcome.

Assume Countable Choice. For every $\mu\ge0$, the measure $d\nu_\mu$ of
[[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]] is locally finite and sigma-finite on $H_\mu^+$.
For every proper orthochronous Lorentz transformation $\Lambda$ and every
nonnegative Borel function $g$ on $H_\mu^+$,
$$\int_{H_\mu^+}g(\Lambda^{-1}p)\,d\nu_\mu(p) =\int_{H_\mu^+}g(p)\,d\nu_\mu(p).$$
The claim applies off the omitted apex when $\mu=0$.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. For every $\mu\ge0$, the
space $H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu)$ of
[[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]] is separable, and
$$\{K_\mu f:f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)\}$$
is dense in $H_\mu$. If $\mu>0$, the range contains every function in
$C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$; if $\mu=0$, it contains every function in
$C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. For every $\mu\ge0$, the
pointwise restriction
$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{ip\circ x}\,d^4x$$
of [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]] maps $\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ continuously
and linearly into $H_\mu$. It also annihilates the Klein–Gordon test operator:
$$K_\mu\bigl((\partial_0^2-\Delta+\mu^2)f\bigr)=0 \qquad(f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)).$$
The coordinates are the fixed length coordinates of that definition and
$\mu$ has inverse-length units.

An **oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space** is a quadruple
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with the following data. In this notation $V$ includes its
specified orientation; forgetting that orientation gives only the underlying
real vector space, not the full datum $V$ of the model.

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

The following terminology is attached to such a quadruple.

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.
- Events $p,q$ are **timelike**, **null**, **spacelike** or **causally
  related** when the displacement $q-p$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal
  in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; they are
  **future-related** when $q-p$ is future causal and **past-related** when
  $q-p$ is past causal in the sense of
  [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**No point of $A$ is distinguished.** For every $v\in V$ the translation
$\tau_v:A\to A$, $\tau_v(p):=p+v$, is a bijection, since it is inverse to
$\tau_{-v}$: $\tau_{-v}(\tau_v(p))=(p+v)+(-v)=p+(v-v)=p$ and symmetrically, by
the affine action axioms ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). Displacements
are translation invariant, $\tau_v(q)-\tau_v(p)=q-p$, so every $\tau_v$ preserves
the interval, the causal classification of every ordered pair, and the sets
$C^+$, $C^-$ (which are subsets of $V$, independent of the point of $A$); it
changes only the labelling of points. The mathematical structure of the model is
exactly the quadruple $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; no derived physical quantity (proper
time, four-velocity, momentum, energy, charge or any field) is part of this
definition, and all later structure of the framework (frames, charts, tensor
fields, worldlines) is built on this model.

**Well-definedness.** The affine-space definition supplies the action and the
unique displacements; the Lorentz-form definition supplies $\eta$ and its
inertia; the determinant-line definition supplies orientations; and the two
components of $T$ between which the time-orientation definition chooses exist by
the components lemma recorded in the well-definedness clause of
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], which is also what makes the
names future and past causal in item 4 well defined.

Let $V$ be a $4$-dimensional real vector space ([[def-vector-space]],
[[def-dimension]]). A **Lorentz form** on $V$ is a symmetric bilinear form
$\eta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]])
such that

1. $\eta$ is nondegenerate: both radicals
   $\operatorname{rad}_L(\eta)=\{u:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }v\}$ and
   $\operatorname{rad}_R(\eta)=\{v:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }u\}$ are
   $\{0\}$ ([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]);
   and
2. $\eta$ has **inertia** $(3,1,0)$: in some (equivalently, in every) basis of
   $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal, exactly three diagonal
   entries are positive, exactly one is negative, and none is zero
   ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]).

The inertia of a symmetric bilinear form is the triple $(p,q,r)$ of numbers of
positive, negative and zero diagonal entries of any diagonalizing basis, and it
is independent of the diagonalizing basis by Sylvester's law of inertia
([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]); hence clause 2
is a property of $\eta$ itself and not of a chosen basis. The **associated
quadratic form** of $\eta$ is

$$q(v):=\eta(v,v),\qquad v\in V .$$

A **Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$** is a pair $(V,\eta)$
consisting of a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$ and a Lorentz form $\eta$
on $V$; the name records that the diagonal normal form of $\eta$ has one
negative entry followed by three positive entries. No positive-definite
structure on $V$ is assumed or implied by this definition, and $q$ takes both
negative and positive values on nonzero vectors: a basis in which
$\eta$ is diagonal with diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$ exists by clause 2, and on
its first vector $q$ is $-1$, while on each of the other three it is $+1$.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

$x=a+\Lambda y$; [F5] gives $|\det\Lambda|=1$ and [F7] justifies the
change of variables. Lorentz invariance of the phase then gives
$$K_\mu f_g(p)=e^{ip\circ a}K_\mu f(\Lambda^{-1}p).$$

Let $h\in C_c^\infty$ in the shell chart, with support away from the
massless apex. If $g\to g_0$ in the Poincare group, $U_\mu(g)h$ converges

lie in one compact chart subset $C$ away from the apex; $\nu_\mu(C)<\infty$
by [F2]. The squared pointwise difference is bounded by
$4\|h\|_\infty^2\mathbf1_C$, so [F8] gives norm continuity for this dense

$h$ with $\|v-h\|<\epsilon$; unitarity gives
$$\|U_\mu(g)v-U_\mu(g_0)v\| \le2\epsilon+\|U_\mu(g)h-U_\mu(g_0)h\|.$$
First take $g\to g_0$ and then $\epsilon\downarrow0$. This proves strong
continuity on all of $H_\mu$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], let $\mu\ge0$, let
$H_\mu$ and $K_\mu$ be as in [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and form
$\mathcal F_s(H_\mu)$ with vacuum $\Omega$ and finite-particle domain
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ define on
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$
$$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu\overline f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f).$$
This is a complex-linear map of test functions into operators
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\to\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For real $f$ it is symmetric
and equals $\sqrt2\,\Phi_{\rm Segal}(K_\mu f)|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}$, where the Segal field of
[[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]] is
$\Phi_{\rm Segal}(h)=\overline{(a^\dagger(h)+a(h))/\sqrt2}$.
Thus its Weyl unitary is
$W_\mu(f):=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2 K_\mu f)$ and, for real $f,g$,
$$W_\mu(f)W_\mu(g)= e^{-i\,\operatorname{Im}\langle K_\mu f,K_\mu g\rangle_2}W_\mu(f+g).$$
For every real $f$ the vacuum Weyl expectation is
$$\langle\Omega,W_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2 =e^{-\|K_\mu f\|_2^2/2}.$$
Here the inner product is second-variable-linear as fixed in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The vacuum has zero one-point function and
two-point function
$$\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(f)\Phi_\mu(g)\Omega\rangle_2 =\langle K_\mu\overline f,K_\mu g\rangle_2,$$
which obeys $\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(\overline f)\Phi_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2=\|K_\mu f\|_2^2\ge0$ for every complex test $f$ (ordinary diagonal positivity holds for real tests); higher vacuum moments of ordered real smeared
fields obey the CCR pairing recursion and hence the free-field Wick pairing
rule. The field is a weak operator-valued tempered distribution on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$: every matrix coefficient $f\mapsto\langle\Psi,\Phi_\mu(f)\Theta\rangle_2$ for $\Psi,\Theta\in\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on Schwartz space. Its adjoint satisfies $\Phi_\mu(f)^*|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}=\Phi_\mu(\overline f)$, and its normalized vacuum defines a positive state on the finite polynomial $*$-algebra generated by these fields.

The relative-coordinate two-point tempered distribution is
$$W_\mu(z)=\int_{H_\mu^+}e^{-ip\circ z}\,d\nu_\mu(p),$$
understood by pairing with Schwartz tests. Its translation-invariant bidistribution is the shell integral of $e^{-ip\circ x}e^{ip\circ y}$; on product tests it is the displayed vacuum covariance.

For $g=(a,\Lambda)$, let $f_g$ and $U_\mu(g)$ be the affine test pullback
and one-particle action of [[lem-qft-scalar-poincare-action]]. Their Fock
lifts implement the same covariance for $\Phi_\mu$ on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$
and for the bounded Weyl operators.

For translations, the joint spectral measure on Fock space is the
second-quantized multiplier measure with one-particle vector
$(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),-\mathbf k)$. Its support is contained in the closed
future cone $\{(E,\mathbf P):E\ge|\mathbf P|\}$; the vacuum is an eigenvector
at $(0,\mathbf0)$. These are conditional mathematical model deductions.
No point field, empirical observation or measurement claim is made.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Here
$\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ is the Schwartz space of smooth complex functions
whose coordinate-weighted derivatives are all bounded, as defined in
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]].
Fix an oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski space and an inertial coordinate
chart as in [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use coordinates
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ and metric $\eta=\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, matching the
$(-+++)$ convention of the SR suppliers. Some QFT sources use its negative
$(+---)$; the Lorentz group is unchanged, and the phase is fixed explicitly
below.
Coordinates $x$ have length units, momenta have inverse-length units, and the
Fourier phase below is dimensionless. A parameter $\mu\ge0$ has inverse-length
units and is only a mathematical shell parameter; it is not identified with a
physical rest mass. For $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, set
$$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2},\qquad p_\mu(\mathbf k)=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k).$$
The future mass shell is
$$H_\mu^+=\{(p^0,\mathbf p): (p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=\mu^2,\ p^0>0\}.$$
When $\mu=0$, its apex is omitted; thus $\mathbf k\ne0$ in the massless
parameterization. The scalar shell pairing is
$$p\circ x:=p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$
Define the measure and one-particle Hilbert space by
$$d\nu_\mu(p_\mu(\mathbf k))= \frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)},\qquad H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C),$$
where the omitted massless apex has measure zero. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb
R^4)$ define its pointwise shell Fourier restriction by
$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{ip\circ x}\,d^4x.$$
The Fourier convention is exactly the displayed integral, with no prefactor.
If $\widehat f(\xi^0,\boldsymbol\xi)=
\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i(x^0\xi^0+\mathbf x\cdot\boldsymbol\xi)}\,d^4x$ denotes
the standard transform in
[[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]],
then
$$\mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p):=\int f(x)e^{i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)}\,d^4x =\widehat f\!\left(-\frac{p^0}{2\pi},\frac{\mathbf p}{2\pi}\right).$$
Its inverse is
$$f(x)=(2\pi)^{-4}\int_{\mathbb R^4} \mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p)e^{-i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)} \,dp^0\,d^3\mathbf p.$$
Thus this convention is a time reflection and rescaling of the cited
Schwartz automorphism and has the stated reciprocal normalization.
The proper orthochronous Lorentz group consists of linear maps preserving
$\eta$, orientation and the chosen future cone. A Poincare map is
$x\mapsto a+\Lambda x$ with $a\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\Lambda$ in that group.

This is a mathematical free scalar one-particle construction. It adopts the
chosen coordinates, measure and Fourier convention; it asserts no experimental
observation, physical mass identification or measurement outcome.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] and let $H$ be a separable
complex Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear convention of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ define the bosonic
creation and annihilation maps $a^\dagger(h)$ and $a(h)$ and the fermionic maps
$c^\dagger(h)$ and $c(h)$ as in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. Write $a_n(h)$ and $a_n^\dagger(h)$ for
their restrictions to the $n$th bosonic sector. For bosons set

$$D(a(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge1}\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\},\qquad D(a^\dagger(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge0}\|a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}.$$

Then $\mathcal F_s(H)$ and $\mathcal F_a(H)$ are Hilbert spaces,
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is dense, and it is a graph core for both maximal
bosonic sector maps. The bosonic operators on their displayed domains are
closed and mutually adjoint, and on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ satisfy

$$[a(h),a^\dagger(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad [a(h),a(k)]=[a^\dagger(h),a^\dagger(k)]=0.$$

The fermionic $c(h)$ and $c^\dagger(h)$ extend to bounded operators on the
whole Fock space, with norms $\|h\|$, and satisfy on the whole space

$$\{c(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad \{c(h),c(k)\}=\{c^\dagger(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=0.$$

This is a mathematical construction of the two Fock representations; it does
not assign particle statistics to a physical species.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$ and its tensor extension is the bounded map of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation
by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction
$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and
$c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the
creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the
finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. No physical statistics assignment or spin–statistics
theorem is part of these mathematical definitions.

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

Fix an integer $n\geq1$.  A **tempered distribution** on $\mathbb R^n$ is a
continuous complex-linear functional

$$u:\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)\longrightarrow\mathbb C,$$

where Schwartz space and its locally convex topology are those of
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]] and
[[def-schwartz-topology-and-convergence]].  The space of all such functionals
is denoted $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.

We write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$.  This pairing is bilinear:
the test variable is not conjugated.  Thus $u(a\varphi+b\psi)=
a\langle u,\varphi\rangle+b\langle u,\psi\rangle$ for $a,b\in\mathbb C$.
The zero functional is tempered.  Continuity is topological continuity, and,
because the Schwartz topology is generated by a countable cofinal family of
seminorms, it is equivalently continuity on every convergent sequence.  No
choice principle is used in this definition.

An **oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space** is a quadruple
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with the following data. In this notation $V$ includes its
specified orientation; forgetting that orientation gives only the underlying
real vector space, not the full datum $V$ of the model.

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

The following terminology is attached to such a quadruple.

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.
- Events $p,q$ are **timelike**, **null**, **spacelike** or **causally
  related** when the displacement $q-p$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal
  in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; they are
  **future-related** when $q-p$ is future causal and **past-related** when
  $q-p$ is past causal in the sense of
  [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**No point of $A$ is distinguished.** For every $v\in V$ the translation
$\tau_v:A\to A$, $\tau_v(p):=p+v$, is a bijection, since it is inverse to
$\tau_{-v}$: $\tau_{-v}(\tau_v(p))=(p+v)+(-v)=p+(v-v)=p$ and symmetrically, by
the affine action axioms ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). Displacements
are translation invariant, $\tau_v(q)-\tau_v(p)=q-p$, so every $\tau_v$ preserves
the interval, the causal classification of every ordered pair, and the sets
$C^+$, $C^-$ (which are subsets of $V$, independent of the point of $A$); it
changes only the labelling of points. The mathematical structure of the model is
exactly the quadruple $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; no derived physical quantity (proper
time, four-velocity, momentum, energy, charge or any field) is part of this
definition, and all later structure of the framework (frames, charts, tensor
fields, worldlines) is built on this model.

**Well-definedness.** The affine-space definition supplies the action and the
unique displacements; the Lorentz-form definition supplies $\eta$ and its
inertia; the determinant-line definition supplies orientations; and the two
components of $T$ between which the time-orientation definition chooses exist by
the components lemma recorded in the well-definedness clause of
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], which is also what makes the
names future and past causal in item 4 well defined.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

derivations.claim:
Assume Countable Choice as required by [F4]. For fixed $t$,
$\sin(\omega_\mu t)/\omega_\mu$ is bounded near
$\mathbf k=0$ when $\mu>0$ and is bounded by $|t|$ when $\mu=0$; at infinity
it is $O(|\mathbf k|^{-1})$. Pairing with a Schwartz function is absolutely
bounded by a Schwartz seminorm times the integral of
$|q(\mathbf k)|(1+|\mathbf k|)^{-4}$, which is finite. Thus it defines a
tempered inverse Fourier transform in $\mathbf x$, and its massless apex
singularity is locally integrable. Differentiating the multiplier in $t$
distributionally shows
$(\partial_t^2-\Delta_{\mathbf x}+\mu^2)\Delta_\mu=0$,
$\Delta_\mu(0,\cdot)=0$, and
$\partial_t\Delta_\mu(0,\cdot)=\delta_0$; the last identity is Fourier
inversion [F4].

Choose a nonnegative smooth spatial mollifier $\rho_\epsilon$ of integral
one supported in $|\mathbf x|<\epsilon$, using [F7], and let
$u_\epsilon(t,\cdot)=\Delta_\mu(t,\cdot)*\rho_\epsilon$. Its Fourier
multiplier is $\widehat\rho_\epsilon(\mathbf k)\sin(\omega_\mu t)/\omega_\mu$;
this is Schwartz in $\mathbf k$ for every fixed $t$, including $\mu=0$
because $\sin(|\mathbf k|t)/|\mathbf k|$ has a power series in
$|\mathbf k|^2$. Thus $u_\epsilon$ and its derivatives are Schwartz and have
finite energy by [F8]. By 1.1 it is a smooth solution of the
Klein–Gordon equation with data
$u_\epsilon(0)=0$, $\partial_tu_\epsilon(0)=\rho_\epsilon$. Its initial
energy is finite. Choose $R>\epsilon$ and for $t\ge0$ set
$$E_R(t)=\frac12\int_{|\mathbf x|>R+t} \bigl(|\partial_tu_\epsilon|^2+|\nabla u_\epsilon|^2+ \mu^2|u_\epsilon|^2\bigr)\,d^3\mathbf x.$$
The equation and integration by parts on the exterior region give
$$E_R'(t)=-\frac12\int_{|\mathbf x|=R+t} \left(|\partial_tu_\epsilon+\partial_ru_\epsilon|^2+ |\nabla_Tu_\epsilon|^2+\mu^2|u_\epsilon|^2\right)dS\le0.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. The finite linear combinations of indicator functions of
half-open boxes with rational endpoints and rational coefficients form a
countable dense subset of $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Here
$\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ is the Schwartz space of smooth complex functions
whose coordinate-weighted derivatives are all bounded, as defined in
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]].
Fix an oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski space and an inertial coordinate
chart as in [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use coordinates
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ and metric $\eta=\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, matching the
$(-+++)$ convention of the SR suppliers. Some QFT sources use its negative
$(+---)$; the Lorentz group is unchanged, and the phase is fixed explicitly
below.
Coordinates $x$ have length units, momenta have inverse-length units, and the
Fourier phase below is dimensionless. A parameter $\mu\ge0$ has inverse-length
units and is only a mathematical shell parameter; it is not identified with a
physical rest mass. For $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, set
$$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2},\qquad p_\mu(\mathbf k)=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k).$$
The future mass shell is
$$H_\mu^+=\{(p^0,\mathbf p): (p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=\mu^2,\ p^0>0\}.$$
When $\mu=0$, its apex is omitted; thus $\mathbf k\ne0$ in the massless
parameterization. The scalar shell pairing is
$$p\circ x:=p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$
Define the measure and one-particle Hilbert space by
$$d\nu_\mu(p_\mu(\mathbf k))= \frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)},\qquad H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C),$$
where the omitted massless apex has measure zero. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb
R^4)$ define its pointwise shell Fourier restriction by
$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{ip\circ x}\,d^4x.$$
The Fourier convention is exactly the displayed integral, with no prefactor.
If $\widehat f(\xi^0,\boldsymbol\xi)=
\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i(x^0\xi^0+\mathbf x\cdot\boldsymbol\xi)}\,d^4x$ denotes
the standard transform in
[[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]],
then
$$\mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p):=\int f(x)e^{i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)}\,d^4x =\widehat f\!\left(-\frac{p^0}{2\pi},\frac{\mathbf p}{2\pi}\right).$$
Its inverse is
$$f(x)=(2\pi)^{-4}\int_{\mathbb R^4} \mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p)e^{-i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)} \,dp^0\,d^3\mathbf p.$$
Thus this convention is a time reflection and rescaling of the cited
Schwartz automorphism and has the stated reciprocal normalization.
The proper orthochronous Lorentz group consists of linear maps preserving
$\eta$, orientation and the chosen future cone. A Poincare map is
$x\mapsto a+\Lambda x$ with $a\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\Lambda$ in that group.

This is a mathematical free scalar one-particle construction. It adopts the
chosen coordinates, measure and Fourier convention; it asserts no experimental
observation, physical mass identification or measurement outcome.
Assume countable choice. The Fourier transform is a topological automorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\mathcal F^2=R$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F$, where $Rf(x)=f(-x)$.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

In the chart $\mathbf k\mapsto p_\mu(\mathbf k)$, write
$w_\mu(\mathbf k)=[2(2\pi)^3\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)]^{-1}$. Multiplication by
$\sqrt{w_\mu}$ is an isometry from $H_\mu$ onto
$L^2(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\},d^3\mathbf k)$ (for $\mu=0$) or
$L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k)$ (for $\mu>0$), with inverse division by
$\sqrt{w_\mu}$; the omitted point is Lebesgue-null. The full $L^2(\mathbb
R^3)$ is separable by [F1]. In the massless case extend any function on the
punctured space by zero at the null point, approximate it by the countable
dense family from [F1], and restrict those approximants back to the punctured
space; restriction does not increase the norm. Thus both chart spaces, and
therefore $H_\mu$, are separable.

Let $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$ for $\mu>0$ and
$\Omega=\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ for $\mu=0$. For
$\Omega_n=\{1/n<|\mathbf k|<n\}$, these sets increase to $\Omega\setminus\{0\}$; its complement in $\Omega$ is null for the shell measure.
For $h\in L^2(\Omega,w_\mu d^3\mathbf k)$, monotone convergence [F5]
shows $\|h\mathbf1_{\Omega\setminus\Omega_n}\|_{L^2(w_\mu)}\to0$.
On each $\Omega_n$, $w_\mu$ is smooth and bounded above and below by
positive constants. Approximate $h|_{\Omega_n}$ in ordinary $L^2(\Omega_n)$
by a function in $C_c^\infty(\Omega_n)$ using [F2]; equivalence of the
weighted and ordinary norms on $\Omega_n$ gives weighted approximation.
Thus $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ is dense in the shell space.

Fix $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$. Choose $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$
with $\rho(0)=1$, using [F4], and put
$$G(q^0,\mathbf q)= \psi(\mathbf q)\rho(q^0-\omega_\mu(\mathbf q)).$$
Because $\psi$ has compact support away from the massless apex, $\omega_\mu$
is smooth on a neighborhood of its support, so this is a smooth compactly
supported function on $\mathbb R^4$. By the Fourier automorphism [F3] there
is $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ with
$\mathcal F_+f(q^0,\mathbf q)=G(q^0,\mathbf q)$ in the convention of
[[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. On the shell,
$K_\mu f(p_\mu(\mathbf k))=G(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k)
=\psi(\mathbf k)$. Hence the test restriction range contains
$C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, which is dense by 2.1.

spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to

2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

For example, $\delta=1$, $r_1=r_2=1$ and $D=5$ give a spatial gap of $3>2$,
so these strict inequalities are attainable.

$r=|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|>0$ and $\tau=t-s$
$$W_\epsilon(\tau,r)= \frac{1}{4\pi^2r}\int_0^\infty e^{-(\epsilon+i\tau)q}\sin(qr)\,dq =\frac{1}{4\pi^2\bigl(r^2+(\epsilon+i\tau)^2\bigr)}.$$

sine and using $\operatorname{Re}(\epsilon+i\tau)>0$. On the compact

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Here
$\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ is the Schwartz space of smooth complex functions
whose coordinate-weighted derivatives are all bounded, as defined in
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]].

The Fourier convention is exactly the displayed integral, with no prefactor.
If $\widehat f(\xi^0,\boldsymbol\xi)=
\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i(x^0\xi^0+\mathbf x\cdot\boldsymbol\xi)}\,d^4x$ denotes
the standard transform in
[[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]],
then
$$\mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p):=\int f(x)e^{i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)}\,d^4x =\widehat f\!\left(-\frac{p^0}{2\pi},\frac{\mathbf p}{2\pi}\right).$$
Its inverse is
$$f(x)=(2\pi)^{-4}\int_{\mathbb R^4} \mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p)e^{-i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)} \,dp^0\,d^3\mathbf p.$$
Thus this convention is a time reflection and rescaling of the cited
Schwartz automorphism and has the stated reciprocal normalization.
The proper orthochronous Lorentz group consists of linear maps preserving
$\eta$, orientation and the chosen future cone. A Poincare map is
$x\mapsto a+\Lambda x$ with $a\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\Lambda$ in that group.

This is a mathematical free scalar one-particle construction. It adopts the
chosen coordinates, measure and Fourier convention; it asserts no experimental
observation, physical mass identification or measurement outcome.

An **oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space** is a quadruple
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with the following data. In this notation $V$ includes its
specified orientation; forgetting that orientation gives only the underlying
real vector space, not the full datum $V$ of the model.

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

The following terminology is attached to such a quadruple.

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.
- Events $p,q$ are **timelike**, **null**, **spacelike** or **causally
  related** when the displacement $q-p$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal
  in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; they are
  **future-related** when $q-p$ is future causal and **past-related** when
  $q-p$ is past causal in the sense of
  [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**No point of $A$ is distinguished.** For every $v\in V$ the translation
$\tau_v:A\to A$, $\tau_v(p):=p+v$, is a bijection, since it is inverse to
$\tau_{-v}$: $\tau_{-v}(\tau_v(p))=(p+v)+(-v)=p+(v-v)=p$ and symmetrically, by
the affine action axioms ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). Displacements
are translation invariant, $\tau_v(q)-\tau_v(p)=q-p$, so every $\tau_v$ preserves
the interval, the causal classification of every ordered pair, and the sets
$C^+$, $C^-$ (which are subsets of $V$, independent of the point of $A$); it
changes only the labelling of points. The mathematical structure of the model is
exactly the quadruple $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; no derived physical quantity (proper
time, four-velocity, momentum, energy, charge or any field) is part of this
definition, and all later structure of the framework (frames, charts, tensor
fields, worldlines) is built on this model.

**Well-definedness.** The affine-space definition supplies the action and the
unique displacements; the Lorentz-form definition supplies $\eta$ and its
inertia; the determinant-line definition supplies orientations; and the two
components of $T$ between which the time-orientation definition chooses exist by
the components lemma recorded in the well-definedness clause of
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], which is also what makes the
names future and past causal in item 4 well defined.

Let $V$ be a $4$-dimensional real vector space ([[def-vector-space]],
[[def-dimension]]). A **Lorentz form** on $V$ is a symmetric bilinear form
$\eta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]])
such that

1. $\eta$ is nondegenerate: both radicals
   $\operatorname{rad}_L(\eta)=\{u:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }v\}$ and
   $\operatorname{rad}_R(\eta)=\{v:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }u\}$ are
   $\{0\}$ ([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]);
   and
2. $\eta$ has **inertia** $(3,1,0)$: in some (equivalently, in every) basis of
   $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal, exactly three diagonal
   entries are positive, exactly one is negative, and none is zero
   ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]).

The inertia of a symmetric bilinear form is the triple $(p,q,r)$ of numbers of
positive, negative and zero diagonal entries of any diagonalizing basis, and it
is independent of the diagonalizing basis by Sylvester's law of inertia
([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]); hence clause 2
is a property of $\eta$ itself and not of a chosen basis. The **associated
quadratic form** of $\eta$ is

$$q(v):=\eta(v,v),\qquad v\in V .$$

A **Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$** is a pair $(V,\eta)$
consisting of a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$ and a Lorentz form $\eta$
on $V$; the name records that the diagonal normal form of $\eta$ has one
negative entry followed by three positive entries. No positive-definite
structure on $V$ is assumed or implied by this definition, and $q$ takes both
negative and positive values on nonzero vectors: a basis in which
$\eta$ is diagonal with diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$ exists by clause 2, and on
its first vector $q$ is $-1$, while on each of the other three it is $+1$.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

derivations.claim:
On $\mathbf k\ne0$ if $\mu=0$, and on all $\mathbf k$ if $\mu>0$,
$F_\mu$ is a smooth chart of the shell. On every compact subset of this chart
the density $[(2\pi)^3 2\omega_\mu]^{-1}$ is bounded; for $\mu=0$ near the
omitted apex it is proportional to $|\mathbf k|^{-1}$, whose integral over a
radius-$r$ ball is proportional to $\int_0^r s\,ds<\infty$. Compact annuli,
and for $\mu>0$ compact balls, give a countable cover by finite-measure sets;
hence $d\nu_\mu$ is locally finite and sigma-finite.

Fix $\Lambda$ and write $F=F_\mu$, $F(\mathbf k')=\Lambda F(\mathbf k)$.
Because $\Lambda$ preserves the future shell, this defines a smooth
diffeomorphism $\mathbf k\mapsto\mathbf k'$ on the chart; let
$J=D\mathbf k'/D\mathbf k$. Put $q_0=(1,0,0,0)$. The columns of
$[q_0,DF(\mathbf k)]$ have determinant $1$. Differentiating
$\Lambda F(\mathbf k)=F(\mathbf k')$ gives
$\Lambda DF(\mathbf k)=DF(\mathbf k')J$, and therefore
$$1=\det[\Lambda q_0,DF(\mathbf k')]\det J.$$
For any $u\in\mathbb R^4$, direct expansion of the determinant gives
$\det[u,DF(\mathbf k')]=-\eta(u,F(\mathbf k'))/\omega_\mu(\mathbf k')$.
Take $u=\Lambda q_0$. Metric preservation and
$F(\mathbf k')=\Lambda F(\mathbf k)$ imply
$-\eta(\Lambda q_0,F(\mathbf k'))=-\eta(q_0,F(\mathbf k))
=\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)$. Thus $\det J=\omega_\mu(\mathbf k')/
\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)>0$.

The change-of-variables theorem [F3] and the Jacobian from 2.1 give
$$\frac{d^3\mathbf k'}{\omega_\mu(\mathbf k')} =\frac{\det J\,d^3\mathbf k}{\omega_\mu(\mathbf k')} =\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)}.$$
Multiplication by the constant $[2(2\pi)^3]^{-1}$ proves invariance for
nonnegative Borel functions. The massless apex is a
single omitted point and was never in the chart; the locally finite density
has no extra point mass there.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], let $\mu\ge0$, let
$H_\mu$ and $K_\mu$ be as in [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and form
$\mathcal F_s(H_\mu)$ with vacuum $\Omega$ and finite-particle domain
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ define on
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$
$$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu\overline f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f).$$
This is a complex-linear map of test functions into operators
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\to\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For real $f$ it is symmetric
and equals $\sqrt2\,\Phi_{\rm Segal}(K_\mu f)|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}$, where the Segal field of
[[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]] is
$\Phi_{\rm Segal}(h)=\overline{(a^\dagger(h)+a(h))/\sqrt2}$.
Thus its Weyl unitary is
$W_\mu(f):=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2 K_\mu f)$ and, for real $f,g$,
$$W_\mu(f)W_\mu(g)= e^{-i\,\operatorname{Im}\langle K_\mu f,K_\mu g\rangle_2}W_\mu(f+g).$$
For every real $f$ the vacuum Weyl expectation is
$$\langle\Omega,W_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2 =e^{-\|K_\mu f\|_2^2/2}.$$
Here the inner product is second-variable-linear as fixed in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The vacuum has zero one-point function and
two-point function
$$\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(f)\Phi_\mu(g)\Omega\rangle_2 =\langle K_\mu\overline f,K_\mu g\rangle_2,$$
which obeys $\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(\overline f)\Phi_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2=\|K_\mu f\|_2^2\ge0$ for every complex test $f$ (ordinary diagonal positivity holds for real tests); higher vacuum moments of ordered real smeared
fields obey the CCR pairing recursion and hence the free-field Wick pairing
rule. The field is a weak operator-valued tempered distribution on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$: every matrix coefficient $f\mapsto\langle\Psi,\Phi_\mu(f)\Theta\rangle_2$ for $\Psi,\Theta\in\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on Schwartz space. Its adjoint satisfies $\Phi_\mu(f)^*|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}=\Phi_\mu(\overline f)$, and its normalized vacuum defines a positive state on the finite polynomial $*$-algebra generated by these fields.

The relative-coordinate two-point tempered distribution is
$$W_\mu(z)=\int_{H_\mu^+}e^{-ip\circ z}\,d\nu_\mu(p),$$
understood by pairing with Schwartz tests. Its translation-invariant bidistribution is the shell integral of $e^{-ip\circ x}e^{ip\circ y}$; on product tests it is the displayed vacuum covariance.

For $g=(a,\Lambda)$, let $f_g$ and $U_\mu(g)$ be the affine test pullback
and one-particle action of [[lem-qft-scalar-poincare-action]]. Their Fock
lifts implement the same covariance for $\Phi_\mu$ on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$
and for the bounded Weyl operators.

For translations, the joint spectral measure on Fock space is the
second-quantized multiplier measure with one-particle vector
$(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),-\mathbf k)$. Its support is contained in the closed
future cone $\{(E,\mathbf P):E\ge|\mathbf P|\}$; the vacuum is an eigenvector
at $(0,\mathbf0)$. These are conditional mathematical model deductions.
No point field, empirical observation or measurement claim is made.

$$\Delta_\mu(t,\mathbf x)= \int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3} \frac{\sin(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)t)}{\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)} e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x},$$
with the massless integrand defined off $\mathbf k=0$; its $1/|\mathbf k|$
behavior is locally integrable in three dimensions. Then
$$\operatorname{supp}\Delta_\mu \subseteq\{(t,\mathbf x):t^2-|\mathbf x|^2\ge0\},$$
the closed causal cone for the $(-+++)$ metric. For real compactly supported
smooth $f,g$, put
$$\Delta_\mu(f,g)= \int_{\mathbb R^4}\!\int_{\mathbb R^4} f(x)g(y)\Delta_\mu(x-y)\,d^4x\,d^4y.$$
On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ the smeared fields of
[[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]] satisfy
$$[\Phi_\mu(f),\Phi_\mu(g)]=-i\Delta_\mu(f,g)I.$$
Consequently spacelike-separated supports give commuting fields.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] and let $H$ be a separable
complex Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear convention of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ define the bosonic
creation and annihilation maps $a^\dagger(h)$ and $a(h)$ and the fermionic maps
$c^\dagger(h)$ and $c(h)$ as in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. Write $a_n(h)$ and $a_n^\dagger(h)$ for
their restrictions to the $n$th bosonic sector. For bosons set

$$D(a(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge1}\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\},\qquad D(a^\dagger(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge0}\|a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}.$$

Then $\mathcal F_s(H)$ and $\mathcal F_a(H)$ are Hilbert spaces,
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is dense, and it is a graph core for both maximal
bosonic sector maps. The bosonic operators on their displayed domains are
closed and mutually adjoint, and on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ satisfy

$$[a(h),a^\dagger(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad [a(h),a(k)]=[a^\dagger(h),a^\dagger(k)]=0.$$

The fermionic $c(h)$ and $c^\dagger(h)$ extend to bounded operators on the

$$\{c(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad \{c(h),c(k)\}=\{c^\dagger(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=0.$$

If $O_1\subseteq O_2$, each real test function supported in $O_1$ is
also a real test function supported in $O_2$. Thus the generators and their
adjoints for $\mathfrak A_\mu(O_1)$ belong to the generating set for
$\mathfrak A_\mu(O_2)$; finite sums and products do too, and norm closure
preserves inclusion. This proves isotony.

Let $f,g$ be real tests supported in the two spacelike-separated
regions. By [F2] their field commutator is zero. Fact [F3], obtained by
expanding the fields with the CCR, then gives
$2i\,\operatorname{Im}\langle K_\mu f,K_\mu g\rangle_2I=0$; hence the
imaginary part vanishes. Substituting it in [F1] gives
$W_\mu(f)W_\mu(g)=W_\mu(f+g)=W_\mu(g)W_\mu(f)$. Taking adjoints shows each
generator from the first region commutes with each generator and adjoint
from the second. Commutation is preserved under finite linear combinations
and products; if bounded sequences $A_n\to A$ and $B_n\to B$ in operator
norm satisfy $A_nB_n=B_nA_n$, then continuity of multiplication gives
$AB=BA$. Taking the two norm closures proves the assertion for the full
local algebras.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Here
$\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ is the Schwartz space of smooth complex functions
whose coordinate-weighted derivatives are all bounded, as defined in
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]].
Fix an oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski space and an inertial coordinate
chart as in [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use coordinates
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ and metric $\eta=\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, matching the
$(-+++)$ convention of the SR suppliers. Some QFT sources use its negative
$(+---)$; the Lorentz group is unchanged, and the phase is fixed explicitly
below.
Coordinates $x$ have length units, momenta have inverse-length units, and the
Fourier phase below is dimensionless. A parameter $\mu\ge0$ has inverse-length
units and is only a mathematical shell parameter; it is not identified with a
physical rest mass. For $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, set
$$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2},\qquad p_\mu(\mathbf k)=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k).$$
The future mass shell is
$$H_\mu^+=\{(p^0,\mathbf p): (p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=\mu^2,\ p^0>0\}.$$
When $\mu=0$, its apex is omitted; thus $\mathbf k\ne0$ in the massless
parameterization. The scalar shell pairing is
$$p\circ x:=p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$
Define the measure and one-particle Hilbert space by
$$d\nu_\mu(p_\mu(\mathbf k))= \frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)},\qquad H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C),$$
where the omitted massless apex has measure zero. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb
R^4)$ define its pointwise shell Fourier restriction by
$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{ip\circ x}\,d^4x.$$
The Fourier convention is exactly the displayed integral, with no prefactor.
If $\widehat f(\xi^0,\boldsymbol\xi)=
\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i(x^0\xi^0+\mathbf x\cdot\boldsymbol\xi)}\,d^4x$ denotes
the standard transform in
[[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]],
then
$$\mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p):=\int f(x)e^{i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)}\,d^4x =\widehat f\!\left(-\frac{p^0}{2\pi},\frac{\mathbf p}{2\pi}\right).$$

Schwartz automorphism and has the stated reciprocal normalization.

$\eta$, orientation and the chosen future cone. A Poincare map is
$x\mapsto a+\Lambda x$ with $a\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\Lambda$ in that group.

This is a mathematical free scalar one-particle construction. It adopts the
chosen coordinates, measure and Fourier convention; it asserts no experimental
observation, physical mass identification or measurement outcome.

$$q_2(f)=\sup_{p\in\mathbb R^4}(1+|p|)^2|\mathcal F_+f(p)|.$$

$|\mathcal F_+f(p_\mu(\mathbf k))|

$|p_\mu(\mathbf k)|\ge|\mathbf k|$. Hence
$$\|K_\mu f\|_{H_\mu}^2 \le\frac{q_2(f)^2}{2(2\pi)^3} \int_{\mathbb R^3} \frac{(1+|\mathbf k|)^{-4}}{\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)}\,d^3\mathbf k.$$

shell therefore gives the asserted Klein–Gordon identity.
