The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and use $\mathcal H_T$ from [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]]. On $\mathcal K=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^4)$ define
$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\epsilon(\mathbf k)^\dagger\eta\,\delta(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,\qquad \eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1).$$
For $\mathbf k\ne0$, let $n=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and set
$$\mathcal K_0=\{\epsilon\in\mathcal K:-\epsilon^0+n\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon=0\text{ a.e.}\},\qquad T\epsilon=\boldsymbol\epsilon-n\epsilon^0.$$
Then $\mathcal K_0$ is closed, $T:\mathcal K_0\to\mathcal H_T$ is bounded and onto, and
$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\langle T\epsilon,T\delta\rangle_2\quad(\epsilon,\delta\in\mathcal K_0).$$
Its radical (the vectors pairing to zero with all of $\mathcal K_0$) is
$$\mathcal N=\ker T=\{b(\mathbf k)(1,n(\mathbf k)):b\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)\}.$$
Consequently $\mathcal K_0/\mathcal N$ with the induced form is a positive Hilbert space isometric to $\mathcal H_T$. The form on the four-component auxiliary space is indefinite; only the subsidiary quotient is the positive physical one-particle space.

Fix an inertial frame of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] and identify its vector coordinates with $\mathbb R^4$ and $\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. For a unit spatial vector $\mathbf n_B$ and $\chi\in\mathbb R$, define the boost $B_{\mathbf n_B}(\chi)$ by $B e_0=\cosh\chi\,e_0+\sinh\chi\,\mathbf n_B$, $B\mathbf n_B=\sinh\chi\,e_0+\cosh\chi\,\mathbf n_B$, and $Bw=w$ for every $w$ Euclidean-orthogonal to $\operatorname{span}(e_0,\mathbf n_B)$. Every proper orthochronous linear Lorentz map $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$, as defined in [[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]], admits $\Lambda=B_{\mathbf n_B}(\chi)R_{\mathbf n_R}(\theta)$, where $R_{\mathbf n_R}(\theta)$ fixes the time axis and $\mathbf n_R$, and sends $\mathbf v_\perp$ to $\cos\theta\,\mathbf v_\perp+\sin\theta\,\mathbf n_R\times\mathbf v_\perp$ on the orthogonal plane, where $\mathbf v_\parallel=(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n_R)\mathbf n_R$ and $\mathbf v_\perp=\mathbf v-\mathbf v_\parallel$; the cross product is [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. If $\Lambda e_0=e_0$, choose $\chi=0$ and $R_{\mathbf n_R}(\theta)=\Lambda$.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space and let
$\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d):X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a
finite-valued measurable map, where $d\ge1$. Put
$H=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ with the second-variable-linear pairing of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and form the bosonic Fock space
$\mathcal F_s(H)$. For $n\ge1$, identify $H_s^{(n)}$ with the symmetric
subspace of $L^2(X^n,\overline{\mu^{\times n}};\mathbb C)$ by iterating
[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]. Set $X^0=\{\star\}$,
$s_0(\star)=0$, and for $n\ge1$ set
$$s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n\boldsymbol\omega(x_r)\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For $1\le j\le d$, define $H_j$ by multiplication by the $j$th coordinate
$s_{n,j}$ on sector $n$, with exact domain
$$D(H_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n): \sum_{n\ge1}\int_{X^n}|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2\,d\overline{\mu^{\times n}}<\infty\right\}.$$
Each $H_j$ is self-adjoint, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_j)$ is a
graph core. The joint projection-valued measure
[[def-projection-valued-measure]] on $\mathbb R^d$ is
$$(E(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}\Psi_n\quad(n\ge1),\qquad (E(B)\Psi)_0=\mathbf1_B(0)\Psi_0.$$
For $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, let $H_\theta$ be multiplication on sector $n$
by $\theta\cdot s_n$, with its maximal square-integrability domain. Then
$$U_\theta(t)\Psi:=\bigl(e^{it\theta\cdot s_n}\Psi_n\bigr)_{n\ge0}$$
is a strongly continuous unitary group on all of Fock space, and its norm
derivative at zero exists exactly for $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, where it is
$iH_\theta\Psi$. The zero-particle sector is the vacuum eigenvector at joint
value $0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) equipped with a time orientation $C^+$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), and let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

**(e) Convention.** In this framework, unless stated otherwise, the term
**Lorentz transformation** means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map.
Improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly.

The composition of two affine Lorentz maps is affine Lorentz with linear part
the composition of the linear parts, and the identity and the inverse of an
affine Lorentz map are again such maps; these facts are part of
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

derivations.claim: By [F5], $\Lambda$ preserves $\eta$ and sends a future null vector $p$ to a future null vector $\Lambda p$. It maps $p^\perp$ onto $(\Lambda p)^\perp$ and $\mathbb Cp$ onto $\mathbb C\Lambda p$, so it induces a well-defined map on the quotient fiber. The induced form is preserved because $\eta(\Lambda v,\Lambda w)=\eta(v,w)$; hence the fiber map is an isometry. Applying two maps successively gives the representation composition law.

For the boost $B_n(\chi)$ in [F2], put $\beta=\tanh\chi$ and $\gamma=\cosh\chi$, so $|\beta|<1$ and $\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$. In Euclidean unit direction $n$ [F5], its spatial cone coordinates satisfy
$$\mathbf k'=\mathbf k+(\gamma-1)(n\cdot\mathbf k)n-\gamma\beta\omega n,\qquad \omega'=\gamma(\omega-\beta n\cdot\mathbf k).$$
Taking $n$ as the third coordinate axis, the first two spatial coordinates are unchanged and
$$\frac{\partial k'_3}{\partial k_3} =\gamma\left(1-\beta\frac{k_3}{\omega}\right)=\frac{\omega'}{\omega}.$$
Thus $\det(\partial\mathbf k'/\partial\mathbf k)=\omega'/\omega$. A rotation has determinant one and preserves $\omega$. By [F2], every proper orthochronous $\Lambda$ is a product of these, so $d^3\mathbf k'/(2\omega')=d^3\mathbf k/(2\omega)$. Combining this change of variables with the fiber isometry in step 1.1 proves unitarity on the quotient-section space and verifies the stated identification with $\mathcal H_T$.

For $v\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$, consider the bundle section $s_v(p)=\sqrt{2\omega}\,P_T(\mathbf k)v(\mathbf k)$; under the stated unitary identification it corresponds exactly to $u=P_Tv\in\mathcal H_T$. Its support stays in a fixed compact set for Lorentz transformations near the identity. Away from an arbitrarily small ball about $\mathbf k=0$, the momentum maps and fiber maps vary uniformly continuously; inside that ball $s_v$ is bounded and the $d\nu$ measure tends to zero with the radius. Such sections are dense: approximate any $u\in\mathcal H_T$ by $v\in C_c^\infty$ using [F4], and apply the bounded projection $P_T$; the transformed maps are unitary by step 2.1, so density extends continuity to every section. The symmetric transverse sector is reducing, so restriction preserves the exact multiplier domain. The vacuum supplies the origin. Thus the joint spectrum is exactly $\overline V_+$, and [F3] gives the exact energy domain.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$$\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3),\qquad \langle u,v\rangle_2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline{u(\mathbf k)}\cdot v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,$$
with the second-variable-linear convention of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]; the dot product and norm on each $\mathbb R^3$ fiber are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and Hilbert completeness follows from [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For $\mathbf k\ne0$, write $n(\mathbf k)=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and
$$P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-n(\mathbf k)n(\mathbf k)^T.$$
Assign any value at $\mathbf k=0$, which is a Lebesgue-null set. Let $M_{P_T}$ be multiplication by this measurable matrix field and define the positive transverse photon space
$$\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T} =\{u\in\mathcal H:\mathbf k\cdot u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for almost every }\mathbf k\ne0\}.$$
The inner product on $\mathcal H_T$ is the restriction of that on $\mathcal H$. Each nonzero momentum fiber is the two-dimensional plane perpendicular to $\mathbf k$; no global continuous polarization frame is part of the definition.

Assume Countable Choice and use $\mathcal H_T$ from [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]]. On $\mathcal K=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^4)$ define
$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\epsilon(\mathbf k)^\dagger\eta\,\delta(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,\qquad \eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1).$$
For $\mathbf k\ne0$, let $n=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and set
$$\mathcal K_0=\{\epsilon\in\mathcal K:-\epsilon^0+n\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon=0\text{ a.e.}\},\qquad T\epsilon=\boldsymbol\epsilon-n\epsilon^0.$$
Then $\mathcal K_0$ is closed, $T:\mathcal K_0\to\mathcal H_T$ is bounded and onto, and
$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\langle T\epsilon,T\delta\rangle_2\quad(\epsilon,\delta\in\mathcal K_0).$$
Its radical (the vectors pairing to zero with all of $\mathcal K_0$) is
$$\mathcal N=\ker T=\{b(\mathbf k)(1,n(\mathbf k)):b\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)\}.$$
Consequently $\mathcal K_0/\mathcal N$ with the induced form is a positive Hilbert space isometric to $\mathcal H_T$. The form on the four-component auxiliary space is indefinite; only the subsidiary quotient is the positive physical one-particle space.

Assume Countable Choice. For $n\in S^2\subset\mathbb R^3$, let $E_n=n^\perp=\operatorname{Ran}(I-nn^T)$ be the real transverse plane. There do not exist continuous maps $e_1,e_2:S^2\to\mathbb R^3$ such that, for every $n$, $(e_1(n),e_2(n))$ is an orthonormal basis of $E_n$. A continuous real orthonormal polarization frame would in particular give a continuous nowhere-zero tangent vector field on $S^2$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

For $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$, $\|u\times v\|_2^2=\det G(u,v)$, and this value is positive exactly when $u$ and $v$ are linearly independent.

Equivalently,
$$\|u\times v\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2\|v\|_2^2-\langle u,v\rangle^2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$ and its tensor extension is the bounded map of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation
by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction
$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and
$c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the
creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the
finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. No physical statistics assignment or spin–statistics
theorem is part of these mathematical definitions.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], the mathematical scalar shell conventions of [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and the second-variable-linear Hilbert pairing of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. In the fixed inertial coordinates $x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] on the affine Minkowski model [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; these coordinates have length units under [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. The parameter $\mu\ge0$ and momentum coordinate $\mathbf k$ have inverse-length units, and $\omega(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ has the same units. The parameter is not identified here with a physical rest mass. Matrix $h_D$ has inverse-length units; the dimensionless spin matrices have no physical unit assignment in this mathematical item.

Use the Pauli matrices $\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, and $\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. On $\mathbb C^4=\mathbb C^2\oplus\mathbb C^2$, define
$$\beta=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&0\\0&-I_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \alpha_j=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_j\\\sigma_j&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \gamma^0=\beta,\qquad \gamma^j=\beta\alpha_j.$$
For a spinor column $z\in\mathbb C^4$, its Dirac adjoint is $\bar z=z^\dagger\beta$. The Clifford contraction is $\Gamma(p):=\gamma^0p^0-\sum_{j=1}^3\gamma^jp_j$; this contraction uses the effective matrix $-\eta$ in the relation $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most

Assume Countable Choice and use $\mathcal H_T$ from [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]]. On $\mathcal K=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^4)$ define
$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\epsilon(\mathbf k)^\dagger\eta\,\delta(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,\qquad \eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1).$$
For $\mathbf k\ne0$, let $n=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and set
$$\mathcal K_0=\{\epsilon\in\mathcal K:-\epsilon^0+n\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon=0\text{ a.e.}\},\qquad T\epsilon=\boldsymbol\epsilon-n\epsilon^0.$$
Then $\mathcal K_0$ is closed, $T:\mathcal K_0\to\mathcal H_T$ is bounded and onto, and
$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\langle T\epsilon,T\delta\rangle_2\quad(\epsilon,\delta\in\mathcal K_0).$$
Its radical (the vectors pairing to zero with all of $\mathcal K_0$) is
$$\mathcal N=\ker T=\{b(\mathbf k)(1,n(\mathbf k)):b\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)\}.$$
Consequently $\mathcal K_0/\mathcal N$ with the induced form is a positive Hilbert space isometric to $\mathcal H_T$. The form on the four-component auxiliary space is indefinite; only the subsidiary quotient is the positive physical one-particle space.

$$F_{ab}=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a,\qquad E_i=-\partial_0A_i,\qquad B_i=\epsilon_{irs}\partial_rA_s,$$
where $\epsilon_{irs}$ is the totally antisymmetric symbol with $\epsilon_{123}=1$. In the commutator formulas below, $\Delta=\sum_{r=1}^3\partial_r^2$ is the spatial Laplacian acting on $x-y$.
For a real compactly supported smooth antisymmetric test tensor $h^{ab}=-h^{ba}$, define
$$F(h)=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^4}F_{ab}(x)h^{ab}(x)\,d^4x =-A_b(\partial_a h^{ab}).$$
The effective test is conserved, $\partial_b\partial_a h^{ab}=0$, and $F(h)$ is unchanged by $A_b\mapsto A_b+\partial_b\lambda$ for smooth $\lambda$. Its one-particle coefficient $g_h$ is the vector $g_j$ of [[lem-qft-photon-smeared-potential]] for $j_i=-\partial_a h^{ai}$, so $F(h)=a(g_h)+a^\dagger(g_h)$ on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$.

Let $C_0=-i\Delta_0$, where $\Delta_0$ is the massless scalar causal commutator of [[lem-qft-scalar-causal-commutator]]. As distributions in $x-y$,
$$[E_i(x),E_j(y)]=[B_i(x),B_j(y)] =(-\delta_{ij}\Delta+\partial_i\partial_j)C_0(x-y),$$
$$[E_i(x),B_j(y)]=\epsilon_{jri}\partial_0\partial_rC_0(x-y).$$
Every right-hand side has support in the closed causal cone. Hence compactly supported tests with spacelike-separated supports give commuting field-strength operators on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. The quotient representation of [[lem-qft-photon-covariance-spectrum]] makes these smeared field strengths Lorentz covariant: their on-shell coefficient depends on a polarization class only through $p_a\epsilon_b-p_b\epsilon_a$. These conclusions concern gauge-invariant free observables and do not assert locality of the Coulomb potential.

complex Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear convention of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ define the bosonic
creation and annihilation maps $a^\dagger(h)$ and $a(h)$ and the fermionic maps

[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. Write $a_n(h)$ and $a_n^\dagger(h)$ for

$$D(a(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge1}\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\},\qquad D(a^\dagger(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge0}\|a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}.$$

Then $\mathcal F_s(H)$ and $\mathcal F_a(H)$ are Hilbert spaces,
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is dense, and it is a graph core for both maximal
bosonic sector maps. The bosonic operators on their displayed domains are
closed and mutually adjoint, and on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ satisfy

$$[a(h),a^\dagger(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad [a(h),a(k)]=[a^\dagger(h),a^\dagger(k)]=0.$$

The fermionic $c(h)$ and $c^\dagger(h)$ extend to bounded operators on the

$$\{c(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad \{c(h),c(k)\}=\{c^\dagger(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=0.$$

This is a mathematical construction of the two Fock representations; it does
not assign particle statistics to a physical species.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. The finite linear combinations of indicator functions of
half-open boxes with rational endpoints and rational coefficients form a
countable dense subset of $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $H$ be a separable
complex Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear convention of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and let $\mathcal F_s(H)$ and
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ be its bosonic Fock space and finite-particle domain.

$$\phi_0(h):=2^{-1/2}\bigl(a^\dagger(h)+a(h)\bigr).$$
For $h\ne0$, this symmetric operator is essentially self-adjoint; write
$\Phi(h)=\overline{\phi_0(h)}$. If $r=\|h\|$, $e=h/r$, $K=e^\perp$,

$$D(\Phi(h))=\left\{(f_j):\sum_{j\in J}\int_{\mathbb R}(1+r^2x^2)|f_j(x)|^2\,dx<\infty\right\},\qquad (\Phi(h)f)_j(x)=rx f_j(x).$$

$$W(h)\epsilon(z)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|h\|^2}{4} +\frac{i}{\sqrt2}\langle h,z\rangle_2\right) \epsilon\!\left(z+\frac{i h}{\sqrt2}\right).$$

generator). Thus the displayed bounded Weyl operators have precisely the
closed Segal fields as their generators; no point-field or measurement claim
is included.

citations.quote:
Use the transverse one-particle space $\mathcal H_T$ and multiplier $\omega(\mathbf k)$ of [[def-qft-qed-photon-energy-multiplier]], and form its symmetric Fock space $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$. Let $H_{\rm ph}:=\hbar c\,d\Gamma(\omega)$, with $\hbar,c>0$ and $d\Gamma(\omega)$ acting on the $n$-particle sector as multiplication by $\sum_{j=1}^n|\mathbf k_j|$, as in [[lem-qft-second-quantized-spectrum]]. For a coherent vector use
$$ \epsilon(f):=\bigoplus_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{f^{\otimes n}}{\sqrt{n!}},\qquad C(f):=e^{-\|f\|^2/2}\epsilon(f), $$
using the tensor and direct-sum conventions of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]].

Let $\kappa>0$. Let $b:S^2\to\mathbb C^3$ be measurable with $b\in L^2(S^2,d\Omega;\mathbb C^3)$, $\mathbf n\cdot b(\mathbf n)=0$ for a.e. $\mathbf n$, and
$$ C_b:=\int_{S^2}|b(\mathbf n)|^2\,d\Omega>0. $$
Take $\mathbf k,\kappa,\epsilon$ in inverse metres and $b$ dimensionless; then $f_\epsilon$ has momentum-wavefunction units $\mathrm m^{3/2}$, $C_b$ is dimensionless, and $\hbar c(\kappa-\epsilon)$ has energy units.
For $0<\epsilon<\kappa$, define $f_\epsilon(0)=0$ and
$$ f_\epsilon(\mathbf k):=\mathbf1_{\{\epsilon<|\mathbf k|<\kappa\}}|\mathbf k|^{-3/2}b\!\left(\frac{\mathbf k}{|\mathbf k|}\right). $$
Then
$$ \|f_\epsilon\|^2=C_b\log\frac{\kappa}{\epsilon},\qquad \langle C(f_\epsilon),H_{\rm ph}C(f_\epsilon)\rangle =\hbar c\,C_b(\kappa-\epsilon). $$
Each $C(f_\epsilon)$ is a unit vector in $D(H_{\rm ph})$. As $\epsilon\downarrow0$, $C(f_\epsilon)\rightharpoonup0$ weakly, but the family has no strong Fock-space limit. The statement is an exact free transverse-mode construction; it asserts no interacting charged sector, continuum QED limit, or empirical observation.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and $n\ge2$. The chart surface measure on $S^{n-1}$ equals the polar measure $\sigma$. Orthogonal transformations preserve it. The map $\omega\mapsto a+R\omega$, $R>0$, multiplies surface measure by $R^{n-1}$, and $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For $b(n)=P_T(n)e$, $|b(n)|^2=1-(n\cdot e)^2$. By [F2], rotate $e$ to the third coordinate axis. The regular sphere chart $X(y,z)=(\sqrt{1-y^2-z^2},y,z)$ on $|y|,|z|<1/4$ lies in the belt $|n\cdot e|<1/2$ and has area density $(1-y^2-z^2)^{-1/2}\ge1$ by [F3]. Its parameter rectangle has area $1/4$, so this belt has positive surface measure. On the belt $|b(n)|^2\ge3/4$, hence $C_b>0$; also $b$ is continuous, square-integrable on the finite sphere measure, and transverse.

Apply [F1] to this $b$. It gives unit vectors with $0\le\langle C(f_\epsilon),H_{\rm ph}C(f_\epsilon)\rangle\le\hbar c\,C_b\kappa<\infty$, yet no strong Fock-space limit. This contradicts the asserted implication and is the required counterexample.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Use the transverse space $\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T}$ of [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]], with $P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-\mathbf n\mathbf n^T$ for $\mathbf k\ne0$ and any assigned value at the null point $\mathbf k=0$. In the QFT length convention, assign $\mathbf k$ units m$^{-1}$ and define the nonnegative measurable multiplier
$$ \omega(\mathbf k):=|\mathbf k|. $$
Its maximal multiplication operator on $\mathcal H_T$ is
$$ (M_\omega f)(\mathbf k):=\omega(\mathbf k)f(\mathbf k),\qquad D(M_\omega):=\{f\in\mathcal H_T:\omega f\in L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3)\}. $$
Because $\omega$ is a scalar multiplier, $\mathbf k\cdot f(\mathbf k)=0$ a.e. implies $\mathbf k\cdot(M_\omega f)(\mathbf k)=0$ a.e.; thus the displayed multiplication maps its stated domain into $\mathcal H_T$. The value $\omega(0)=0$ is immaterial to the $L^2$ operator. For $\hbar,c>0$, the corresponding one-particle energy convention is $E_1:=\hbar c M_\omega$, in joules.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space and let
$\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d):X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a
finite-valued measurable map, where $d\ge1$. Put
$H=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ with the second-variable-linear pairing of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and form the bosonic Fock space
$\mathcal F_s(H)$. For $n\ge1$, identify $H_s^{(n)}$ with the symmetric
subspace of $L^2(X^n,\overline{\mu^{\times n}};\mathbb C)$ by iterating
[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]. Set $X^0=\{\star\}$,
$s_0(\star)=0$, and for $n\ge1$ set
$$s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n\boldsymbol\omega(x_r)\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For $1\le j\le d$, define $H_j$ by multiplication by the $j$th coordinate
$s_{n,j}$ on sector $n$, with exact domain
$$D(H_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n): \sum_{n\ge1}\int_{X^n}|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2\,d\overline{\mu^{\times n}}<\infty\right\}.$$
Each $H_j$ is self-adjoint, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_j)$ is a
graph core. The joint projection-valued measure
[[def-projection-valued-measure]] on $\mathbb R^d$ is
$$(E(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}\Psi_n\quad(n\ge1),\qquad (E(B)\Psi)_0=\mathbf1_B(0)\Psi_0.$$
For $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, let $H_\theta$ be multiplication on sector $n$
by $\theta\cdot s_n$, with its maximal square-integrability domain. Then
$$U_\theta(t)\Psi:=\bigl(e^{it\theta\cdot s_n}\Psi_n\bigr)_{n\ge0}$$
is a strongly continuous unitary group on all of Fock space, and its norm
derivative at zero exists exactly for $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, where it is
$iH_\theta\Psi$. The zero-particle sector is the vacuum eigenvector at joint
value $0$.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$ and its tensor extension is the bounded map of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation
by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction
$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and
$c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the
creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the
finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. No physical statistics assignment or spin–statistics
theorem is part of these mathematical definitions.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and $n\ge2$. The chart surface measure on $S^{n-1}$ equals the polar measure $\sigma$. Orthogonal transformations preserve it. The map $\omega\mapsto a+R\omega$, $R>0$, multiplies surface measure by $R^{n-1}$, and $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].
For every $z\in\mathbb C$, the series $\sum z^n/n!$ converges absolutely.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

derivations.claim: For $\mathbf n\in S^2$, $P_T(\mathbf n)=I-\mathbf n\mathbf n^\top$ is an orthogonal projection and [A2] gives $\mathbf n\cdot b(\mathbf n)=0$; hence $\mathbf k\cdot f_\epsilon(\mathbf k)=0$ a.e. Since $\epsilon<|\mathbf k|<\kappa$ on the support, the radial norm integrals in [F4]–[F6] are finite on these strictly positive finite bounds, so both $f_\epsilon$ and $\omega f_\epsilon$ are square-integrable.

By [F4]–[F6], spherical coordinates give $d^3k=r^2dr\,d\Omega$, so $\|f_\epsilon\|^2=C_b\int_\epsilon^\kappa r^{-1}dr=C_b\log(\kappa/\epsilon)$, $\langle f_\epsilon,\omega f_\epsilon\rangle=C_b(\kappa-\epsilon)$, and $\|\omega f_\epsilon\|^2=C_b(\kappa^2-\epsilon^2)/2$.

For any $u,v\in\mathcal H_T$, [F2] gives $\langle u^{\otimes n},v^{\otimes n}\rangle=\langle u,v\rangle^n$ and $\|u^{\otimes n}\|^2=\|u\|^{2n}$. By [F7]–[F8], $\sum_{n\ge0}\|u\|^{2n}/n!=e^{\|u\|^2}<\infty$, so the displayed $\epsilon(u)$ belongs to symmetric Fock space. Its direct-sum pairing with $\epsilon(v)$ is the absolutely convergent series $\sum_{n\ge0}\langle u,v\rangle^n/n!=e^{\langle u,v\rangle}$, by [F7]. The addition and modulus laws [F8]–[F9] therefore give that $C(u)$ has norm one and $|\langle C(u),C(v)\rangle|=e^{-\|u-v\|^2/2}$. This direct tensor calculation requires no separability hypothesis on $\mathcal H_T$. On the full vector space $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$, multiplication by $\omega$ commutes with the multiplier $P_T$. Its tensor-power projections therefore commute with the sector multiplier $\sum_j|\mathbf k_j|$; the transverse symmetric Fock space is a reducing subspace for the second-quantized multiplier of [F3]. If $r=\|f_\epsilon\|^2$, $q=\langle f_\epsilon,\omega f_\epsilon\rangle$, and $s=\|\omega f_\epsilon\|^2$, the sector formulas give
$$ \|d\Gamma(\omega)C(f_\epsilon)\|^2 =e^{-r}\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{n s r^{n-1}+n(n-1)q^2r^{n-2}}{n!} =s+q^2<\infty. $$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Use the transverse space $\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T}$ of [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]], with $P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-\mathbf n\mathbf n^T$ for $\mathbf k\ne0$ and any assigned value at the null point $\mathbf k=0$. In the QFT length convention, assign $\mathbf k$ units m$^{-1}$ and define the nonnegative measurable multiplier
$$ \omega(\mathbf k):=|\mathbf k|. $$
Its maximal multiplication operator on $\mathcal H_T$ is
$$ (M_\omega f)(\mathbf k):=\omega(\mathbf k)f(\mathbf k),\qquad D(M_\omega):=\{f\in\mathcal H_T:\omega f\in L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3)\}. $$
Because $\omega$ is a scalar multiplier, $\mathbf k\cdot f(\mathbf k)=0$ a.e. implies $\mathbf k\cdot(M_\omega f)(\mathbf k)=0$ a.e.; thus the displayed multiplication maps its stated domain into $\mathcal H_T$. The value $\omega(0)=0$ is immaterial to the $L^2$ operator. For $\hbar,c>0$, the corresponding one-particle energy convention is $E_1:=\hbar c M_\omega$, in joules.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space and let
$\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d):X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a
finite-valued measurable map, where $d\ge1$. Put
$H=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ with the second-variable-linear pairing of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and form the bosonic Fock space
$\mathcal F_s(H)$. For $n\ge1$, identify $H_s^{(n)}$ with the symmetric
subspace of $L^2(X^n,\overline{\mu^{\times n}};\mathbb C)$ by iterating
[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]. Set $X^0=\{\star\}$,
$s_0(\star)=0$, and for $n\ge1$ set
$$s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n\boldsymbol\omega(x_r)\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For $1\le j\le d$, define $H_j$ by multiplication by the $j$th coordinate
$s_{n,j}$ on sector $n$, with exact domain
$$D(H_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n): \sum_{n\ge1}\int_{X^n}|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2\,d\overline{\mu^{\times n}}<\infty\right\}.$$
Each $H_j$ is self-adjoint, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_j)$ is a
graph core. The joint projection-valued measure
[[def-projection-valued-measure]] on $\mathbb R^d$ is
$$(E(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}\Psi_n\quad(n\ge1),\qquad (E(B)\Psi)_0=\mathbf1_B(0)\Psi_0.$$
For $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, let $H_\theta$ be multiplication on sector $n$
by $\theta\cdot s_n$, with its maximal square-integrability domain. Then
$$U_\theta(t)\Psi:=\bigl(e^{it\theta\cdot s_n}\Psi_n\bigr)_{n\ge0}$$
is a strongly continuous unitary group on all of Fock space, and its norm
derivative at zero exists exactly for $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, where it is
$iH_\theta\Psi$. The zero-particle sector is the vacuum eigenvector at joint
value $0$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$ and its tensor extension is the bounded map of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation
by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction
$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and
$c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the
creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the
finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. No physical statistics assignment or spin–statistics
theorem is part of these mathematical definitions.

Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

Use the $(-+++)$ coordinate convention, $h=-\eta=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$, and the Clifford matrices of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]]; the shell parameter $\mu>0$ has inverse-length units as in [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. For $p=(p^0,\mathbf p)\in\mathbb R^4$, write
$$ \Gamma(p):=\gamma^0p^0-\sum_{j=1}^3\gamma^jp_j,\qquad K(p):=\Gamma(p)-\mu I_4. $$
When $h(p,p)\ne\mu^2$, define the finite rational inverse
$$ S_0(p):=\frac{\Gamma(p)+\mu I_4}{h(p,p)-\mu^2}. $$
For $p,p+k$ with both denominators nonzero,
$$ S_0(p+k)\Gamma(k)S_0(p)=S_0(p)-S_0(p+k). $$
For any finite chain of off-shell momenta, the corresponding insertion differences telescope with both endpoint terms retained. If $u(p),u(p')$ satisfy $(\Gamma(p)-\mu)u(p)=0$, $(\Gamma(p')-\mu)u(p')=0$ and $p,p'$ lie on the future shell, then $\bar u(p')\Gamma(p-p')u(p)=0$, where $\bar u=u^\dagger\beta$. These are finite rational/tree identities; no Feynman boundary value, singular distribution product, loop theorem, or all-diagram gauge-independence claim is included.

Use the finite graph phase data of [[def-qft-qed-finite-graph-gauge-data]] and the planned QED $U(1)$, Clifford, and natural-unit conventions of [[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]]. Let $K_0(\zeta)\in GL_d(\mathbb C)$ be an invertible base matrix and let $V(\zeta)\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ be its finite link-hopping matrix. The admissible covariant families satisfy
$$
K_0(\zeta^\alpha)=D_\alpha K_0(\zeta)D_\alpha^{-1},\qquad
V(\zeta^\alpha)=D_\alpha V(\zeta)D_\alpha^{-1}.
$$
The scalar base $K_0=mI_d$, $m\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, is an explicit admissible case. Define
$$
K(z;\zeta):=K_0(\zeta)+zV(\zeta),\qquad
S(z;\zeta):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-zK_0(\zeta)^{-1}V(\zeta))^nK_0(\zeta)^{-1}.
$$
The coefficient of each power $z^n$ in $S$ is one finite matrix. The item defines this formal candidate; the following lemma proves its two-sided inverse and covariance properties. Define $\det A$ for a finite matrix $A$ over $\mathbb C\llbracket z\rrbracket$ by the Leibniz formula $\det A=\sum_{\sigma\in S_d}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{j=1}^d A_{j,\sigma(j)}$.

For a real vertex phase $\theta=(\theta_x)_{x\in X}\in\mathbb R^X$, define
$$
\zeta_e^\theta:=e^{i(\theta_{s(e)}-\theta_{t(e)})}\zeta_e,\qquad
D_\theta:=\operatorname{diag}_{x\in X}(e^{i\theta_x}I_r)\in GL_d(\mathbb C).
$$
Define the link-hopping matrix $V(\zeta)\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ by its $x,y$ block indexed by $x,y\in X$
$$
V(\zeta)_{xy}:=\sum_{\substack{e\in E\\s(e)=x,\ t(e)=y}}T_e\zeta_e .
$$
An empty sum is the zero $r\times r$ matrix. Additional fixed diagonal blocks belong to a separate base matrix. These data are finite-dimensional algebraic data; the phases are external parameters, not rotor multiplication operators on $L^2(\mathbb T^E)$.

For a real smooth gauge parameter $\chi$ in webers, put $\alpha=\chi/S_0$ (dimensionless) and use
$$A'_a=A_a+\partial_a\chi,\qquad a'_a=a_a+\partial_a\alpha,\qquad \psi'=e^{ig\alpha}\psi.$$
The induced covariant derivative is $D'_a=\partial_a-ig a'_a$. These are formal mathematical conventions for the later conditional deductions. They do not adopt a measured value of $\mu_0$, identify $q$ with an electron charge, impose charge quantization, or assert that interacting continuum fields exist.

derivations.claim: Put $B:=K_0^{-1}V$. The coefficient of $z^n$ in $S$ is $(-B)^nK_0^{-1}$, a finite matrix, so the series defines an element of $M_d(\mathbb C\llbracket z\rrbracket)$ without an analytic convergence assumption.

Since $K=K_0(I+zB)$, multiplication gives $KS=K_0(I+zB)\sum_{n\ge0}(-zB)^nK_0^{-1}$. In the product $(I+zB)\sum_{n\ge0}(-zB)^n$, the constant coefficient is $I$ and the two contributions to every positive-degree coefficient cancel; hence $KS=I$.
Also $K_0^{-1}K=I+zB$, so $SK=\sum_{n\ge0}(-zB)^n(I+zB)=I$ by the same coefficientwise cancellation. Thus $S$ is the two-sided formal inverse.

Each link block transforms as $T_e\zeta_e^\theta=e^{i\theta_{s(e)}}(T_e\zeta_e)e^{-i\theta_{t(e)}}$; summing links in each block gives $V(\zeta^\theta)=D_\theta V(\zeta)D_\theta^{-1}$. With [A1], the assumed covariance of $K_0$ gives the same conjugation for each coefficient of $K$; the QED phase interpretation is exactly $\theta_x=g\alpha_x$ from [F3].
Substituting the conjugated $K_0,V$ into the defining series for $S$ conjugates each finite coefficient by $D_\theta$, proving $S(z;\zeta^\theta)=D_\theta S(z;\zeta)D_\theta^{-1}$.
Differentiate $K_sS_s=I$ coefficientwise at $s=0$. This gives $(\delta K)S+K(\delta S)=0$, hence $\delta S=-S(\delta K)S$ using $K^{-1}=S$.
From $D_s=e^{is\Theta}$, direct differentiation gives $\delta K=i[\Theta,K]$. Therefore $-S\,i[\Theta,K]\,S=-iS\Theta KS+iSK\Theta S=-iS\Theta+i\Theta S=i[\Theta,S]$.

Take $\mathbf k,\kappa,\epsilon$ in inverse metres and $b$ dimensionless; then $f_\epsilon$ has momentum-wavefunction units $\mathrm m^{3/2}$, $C_b$ is dimensionless, and $\hbar c(\kappa-\epsilon)$ has energy units.

Order the generators as $\bar\psi_1,\ldots,\bar\psi_d,\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_d$. The corresponding ordered monomials form the $R$-basis of $\Lambda_d(R)$. Let
$$
M_d:=\bar\psi_1\cdots\bar\psi_d\psi_1\cdots\psi_d
$$
and let $[M_d]P\in R$ denote the coefficient of $M_d$ in $P\in\Lambda_d(R)$. Define the finite Grassmann integral by the $R$-linear functional
$$
\mathcal I_d(P):=(-1)^{d(d+1)/2}[M_d]P .
$$
For $K\in M_d(R)$, put $B_K:=\sum_{i,j=1}^d\bar\psi_iK_{ij}\psi_j$. Since every monomial of degree greater than $2d$ vanishes, its exponential is the finite sum
$$
\exp(-B_K):=\sum_{n=0}^{d}\frac{(-B_K)^n}{n!}.
$$
The sign factor in $\mathcal I_d$ is the chosen normalization. Its Gaussian determinant identity, including the value at $K=I_d$, is proved separately.

V(\zeta^\alpha)=D_\alpha V(\zeta)D_\alpha^{-1}.
$$

$$
K(z;\zeta):=K_0(\zeta)+zV(\zeta),\qquad
S(z;\zeta):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-zK_0(\zeta)^{-1}V(\zeta))^nK_0(\zeta)^{-1}.
$$

Define $\det A$ for a finite matrix $A$ over $\mathbb C\llbracket z\rrbracket$ by the Leibniz formula $\det A=\sum_{\sigma\in S_d}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{j=1}^d A_{j,\sigma(j)}$.

derivations.claim: Put $B_K=\sum_{i,j}\bar\psi_iK_{ij}\psi_j$. Every factor has Grassmann degree two, so a product of more than $d$ such factors has degree greater than $2d$ and vanishes. Hence the exponential is the finite sum $\sum_{n=0}^d(-B_K)^n/n!$, and only its degree-$2d$ term contributes to $[M_d]$.

In $B_K^d/d!$, any term with a repeated row or column index vanishes. The surviving terms are indexed by permutations $\sigma\in S_d$. Reordering $\bar\psi_1\psi_{\sigma(1)}\cdots\bar\psi_d\psi_{\sigma(d)}$ into $M_d$ contributes $(-1)^{d(d-1)/2}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$; the exponential contributes $(-1)^d$. Therefore
$$ [M_d]\exp(-B_K)=(-1)^{d(d+1)/2}\sum_{\sigma\in S_d}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i=1}^dK_{i,\sigma(i)} =(-1)^{d(d+1)/2}\det K . $$
Applying the normalization in [F1] proves the Gaussian identity.

For diagonal $D$, $K'_{ij}=u_iK_{ij}u_j^{-1}$. In each Leibniz term, $\prod_i u_i\prod_i u_{\sigma(i)}^{-1}=1$, since $\sigma$ permutes the indices; thus $\det K'=\det K$. The Gaussian identity from [step 2.1] then gives the same equality for the finite Grassmann integral.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Order the generators as $\bar\psi_1,\ldots,\bar\psi_d,\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_d$. The corresponding ordered monomials form the $R$-basis of $\Lambda_d(R)$. Let
$$
M_d:=\bar\psi_1\cdots\bar\psi_d\psi_1\cdots\psi_d
$$
and let $[M_d]P\in R$ denote the coefficient of $M_d$ in $P\in\Lambda_d(R)$. Define the finite Grassmann integral by the $R$-linear functional
$$
\mathcal I_d(P):=(-1)^{d(d+1)/2}[M_d]P .
$$
For $K\in M_d(R)$, put $B_K:=\sum_{i,j=1}^d\bar\psi_iK_{ij}\psi_j$. Since every monomial of degree greater than $2d$ vanishes, its exponential is the finite sum
$$
\exp(-B_K):=\sum_{n=0}^{d}\frac{(-B_K)^n}{n!}.
$$
The sign factor in $\mathcal I_d$ is the chosen normalization. Its Gaussian determinant identity, including the value at $K=I_d$, is proved separately.

R^4)$ define its pointwise shell Fourier restriction by
$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{ip\circ x}\,d^4x.$$

Consequently $\Gamma(p)^2=h(p,p)I_4$ and $\beta\Gamma(p)^\dagger\beta=\Gamma(p)$ for every real $p$.

Use the finite Dirac matrices and adjoint of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]], and the separate geometric metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and algebraic contraction $h=-\eta=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$ of [[def-qft-example-data]]. Write $p=(E,\mathbf p)$ for an energy four-vector with components in joules, $M\geq0$ for a rest-energy parameter in joules, and $E=\sqrt{|\mathbf p|^2+M^2}>0$. In the natural-length variables of the Dirac definition, $\mathbf k=\mathbf p/(\hbar c)$, $\mu=M/(\hbar c)$, and $\omega=E/(\hbar c)$.

Let $\beta=\gamma^0$, $\alpha_j=\beta\gamma^j$, $\Sigma_j=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_j,\sigma_j)$, and $\gamma_5=i\gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3$. Define $H_\pm=\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot\mathbf p\pm\beta M$ and $P_\pm=(I_4+H_\pm/E)/2$. Each $P_\pm$ is a Hermitian rank-two projection. derivations.claim: Direct multiplication of the displayed Pauli matrices gives $\sigma_j^2=I_2$, $\sigma_1\sigma_2=i\sigma_3$, $\sigma_2\sigma_3=i\sigma_1$, $\sigma_3\sigma_1=i\sigma_2$, and the reversed products have the opposite signs. Block multiplication then gives $\alpha_i^\dagger=\alpha_i$, $\beta^\dagger=\beta$, $\alpha_i\alpha_j=\delta_{ij}I_4+i\epsilon_{ijk}\Sigma_k$, and $\alpha_i\beta=-\beta\alpha_i$. The explicit blocks have trace zero, so $\operatorname{Tr}\gamma^a=0$, and $\operatorname{Tr}I_4=4$. The Clifford relation is $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=2h^{ab}I_4$. Cyclicity of trace follows by expanding matrix entries; averaging $\operatorname{Tr}(\gamma^a\gamma^b)$ with its cyclic rearrangement gives $4h^{ab}$. For the four-factor trace, anticommute $\gamma^a$ successively past $\gamma^b,\gamma^c,\gamma^d$; cyclicity makes the final four-factor term the negative of the original, yielding $4(h^{ab}h^{cd}-h^{ac}h^{bd}+h^{ad}h^{bc})$. Finally $\gamma_5^2=I_4$ and $\gamma_5\gamma^a=-\gamma^a\gamma_5$ by the same Clifford relations, so cyclicity gives $\operatorname{Tr}(\gamma^a\gamma^b\gamma^c)=-\operatorname{Tr}(\gamma^a\gamma^b\gamma^c)$, hence the three-factor trace is zero.

Multiplying on the right by $\beta$ yields $EI_4\beta+H_+\beta=E\beta-\beta\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot\mathbf p+MI_4=\not p+M$ and $EI_4\beta+H_-\beta=E\beta-\beta\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot\mathbf p-MI_4=\not p-M$, using $\alpha_i\beta=-\beta\alpha_i$ and $\gamma^j=\beta\alpha_j$.

Let $m\geq0$ be a scalar rest energy in joules and $s>4m^2$. For one scalar initial label of weight $1$ and one specified final channel, take the dimensionless real quartic tree amplitude $\mathcal A=-\lambda$. The coefficient map of [[lem-qft-example-two-body-phase-space]] gives
$$\frac{d\sigma_{\mathrm{coeff}}}{d\Omega} =\frac{\lambda^2(\hbar c)^2}{128\pi^2s}, \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{coeff}}=\frac{\lambda^2(\hbar c)^2}{32\pi s}$$
for identical final scalars integrated over the full labeled sphere. For distinguishable final scalars the two coefficients are twice these values.

For a parent at rest with energy $\mathsf M_0>2m$ decaying through a specified single channel to two identical scalars of rest energy $m$ under a constant amplitude $G_E$ in joules, the rate coefficient is
$$\Gamma_{\mathrm{coeff}} =\frac{|G_E|^2}{32\pi\hbar\mathsf M_0} \sqrt{1-\frac{4m^2}{\mathsf M_0^2}}.$$
This result concerns the defined formal coefficients. It does not assert an exact exponential survival law.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], and use [[def-qft-example-data]] and [[def-qft-example-two-body-phase-space-data]]. A proper orthochronous linear $h$-Lorentz map is a real linear $\Lambda$ with $\Lambda^Th\Lambda=h$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and $\Lambda$ preserving the future cone $E>0$. For future energy four-vectors in the algebraic metric $h=(+,-,-,-)$, the shell measure $d^3\mathbf p/((2\pi)^3\,2E)$ is invariant under every such map. Write $E_i(r)=\sqrt{r^2+\mathsf M_i^2}$. Let $f$ be a nonnegative Borel function on the product of the positive shells of [[def-qft-example-two-body-phase-space-data]]. The standard two-body on-shell integral
$$(2\pi)^4\int d\nu_{\mathsf M_1}(k_1)d\nu_{\mathsf M_2}(k_2)\, \delta^{(4)}(P-k_1-k_2)\,f(k_1,k_2)$$
is interpreted by first evaluating the spatial delta in $k_2$, then the one-dimensional energy delta by the increasing radial change of variable $r\mapsto E_1(r)+E_2(r)$. Explicitly, after the spatial evaluation its radial action is $\int_0^\infty g(r)\delta(\sqrt{s}-E_1(r)-E_2(r))\,dr=g(k_*)/(d(E_1+E_2)/dr|_{k_*})$ for nonnegative Borel $g$; this is the pushforward evaluation under that $C^1$ diffeomorphism, not a product of distributions. It equals $\int f\,d\Phi_2$ from the Definition. The threshold root is $k_*$ in that Definition, and
$$\int d\Phi_2=\frac{k_*}{4\pi\sqrt{s}}.$$
For equal rest energies $\mathsf M_1=\mathsf M_2=\mathsf M$, set $\beta=\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M^2/s}$; then $k_*=\sqrt{s}\beta/2$ and $\int d\Phi_2=\beta/(8\pi)$. For future incoming energy four-vectors $p_1,p_2$ with $p_1+p_2=P$ and nonnegative rest energies $\mathsf M_{1,\mathrm{in}},\mathsf M_{2,\mathrm{in}}\geq0$, let $p_*$ be their center-of-momentum spatial momentum magnitude. Their invariant flux is $F=4p_*\sqrt{s}$. For equal incoming rest energies $\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}\geq0$ with $s\geq4\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}^2$, define $\beta_{\mathrm{in}}=\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}^2/s}$; then $p_*=\sqrt{s}\beta_{\mathrm{in}}/2$ and $F=2s\beta_{\mathrm{in}}$. For finite nonempty incoming and outgoing label sets, normalized initial weights, and the Borel amplitude family of the Definition, whenever $F>0$ the cross-section coefficient map gives
$$\frac{d\sigma_{\mathrm{coeff}}}{d\Omega} =\frac{(\hbar c)^2}{64\pi^2s}\, \frac{k_*}{p_*}\, \frac{\overline{|\mathcal A|^2}}{S_f}.$$
For a parent at rest with energy $\mathsf M_0>2\mathsf M$ decaying to two equal rest-energy daughters with constant amplitude $G_E$ in joules, the rate coefficient is $|G_E|^2\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M^2/\mathsf M_0^2}/(32\pi\hbar\mathsf M_0)$ when the daughters are identical. Finite-matrix examples act on $\mathbb C^d$ with the operator norm. For Hilbert spaces, use the first-variable-linear pairing $(u,v)_1=v^\dagger u$; a displayed coordinate contraction $u^\dagger v$ is second-variable-linear and equals $\overline{(u,v)_1}$. Thus norms, traces, and modulus-squared amplitudes agree under conversion, although the unsquared pairing is conjugated. No amplitude is assigned a probability by these conventions.

Write $p=(E,\mathbf p)$ for an energy four-vector with components in joules, $M\geq0$ for a rest-energy parameter in joules, and $E=\sqrt{|\mathbf p|^2+M^2}>0$. In the natural-length variables of the Dirac definition, $\mathbf k=\mathbf p/(\hbar c)$, $\mu=M/(\hbar c)$, and $\omega=E/(\hbar c)$.

Let $\beta=\gamma^0$, $\alpha_j=\beta\gamma^j$, $\Sigma_j=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_j,\sigma_j)$, and $\gamma_5=i\gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3$. Define $H_\pm=\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot\mathbf p\pm\beta M$ and $P_\pm=(I_4+H_\pm/E)/2$. Each $P_\pm$ is a Hermitian rank-two projection. $$\operatorname{Tr}I_4=4,\quad \operatorname{Tr}\gamma^a=0,\quad \operatorname{Tr}(\gamma^a\gamma^b)=4h^{ab},\quad \operatorname{Tr}(\gamma^a\gamma^b\gamma^c)=0,$$

$$\operatorname{Tr}(\gamma^a\gamma^b\gamma^c\gamma^d) =4(h^{ab}h^{cd}-h^{ac}h^{bd}+h^{ad}h^{bc}), \qquad \sum_s u_s\bar u_s=\not p+M,\quad \sum_s v_s\bar v_s=\not p-M.$$

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], and use [[def-qft-example-data]] and [[def-qft-example-two-body-phase-space-data]]. A proper orthochronous linear $h$-Lorentz map is a real linear $\Lambda$ with $\Lambda^Th\Lambda=h$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and $\Lambda$ preserving the future cone $E>0$. For future energy four-vectors in the algebraic metric $h=(+,-,-,-)$, the shell measure $d^3\mathbf p/((2\pi)^3\,2E)$ is invariant under every such map. Write $E_i(r)=\sqrt{r^2+\mathsf M_i^2}$. Let $f$ be a nonnegative Borel function on the product of the positive shells of [[def-qft-example-two-body-phase-space-data]]. The standard two-body on-shell integral
$$(2\pi)^4\int d\nu_{\mathsf M_1}(k_1)d\nu_{\mathsf M_2}(k_2)\, \delta^{(4)}(P-k_1-k_2)\,f(k_1,k_2)$$
is interpreted by first evaluating the spatial delta in $k_2$, then the one-dimensional energy delta by the increasing radial change of variable $r\mapsto E_1(r)+E_2(r)$. Explicitly, after the spatial evaluation its radial action is $\int_0^\infty g(r)\delta(\sqrt{s}-E_1(r)-E_2(r))\,dr=g(k_*)/(d(E_1+E_2)/dr|_{k_*})$ for nonnegative Borel $g$; this is the pushforward evaluation under that $C^1$ diffeomorphism, not a product of distributions. It equals $\int f\,d\Phi_2$ from the Definition. The threshold root is $k_*$ in that Definition, and
$$\int d\Phi_2=\frac{k_*}{4\pi\sqrt{s}}.$$
For equal rest energies $\mathsf M_1=\mathsf M_2=\mathsf M$, set $\beta=\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M^2/s}$; then $k_*=\sqrt{s}\beta/2$ and $\int d\Phi_2=\beta/(8\pi)$. For future incoming energy four-vectors $p_1,p_2$ with $p_1+p_2=P$ and nonnegative rest energies $\mathsf M_{1,\mathrm{in}},\mathsf M_{2,\mathrm{in}}\geq0$, let $p_*$ be their center-of-momentum spatial momentum magnitude. For equal incoming rest energies $\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}\geq0$ with $s\geq4\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}^2$, define $\beta_{\mathrm{in}}=\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}^2/s}$; then $p_*=\sqrt{s}\beta_{\mathrm{in}}/2$ and $F=2s\beta_{\mathrm{in}}$. For finite nonempty incoming and outgoing label sets, normalized initial weights, and the Borel amplitude family of the Definition, whenever $F>0$ the cross-section coefficient map gives
$$\frac{d\sigma_{\mathrm{coeff}}}{d\Omega} =\frac{(\hbar c)^2}{64\pi^2s}\, \frac{k_*}{p_*}\, \frac{\overline{|\mathcal A|^2}}{S_f}.$$

This is a coefficient calculation, not a claim of exponential survival.

Let $K(z;\zeta)=K_0(\zeta)+zV(\zeta)$ and $S(z;\zeta)$ be the finite-dimensional formal matrices of [[def-qft-qed-formal-ring]], with $d\ge1$, $K_0(\zeta)$ invertible, and both coefficient matrices covariant under the vertex phase angles of [[def-qft-qed-finite-graph-gauge-data]]. Then $S$ is a two-sided inverse of $K$ in $M_d(\mathbb C\llbracket z\rrbracket)$, and
$$ S(z;\zeta^\theta)=D_\theta S(z;\zeta)D_\theta^{-1} $$
coefficientwise. For a differentiable phase path $D_s=e^{is\Theta}$, where the real vertex-angle path is $s\theta$, the variations satisfy
$$ \delta K=i[\Theta,K],\qquad \delta S=i[\Theta,S]=-S(\delta K)S . $$
For ordinary finite matrices $A,B\in GL_d(\mathbb C)$, the corresponding resolvent identity is $B^{-1}(B-A)A^{-1}=A^{-1}-B^{-1}$. These are formal or finite algebraic statements; they assert no convergence of a perturbation series, continuum limit, or loop Ward identity.
