citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Use the finite data and notation of
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]: $N\ge1$,
$H_N=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, $D_0=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
and $W=V+C_0+1\ge1+c|q|^2$. For $u,v\in D_0$ define
$$a(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int_{\mathbb R^N}(\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv}\,dq+\int_{\mathbb R^N}(W+1)u\overline v\,dq,$$
and $\|u\|_Q:=a(u,u)^{1/2}$. Let $Q$ be the completion of this inner-product
space, constructed as equivalence classes of $\|\cdot\|_Q$-Cauchy sequences.
Then $Q$ is a complex Hilbert space and the map sending a Cauchy class to its
$L^2$ limit is a continuous injective linear map $Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ with
dense image. Each $u\in Q$ has weak derivatives $\partial_j u\in L^2$ and a
weighted function $\sqrt{W+1}\,u\in L^2$, and
$$\|u\|_Q^2=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2.$$
Here $g_j=\partial_j u$ means explicitly that
$\int u\,\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$ for every
$\varphi\in D_0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $d\ge1$. For each $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ put $K_j^y:=L^2(\mathbb R,dy_j)$ and take a copy $(g^{(j)}_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of the Hermite family of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $K_j^y$. Define the left-associated completed tensor products by $\mathcal K_1^y:=K_1^y$ and $\mathcal K_r^y:=\mathcal K_{r-1}^y\widehat\otimes K_r^y$ for $2\le r\le d$. Let $\Theta_y^{(1)}:K_1^y\to L^2(\mathbb R,dy_1)$ be the identity; recursively, for $2\le r\le d$, let

$$\Theta_y^{(r)}:=\Theta_{r-1,1}^y\circ\bigl(\Theta_y^{(r-1)}\otimes I_{K_r^y}\bigr):\mathcal K_r^y\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^r,dy),$$

where $\Theta_{r-1,1}^y:L^2(\mathbb R^{r-1},dy)\widehat\otimes K_r^y\to L^2(\mathbb R^r,dy)$ is the two-factor Euclidean product unitary of [[lem-nrqm-composites-euclidean-l2-product-unitary]], and $\Theta_y^{(r-1)}\otimes I_{K_r^y}$ is the bounded tensor map of [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]]. Thus $\Theta_y^{(r)}$ is a specified unitary, with $\Theta_y^{(r)}(u\otimes v)(y',y_r)=\Theta_y^{(r-1)}u(y')v(y_r)$ almost everywhere. For $N=(n_1,\dots,n_d)\in\mathbb N^d$, set $G_N^{y,1}:=g^{(1)}_{n_1}$ and recursively $G_N^{y,r}:=G_N^{y,r-1}\otimes g^{(r)}_{n_r}$; define $g_N:=\Theta_y^{(d)}G_N^{y,d}\in L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$.

Let $\varphi:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N^d$ list the multi-indices by increasing total degree $M=\sum_jn_j$ and, within each finite level, in lexicographic order. By [[thm-stars-and-bars]] each level is finite and the levels exhaust $\mathbb N^d$, so this specifies a bijection. All sums indexed by $\mathbb N^d$ below are taken in this order; nonnegative sums equivalently mean the supremum of finite subsums.

The functions $g_N$ have smooth product representatives from the recursive construction. These representatives are unique: a continuous difference that is nonzero at a point remains nonzero on a ball of positive Lebesgue measure. The coordinate derivatives in (b) and (c) are taken on these representatives and their scaled products.

Then:

(a) $(g_N)_{N\in\mathbb N^d}$ is a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$: $\langle g_N,g_M\rangle=\delta_{NM}$ and every $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$ has $f=\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}\langle f,g_N\rangle g_N$ with $\|f\|^2=\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}|\langle f,g_N\rangle|^2$, the sum being the supremum over finite subfamilies ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]]);

(b) with the eigenvalues $\lambda_N:=\sum_{j=1}^d(2n_j+1)=2M+d$, $M:=\sum_jn_j$, let $A_d$ be the diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the enumerated family $e_m:=g_{\varphi(m)}$ and eigenvalue sequence $\lambda_{\varphi(m)}$. Then $A_d$ is self-adjoint with

$$A_dg_N=\lambda_Ng_N,\qquad D(A_d)=\Bigl\{f:\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}\lambda_N^2|\langle f,g_N\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad \sigma(A_d)=\{2M+d:M\in\mathbb N\}$$

(the spectrum by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]); the algebraic span of the $g_N$ is a core, and on that span

$$A_d=\sum_{j=1}^d\bigl(-\partial_{y_j}^2+y_j^2\bigr)$$

as operators, the $j$-th summand acting in the $j$-th coordinate;

(c) for real $m_j,\omega_j,\hbar>0$ put $\ell_j:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m_j\omega_j)}$ and let $D_j:K_j^y\to K_j^x:=L^2(\mathbb R,dx_j)$ be the one-dimensional unitary of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]]. Define $\mathcal K_1^x:=K_1^x$ and $\mathcal K_r^x:=\mathcal K_{r-1}^x\widehat\otimes K_r^x$ for $2\le r\le d$, and define $\Theta_x^{(1)}$ and $\Theta_x^{(r)}$ by the same recursion as $\Theta_y^{(r)}$, using the two-factor Euclidean product unitaries on the $x$-coordinate spaces. Let $\mathcal D_1:=D_1$ and recursively $\mathcal D_r:=\mathcal D_{r-1}\otimes D_r:\mathcal K_r^y\to\mathcal K_r^x$; each $\mathcal D_r$ is unitary by [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]]. Put $D_d:=\Theta_x^{(d)}\mathcal D_d(\Theta_y^{(d)})^{-1}:L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R^d,dx)$. For $N\in\mathbb N^d$, define $G_N^{x,1}:=D_1g^{(1)}_{n_1}=:\psi^{(1)}_{n_1}$ and recursively $G_N^{x,r}:=G_N^{x,r-1}\otimes\psi^{(r)}_{n_r}$; then $\psi_N:=D_dg_N=\Theta_x^{(d)}G_N^{x,d}$. Let $H$ be the diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the enumerated family $\psi_{\varphi(m)}$ and eigenvalue sequence $E_{\varphi(m)}$, where $E_N:=\hbar\sum_{j=1}^d\omega_j(n_j+\frac12)$. Then $H$ is self-adjoint with

$$H\psi_N=E_N\psi_N,\qquad D(H)=\Bigl\{f:\sum_N E_N^2|\langle f,\psi_N\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad \sigma(H)=\overline{\{E_N:N\in\mathbb N^d\}},$$

the span of the $\psi_N$ is a core, and on that core

$$H=\sum_{j=1}^d\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_j}\partial_{x_j}^2+\frac{m_j\omega_j^2}{2}x_j^2\Bigr);$$

(d) if $\omega_1=\cdots=\omega_d=\omega$, then $\sigma(H)=\{\hbar\omega(M+\frac d2):M\in\mathbb N\}$, and the eigenvalue $\hbar\omega(M+\frac d2)$ has multiplicity

$$\bigl|\{(n_1,\dots,n_d)\in\mathbb N^d:n_1+\cdots+n_d=M\}\bigr|=\binom{M+d-1}{d-1};$$

in particular for $d=3$ the multiplicity is $(M+1)(M+2)/2$ ([[thm-stars-and-bars]]). All parameters are positive real numbers; no physical interpretation is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L^2=L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ be the complex Lebesgue space with inner product $\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(y)\overline{\psi(y)}\,dy$ linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); this pairing makes $L^2$ a complex Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For complex-valued functions, smoothness and derivatives use the componentwise convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Write $g_0$ for the function $g_0(y):=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-y^{2}/2}$ and also for its class in $L^2$. Put

$$P:=\{p\,g_0:\ p\in\mathbb C[y]\}\subseteq L^2 ,$$

the set of classes of polynomial multiples of $g_0$. Each class in $P$ has a unique representative of the form $p g_0$: if $p g_0=qg_0$ almost everywhere, the continuous function $(p-q)g_0$ vanishes almost everywhere and therefore everywhere, and $g_0(y)>0$ for every $y$, so $p=q$. Let $Y$ be multiplication by $y$ and $\partial_y$ the derivative, acting on this unique smooth representative. Set $g_{-1}:=0$ for use in the recurrence formulas at $n=0$. Define

$$a:=\frac{Y+\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad a^\dagger:=\frac{Y-\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad g_n:=\frac{(a^\dagger)^ng_0}{\sqrt{n!}}\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then:

(a) $g_0\in L^2$ with $\|g_0\|=1$; more generally $y^kg_0\in L^2$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$, so $P$ is a linear subspace of $L^2$ all of whose members are represented by $C^\infty$ functions;

(b) $Y,\partial_y,a,a^\dagger$ map $P$ into $P$, and $\partial_y(pg_0)=(p'-yp)g_0$ for every polynomial $p$;

(c) for all $\varphi,\psi\in P$, $\langle a^\dagger\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a\psi\rangle$ and $\langle a\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a^\dagger\psi\rangle$;

(d) $a^\dagger a-a a^\dagger=-I$ on $P$, i.e. $[a,a^\dagger]=aa^\dagger-a^\dagger a=I$ on $P$, and $ag_0=0$;

(e) for every $n\in\mathbb N$: $ag_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}$ (with $ag_0=0$), $a^\dagger g_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}$, $a^\dagger ag_n=ng_n$ and $aa^\dagger g_n=(n+1)g_n$;

(f) the polynomials

$$H_n(y):=(-1)^ne^{y^2}\frac{d^n}{dy^n}e^{-y^2}$$

are polynomials of degree $n$ with leading coefficient $2^n$, $H_0=1$, $H_1(y)=2y$, $H_n(-y)=(-1)^nH_n(y)$, and they satisfy

$$H_n'=2nH_{n-1},\qquad H_{n+1}=2yH_n-2nH_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1);$$

moreover

$$g_n=\frac{H_ng_0}{\sqrt{2^nn!}};$$

(g) consequently

$$\sqrt2\,y\,g_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1},\qquad \sqrt2\,g_n'=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}-\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix real parameters $m>0$, $\omega>0$, $\hbar>0$, put $\ell:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}>0$, and let $g_0,P,(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be the Hermite data of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$, so that $(g_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-completeness]]. Define

$$D:L^2(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R,dx),\qquad (Df)(x):=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell),$$

and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=2n+1$, with the core $P$ and spectrum $\{2n+1:n\in\mathbb N\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]).

Then:

(a) $D$ is a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with two-sided inverse $(D^{-1}g)(y)=\ell^{1/2}g(\ell y)$; the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$;

(b) the operator

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,DAD^{-1},\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{osc}}):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R,dx):D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$

is self-adjoint, satisfies $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$ for every $n$, and has

$$D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\Bigl\{f:\sum_n\hbar^2\omega^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n,$$

where $c_n:=\langle D^{-1}f,g_n\rangle=\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$; its spectrum is $\sigma(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\{\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12):n\in\mathbb N\}$, its ground energy is $\hbar\omega/2$ with eigenvector $\psi_0$, and $\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}f,f\rangle\ge\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\|f\|^2$ for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$;

(c) $D(P)=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n\}$ is a core for $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and for every polynomial $p$ the function $f:=D(pg_0)$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ with

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}f''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2f$$

pointwise on $\mathbb R$;

(d) for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and every test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R}(H_{\mathrm{osc}}f)(x)\varphi(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\varphi''(x)+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2\varphi(x)\Bigr)dx,$$

so $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is the self-adjoint realization of the differential expression $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2$ in the weak sense; no identification of $D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ with a separately defined maximal differential-operator domain is asserted.

All parameters enter as positive real numbers; no physical identification of $m,\omega,\hbar$ with measured quantities is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be a complete orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert
space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]) and
let $x\in H$, with partial sums
$P_Fx=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$ over finite $F\subseteq I$. Then:

1. $x$ is the norm limit of the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)$, that is
   $$x=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$$
   in the sense of convergence of the net of finite subsums;
2. **the coefficients are unique**: if $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ is a family in
   $\mathbb F$ whose finite-subset net $\sum_{i\in F}a_ie_i$ converges to $x$,
   then $a_i=\langle x,e_i\rangle$ for every $i\in I$;
3. the support $\{i : \langle x,e_i\rangle\ne0\}$ is at most countable, and the
   expansion does not depend on an ordering: if $(i_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ is a
   sequence of pairwise distinct elements of $I$ whose image contains the
   support, then the sequence of partial sums
   $\sum_{k<n}\langle x,e_{i_k}\rangle e_{i_k}$ also converges to $x$.

Claim 3 is the sense in which the expansion is **unconditional**: the sum is
independent of any ordering, because the finite-subset net converges and any
enumeration of a set containing the support by pairwise distinct indices is
cofinal in the squared mass.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: In [F2] choose $\hbar=1$, $m_j=(2a_j)^{-1}$ and $\omega_j=2\sqrt{a_jc}$. Then $\hbar^2/(2m_j)=a_j$ and $m_j\omega_j^2/2=c$. The eigenvalue from [F2] in coordinate $j$ is $\omega_j(n_j+1/2)=(2n_j+1)\sqrt{a_jc}$. Summing over the $N$ coordinates gives the displayed differential eigenvalue $\epsilon_{\mathbf n}$. In the same scaling, $b_j=m_j\omega_j=\sqrt{c/a_j}$ and the normalized $n_j=0$ Gaussian becomes $(b_j/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-b_jq_j^2/2}$; taking the product gives the stated ground representative.

Each product Hermite function is a polynomial times a Gaussian, so it and all first derivatives have finite squared integrals after multiplication by any fixed polynomial. Choose a smooth radial cutoff $\chi_R(q)=\chi(q/R)$ with $\chi=1$ on $|q|\le1$, $\chi=0$ on $|q|\ge2$, and $|\nabla\chi_R|\le C/R$. Such a $\chi$ can be formed from $\eta(s)=e^{-1/s}$ for $s>0$ and $\eta(s)=0$ for $s\le0$, by taking $\chi(q)=\eta(4-|q|^2)/(\eta(4-|q|^2)+\eta(|q|^2-1))$. Then $0\le\chi_R\le1$ and $\chi_R\psi_{\mathbf n}\in C_c^\infty$. The weighted-function error is supported on $|q|>R$ and bounded in squared integral by the integrable tail $(c|q|^2+2)|\psi_{\mathbf n}|^2$, so its $L^2$ norm tends to zero. For each derivative,
$$\partial_j((1-\chi_R)\psi_{\mathbf n})=(1-\chi_R)\partial_j\psi_{\mathbf n}-(\partial_j\chi_R)\psi_{\mathbf n};$$
the first term tends to zero by its Gaussian tail and the second has norm at most $C\|\psi_{\mathbf n}\|_2/R$. Thus $\chi_R\psi_{\mathbf n}$ converges in the form norm, proving $\psi_{\mathbf n}\in Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$.

For $v\in C_c^\infty$, integration by parts and the eigenvalue identity in step 1.1 give
$$a_{\mathrm{osc}}(\psi_{\mathbf n},v)=(\epsilon_{\mathbf n}+2) \langle\psi_{\mathbf n},v\rangle.$$
The left side is continuous in the form norm of $v$ by Cauchy--Schwarz [F4] in $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and the right side is continuous since $\|v\|_2\le\|v\|_{Q_{\mathrm{osc}}}$. Density of $C_c^\infty$ in its defining completion extends the identity to every $v\in Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$. Taking $v=\psi_{\mathbf m}$ proves that $\xi_{\mathbf n}:=(\epsilon_{\mathbf n}+2)^{-1/2}\psi_{\mathbf n}$ is orthonormal in $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$. If $u\in Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is orthogonal in this form inner product to every $\xi_{\mathbf n}$, conjugating the displayed identity gives $\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle=0$ for every $\mathbf n$. Completeness in $L^2$ from [F2] makes the image of $u$ zero, and the injective inclusion in [F1] makes $u=0$ in $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$. Thus $(\xi_{\mathbf n})$ is complete there.

Parseval in $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ with the complete orthonormal family $(\xi_{\mathbf n})$ gives
$$a_{\mathrm{osc}}(u,u)=\sum_{\mathbf n}(\epsilon_{\mathbf n}+2) |\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2.$$
Parseval in $L^2$ gives $\|u\|_2^2=\sum_{\mathbf n}|\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2$. Subtracting $2\|u\|_2^2$ from the first identity yields the asserted expansion of the unshifted oscillator form.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and the data of
[[lem-qft-polynomial-positive-compact-resolvent]]. Its variational operator $R$
is compact, self-adjoint, positive, and injective on the infinite-dimensional
complex Hilbert space $H_N$. Let $(\mu_n)_{n\ge1}$ be its positive eigenvalues
in nonincreasing order, with multiplicity, and choose corresponding
orthonormal eigenvectors $(\psi_n)_{n\ge1}$. Put
$E_n:=\mu_n^{-1}-1$ and define
$$D(S):=\left\{u=\sum_{n\ge1}c_n\psi_n\in H_N:\sum_{n\ge1}E_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad Su:=\sum_{n\ge1}E_nc_n\psi_n.$$
The series for $u$ converges in $H_N$ by the Hilbert-space expansion theorem.
Then $S$ is self-adjoint and satisfies $\langle Su,u\rangle\ge\|u\|_2^2$
for every $u\in D(S)$; also $(S+I)^{-1}=R$ is compact. For every
$u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
$$Su=-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2u+Wu.$$
Consequently $h:=S-(C_0+1)I$, on the same domain, is a self-adjoint realization
of the differential expression in
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]] and satisfies
$\langle hu,u\rangle\ge-C_0\|u\|_2^2$ for every $u\in D(h)$.
It has compact resolvent, meaning that for some $z\in\mathbb C$ the map
$h-zI:D(h)\to H_N$ is bijective with bounded inverse on $H_N$, and that
inverse is compact; here $z=-(C_0+2)$ and $(h+(C_0+2)I)^{-1}=R$. Put
$\lambda_n:=E_n-C_0-1$, the eigenvalues of $h$; equivalently,
$$D(h)=\left\{u=\sum_nc_n\psi_n:\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
For every $u\in Q$,
$$a(u,u)=\sum_{n\ge1}(E_n+1)|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2,\qquad q_h(u):=a(u,u)-(C_0+2)\|u\|_2^2 =\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2.$$
The lowest eigenvalue is attained and has finite multiplicity. This selects a
form realization; it does not assert that the differential expression on
$C_c^\infty$ is essentially self-adjoint or that it has no other self-adjoint
extensions.

$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be a complete orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert
space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]) and
let $x\in H$, with partial sums
$P_Fx=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$ over finite $F\subseteq I$. Then:

1. $x$ is the norm limit of the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)$, that is
   $$x=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$$
   in the sense of convergence of the net of finite subsums;
2. **the coefficients are unique**: if $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ is a family in
   $\mathbb F$ whose finite-subset net $\sum_{i\in F}a_ie_i$ converges to $x$,
   then $a_i=\langle x,e_i\rangle$ for every $i\in I$;
3. the support $\{i : \langle x,e_i\rangle\ne0\}$ is at most countable, and the
   expansion does not depend on an ordering: if $(i_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ is a
   sequence of pairwise distinct elements of $I$ whose image contains the
   support, then the sequence of partial sums
   $\sum_{k<n}\langle x,e_{i_k}\rangle e_{i_k}$ also converges to $x$.

Claim 3 is the sense in which the expansion is **unconditional**: the sum is
independent of any ordering, because the finite-subset net converges and any
enumeration of a set containing the support by pairwise distinct indices is
cofinal in the squared mass.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: Parseval gives $\sum_n|c_n|^2=\|f\|^2$. Since $|e^{-it\lambda_n}|=1$, the finite partial sums defining $U(t)f$ are Cauchy in $H_N$, so converge; Parseval gives $\|U(t)f\|^2=\sum_n|c_n|^2=\|f\|^2$. The coefficient formula shows $U(-t)U(t)f=f=U(t)U(-t)f$ and $U(s)U(t)f=U(s+t)f$, first on finite sums and then on all of $H_N$ by norm convergence and the norm bound. Thus $U(t)$ is a surjective isometry, hence unitary, and $U(0)=I$.

Fix $s\in\mathbb R$ and $f\in H_N$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose a finite set $F\subset\mathbb N$ with $\sum_{n\notin F}|c_n|^2<\varepsilon^2/64$, possible by convergence of the nonnegative series in [F2]. The norm of the difference on the complement is at most $2(\sum_{n\notin F}|c_n|^2)^{1/2}<\varepsilon/4$. On the finite set $F$, each scalar $e^{-it\lambda_n}$ is continuous in $t$, so the finite partial difference has norm below $3\varepsilon/4$ for $t$ sufficiently close to $s$. The triangle inequality proves $\|U(t)f-U(s)f\|<\varepsilon$, establishing strong continuity.

Let $f\in D(h)$, so $\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty$. Since $|e^{-it\lambda_n}|=1$, $U(t)f$ has the same finite weighted coefficient sum and belongs to $D(h)$. For $r\ne0$,
$$\frac{U(t+r)f-U(t)f}{r} =\sum_ne^{-it\lambda_n}\frac{e^{-ir\lambda_n}-1}{r}c_n\psi_n.$$
The scalar integral identity $e^{-ir\lambda}-1=\int_0^r(-i\lambda)e^{-is\lambda}\,ds$ gives $|(e^{-ir\lambda}-1)/r|\le|\lambda|$. Thus the difference quotient coefficients are dominated in square sum by $\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2$. On each finite set they converge to $-i\lambda_ne^{-it\lambda_n}c_n$; choosing a finite set with small tail in that dominating series and then taking $r\to0$ proves convergence in $H_N$ to $-i\sum_n\lambda_ne^{-it\lambda_n}c_n\psi_n=-ihU(t)f$.

Conversely, suppose the norm derivative at $t=0$ exists and equals $g\in H_N$. Continuity of the coefficient functional $v\mapsto\langle v,\psi_n\rangle$ from [F3] makes its value on the difference quotient converge to $-i\lambda_nc_n$. Hence $\langle g,\psi_n\rangle=-i\lambda_nc_n$ for every $n$. Parseval for $g$ implies $\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2=\|g\|^2<\infty$, so $f\in D(h)$ by [F1]. If the derivative exists at any other $t$, the same coefficient argument multiplies each coefficient by a unit phase and yields the identical summability condition. Thus the differentiability domain is exactly $D(h)$ at every $t$.

Assume Countable Choice. Use the finite data and notation of
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]: $N\ge1$,
$H_N=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, $D_0=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
and $W=V+C_0+1\ge1+c|q|^2$. For $u,v\in D_0$ define
$$a(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int_{\mathbb R^N}(\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv}\,dq+\int_{\mathbb R^N}(W+1)u\overline v\,dq,$$
and $\|u\|_Q:=a(u,u)^{1/2}$. Let $Q$ be the completion of this inner-product
space, constructed as equivalence classes of $\|\cdot\|_Q$-Cauchy sequences.
Then $Q$ is a complex Hilbert space and the map sending a Cauchy class to its
$L^2$ limit is a continuous injective linear map $Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ with
dense image. Each $u\in Q$ has weak derivatives $\partial_j u\in L^2$ and a
weighted function $\sqrt{W+1}\,u\in L^2$, and
$$\|u\|_Q^2=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2.$$
Here $g_j=\partial_j u$ means explicitly that
$\int u\,\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$ for every
$\varphi\in D_0$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$
([[def-linear-map]]) is a **compact operator** when the image of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]); explicitly, for every bounded $A\subseteq X$ the
closure $\overline{T(A)}$ in $Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$. The set of compact
operators $X\to Y$ is written $\mathcal K(X,Y)$.

**The closed unit ball suffices.** Put
$\overline B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le 1\}$
([[def-metric-ball]]). Then $T$ is compact if and only if
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$.

Indeed, if $T$ is compact then $\overline B_X$ is bounded, because
$\overline B_X\subseteq B(0,2)$ while $B(0,2)$ is bounded and a subset of a
bounded set is bounded, so $T(\overline B_X)$ has compact closure. Conversely
assume $\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ compact and let $A\subseteq X$ be bounded.
If $A=\varnothing$ then $T(A)=\varnothing$, whose closure is empty and hence
compact. Otherwise $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ for some $x_0\in X$ and real $r>0$, so
every $x\in A$ satisfies $\|x\|\le\|x_0\|+r=:R$; if $R>0$ then
$A\subseteq R\,\overline B_X$ and if $R=0$ then $A\subseteq\{0\}$, so in either
case $T(A)\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$. Scalar multiplication by
$R$ is continuous ([[lem-vector-operations-are-continuous-in-a-normed-space]]),
so $R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$
([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), hence closed
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]); therefore
$\overline{T(A)}\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a closed subset of a
compact set, hence compact, and $T$ is compact.

**A compact operator is bounded.** If $T$ is compact then the compact set
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is bounded
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]), so there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|Tx\|\le C$ for every $x\in\overline B_X$ and hence $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for
every $x\in X$; thus $T$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). This is a consequence of compactness, not a
hypothesis of the definition.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim:
Let $C$ be a cube of side $\delta>0$ and $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$, with $u_C:=|C|^{-1}\int_Cu$. Expanding the square and using Fubini on the finite cube gives
$$\int_C|u-u_C|^2=\frac1{2|C|}\int_C\int_C|u(x)-u(y)|^2\,dx\,dy.$$
Telescope $u(x)-u(y)$ through the $N$ coordinate changes and use $|\sum_{j=1}^Nz_j|^2\le N\sum_j|z_j|^2$. For the $j$th change, the fundamental theorem of calculus and Cauchy–Schwarz give $|D_j(x,y)|^2\le\delta\int_{\min(x_j,y_j)}^{\max(x_j,y_j)}|\partial_ju|^2$. For fixed values of the other coordinates and fixed $s\in[0,\delta]$, the measure of pairs $(x_j,y_j)$ whose segment contains $s$ is $2s(\delta-s)\le\delta^2/2$; integrating the displayed bound over the cube variables and dividing by $2|C|$ therefore yields the safe estimate
$$\|u-u_C\|_{L^2(C)}^2\le N\delta^2\sum_{j=1}^N\|\partial_j u\|_{L^2(C)}^2.$$
It applies to complex $u$ because the squared-modulus Cauchy–Schwarz inequality is used.

For $R>0$ and $u\in Q$, the coercive weight gives
$$\int_{|q|>R}|u(q)|^2\,dq\le\frac1{cR^2}\int_{|q|>R}c|q|^2|u(q)|^2\,dq\le\frac1{cR^2}\|u\|_Q^2.$$
Thus the $L^2$ tails of the $Q$ unit ball are uniformly small for large $R$.

The estimate of step 1.1 passes to every $u\in Q$: approximate $u$ in the $Q$ norm by elements of $C_c^\infty$ (the defining completion), restrict to $C$, and use [F1] to pass the $L^2$ and derivative limits.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $R$ so the squared tail in step 1.2 is below $\varepsilon^2/16$. For the $Q$ unit ball, [F1] gives $\sum_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2\le\sum_j a_j^{-1}$. Choose an integer $M$ large enough that $\delta:=2R/M$ satisfies $N\delta^2\sum_j a_j^{-1}<\varepsilon^2/16$, and partition $[-R,R]^N$ into the resulting finitely many cubes of side $\delta$. Summing the squared estimates of step 2.1 over these disjoint cubes bounds the total mean-approximation error by $N\delta^2\sum_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2<\varepsilon^2/16$. The squared error outside $[-R,R]^N$ is the tail from step 1.2; thus replacing $u$ on each cube by its mean and setting it to zero outside the large cube has total squared $L^2$ error below $\varepsilon^2/8$, hence norm error below $\varepsilon/2$.

For the finite partition in step 3.1, the piecewise-constant mean function $m_u$ satisfies $\|m_u\|_2^2=\sum_C|C||u_C|^2\le\sum_C\|u\|_{L^2(C)}^2\le\|u\|_2^2\le1$ by Cauchy--Schwarz [F3]. Thus each mean coordinate has modulus at most $|C|^{-1/2}$, so the vectors of means lie in a bounded box in a finite-dimensional complex coordinate space. Subdivide its real-and-imaginary coordinates into finitely many boxes of sufficiently small side length so that the associated piecewise-constant functions approximate every mean vector to $L^2$ error below $\varepsilon/2$. Combining with step 3.1 gives a finite $\varepsilon$-net for the image of the $Q$ unit ball. Scaling shows that the image of every bounded $Q$ set is totally bounded.

Let $K$ be the $H_N$ closure of the image of the $Q$ unit ball. It is complete because it is closed in the complete space $H_N$ [F1]. Suppose an open cover of $K$ has no finite subcover. For each $n\ge1$, step 4.1 supplies a finite $2^{-n-2}$-net for the image of the $Q$ unit ball with centers in $H_N$; the corresponding closed balls of radius $2^{-n-1}$ cover its closure $K$. Starting with $C_0=K$, choose the least ball index for which $C_n:=C_{n-1}\cap\overline B(p_n,2^{-n-1})$ has no finite subcover. Such an index exists, since otherwise finitely many finite subcovers would cover $C_{n-1}$. Each $C_n$ is nonempty, closed, nested, and has diameter at most $2^{-n}$. For $m>n$, any point of nonempty $C_m$ lies in both selected balls, so $\|p_m-p_n\|_2\le2^{-m-1}+2^{-n-1}$; hence $(p_n)$ is Cauchy and converges to some $p\in H_N$. Since $C_n$ is nonempty and is contained in both $K$ and $\overline B(p_n,2^{-n-1})$, the distance from $p_n$ to $K$ is at most $2^{-n-1}$. Therefore $\operatorname{dist}(p,K)\le\|p-p_n\|_2+2^{-n-1}\to0$; closedness of $K$ gives $p\in K$. For fixed $n$ and every $m>n$, nonempty $C_m\subseteq C_n$ has a point $y\in C_m$ with $\|p_m-y\|_2\le2^{-m-1}$. Thus there are points of $C_n$ arbitrarily close to $p$, and closedness gives $p\in C_n$. An open set of the cover containing $p$ contains $K\cap B(p,r)$ for some $r>0$; for large $n$, $\operatorname{diam}(C_n)<r$, so that one open set covers $C_n$, a contradiction. Thus $K$ is compact. All recursive ball choices are least admissible indices in finite lists.
Step 5.1 proves that the closed-unit-ball image under $J$ has compact closure; applying the equivalent criterion in [F2] to the linear inclusion proves that $J:Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ is compact.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $N\ge1$ be finite and let $C$ be a real symmetric positive-semidefinite $N\times N$ matrix; positive-semidefinite means $u^{\mathsf T}Cu\ge0$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^N$. The centered multivariate normal Borel probability law with covariance $C$ is $\gamma_C:=N_N(0,C)$ as defined by [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: every linear projection $q\mapsto u^{\mathsf T}q$ has scalar normal law $N(0,u^{\mathsf T}Cu)$, and the law exists even when $C$ is singular. Here $N(0,\sigma^2)$ is the law specified in [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], with density $e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ for the standard case.

Let $U:\mathbb R^N\to[0,\infty)$ be a real homogeneous quartic polynomial, meaning $U$ is a polynomial and $U(sq)=s^4U(q)$ for all $s\in\mathbb R$ and $q\in\mathbb R^N$. For a coupling $\lambda\ge0$, define the partition integral and its weighted measure by

$$Z_{C,U}(\lambda):=\int_{\mathbb R^N}e^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q),\qquad \nu_{C,U,\lambda}(A):=\int_Ae^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q)$$

for Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R^N$. Whenever $0<Z_{C,U}(\lambda)<\infty$, the **finite Euclidean interacting measure** is the Borel probability measure

$$d\mu_{C,U,\lambda}(q):=Z_{C,U}(\lambda)^{-1}e^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q).$$

For a polynomial $P:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R$ with finite integral, write $\langle P\rangle_{C,U,\lambda}:=\int P\,d\mu_{C,U,\lambda}$. The exact supplier [[thm-qft-finite-euclidean-polynomial-measure]] proves that $Z_{C,U}(\lambda)$ is positive and finite and that every polynomial insertion is integrable. This is a Borel measure on finite-dimensional $\mathbb R^N$; it is not a measure on distributions on continuum Euclidean spacetime and does not by itself assert reflection positivity or reconstruction of a continuum field.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $N\ge1$ be finite, let $C$ be a real symmetric positive-semidefinite $N\times N$ covariance matrix, and let $Q\sim\gamma_C=N_N(0,C)$ be the law of [[def-qft-finite-euclidean-interacting-measure]]. For $k\ge0$ and vectors $u_1,\ldots,u_k\in\mathbb R^N$, every product $\prod_{j=1}^k(u_j^{\mathsf T}Q)$ is integrable. For $k=0$ its expectation is $1$. If $k$ is odd, its expectation is $0$; if $k=2m$, then

$$\mathbb E\!\left[\prod_{j=1}^{2m}u_j^{\mathsf T}Q\right]=\sum_{\pi\in\operatorname{Pair}(2m)}\prod_{\{a,b\}\in\pi}u_a^{\mathsf T}Cu_b,$$

where $\operatorname{Pair}(2m)$ is the finite set of partitions of $\{1,\ldots,2m\}$ into unordered two-element subsets. Thus every polynomial in $Q$ has a finite absolute moment, computed by finitely many covariance pairings.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and

derivations.claim: Since $U(q)\ge0$ and $\lambda\ge0$, [F5] gives $0<\exp(-\lambda U(q))\le1$ for every $q$, so $Z(\lambda)\le1$. Since $\gamma_C$ is a probability measure, not all $E_n$ can have measure zero: otherwise countable subadditivity would give $\gamma_C(\mathbb R^N)=0$. Thus some $E_n$ has positive measure, and $Z(\lambda)\ge\gamma_C(E_n)/n>0$.

For any polynomial $P$, [F2] gives $\int|P|\,d\gamma_C<\infty$; since [F5] gives $\exp(-\lambda U)\le1$ and step 1.1 gives $Z(\lambda)>0$, $$\int|P|\,d\mu_\lambda\le Z(\lambda)^{-1}\int|P|\,d\gamma_C<\infty.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, let $Q\sim N_N(0,C)$ be the centered finite-dimensional Gaussian vector of [[lem-qft-finite-gaussian-wick-moments]], and write $C_{jj}=\mathbb E[Q_j^2]\ge0$ for the variance of its $j$th coordinate. For each coordinate $j$ and integer $n\ge0$, its **finite covariance Wick normal power** is the polynomial $:Q_j^n:_C$ defined by the formal generating identity

$$\exp\!\left(tQ_j-\frac12t^2C_{jj}\right)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}:Q_j^n:_C\,\frac{t^n}{n!}.$$

Equivalently,

$$:Q_j^n:_C=n!\sum_{s=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\frac{(-C_{jj}/2)^sQ_j^{n-2s}}{s!(n-2s)!},\qquad :Q_j^4:_C=Q_j^4-6C_{jj}Q_j^2+3C_{jj}^2.$$

This is a finite-dimensional polynomial definition; it does not define a product of unsmeared continuum fields.

Assume Countable Choice. Use the finite data and notation of
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]: $N\ge1$,
$H_N=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, $D_0=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
and $W=V+C_0+1\ge1+c|q|^2$. For $u,v\in D_0$ define
$$a(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int_{\mathbb R^N}(\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv}\,dq+\int_{\mathbb R^N}(W+1)u\overline v\,dq,$$
and $\|u\|_Q:=a(u,u)^{1/2}$. Let $Q$ be the completion of this inner-product
space, constructed as equivalence classes of $\|\cdot\|_Q$-Cauchy sequences.
Then $Q$ is a complex Hilbert space and the map sending a Cauchy class to its
$L^2$ limit is a continuous injective linear map $Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ with
dense image. Each $u\in Q$ has weak derivatives $\partial_j u\in L^2$ and a
weighted function $\sqrt{W+1}\,u\in L^2$, and
$$\|u\|_Q^2=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2.$$
Here $g_j=\partial_j u$ means explicitly that
$\int u\,\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$ for every
$\varphi\in D_0$.

The centered multivariate normal Borel probability law with covariance $C$ is $\gamma_C:=N_N(0,C)$ as defined by [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: every linear projection $q\mapsto u^{\mathsf T}q$ has scalar normal law $N(0,u^{\mathsf T}Cu)$, and the law exists even when $C$ is singular. Here $N(0,\sigma^2)$ is the law specified in [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], with density $e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ for the standard case.

Let $U:\mathbb R^N\to[0,\infty)$ be a real homogeneous quartic polynomial, meaning $U$ is a polynomial and $U(sq)=s^4U(q)$ for all $s\in\mathbb R$ and $q\in\mathbb R^N$. For a coupling $\lambda\ge0$, define the partition integral and its weighted measure by

$$Z_{C,U}(\lambda):=\int_{\mathbb R^N}e^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q),\qquad \nu_{C,U,\lambda}(A):=\int_Ae^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q)$$

for Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R^N$. Whenever $0<Z_{C,U}(\lambda)<\infty$, the **finite Euclidean interacting measure** is the Borel probability measure

$$d\mu_{C,U,\lambda}(q):=Z_{C,U}(\lambda)^{-1}e^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q).$$

For a polynomial $P:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R$ with finite integral, write $\langle P\rangle_{C,U,\lambda}:=\int P\,d\mu_{C,U,\lambda}$. The exact supplier [[thm-qft-finite-euclidean-polynomial-measure]] proves that $Z_{C,U}(\lambda)$ is positive and finite and that every polynomial insertion is integrable. This is a Borel measure on finite-dimensional $\mathbb R^N$; it is not a measure on distributions on continuum Euclidean spacetime and does not by itself assert reflection positivity or reconstruction of a continuum field.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $N\ge1$ be finite, let $C$ be a real symmetric positive-semidefinite $N\times N$ covariance matrix, and let $Q\sim\gamma_C=N_N(0,C)$ be the law of [[def-qft-finite-euclidean-interacting-measure]]. For $k\ge0$ and vectors $u_1,\ldots,u_k\in\mathbb R^N$, every product $\prod_{j=1}^k(u_j^{\mathsf T}Q)$ is integrable. For $k=0$ its expectation is $1$. If $k$ is odd, its expectation is $0$; if $k=2m$, then

$$\mathbb E\!\left[\prod_{j=1}^{2m}u_j^{\mathsf T}Q\right]=\sum_{\pi\in\operatorname{Pair}(2m)}\prod_{\{a,b\}\in\pi}u_a^{\mathsf T}Cu_b,$$

where $\operatorname{Pair}(2m)$ is the finite set of partitions of $\{1,\ldots,2m\}$ into unordered two-element subsets. Thus every polynomial in $Q$ has a finite absolute moment, computed by finitely many covariance pairings.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $N\ge1$ be finite, let $C$ be a real symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance matrix, let $\gamma_C=N_N(0,C)$, let $U:\mathbb R^N\to[0,\infty)$ be a real homogeneous quartic polynomial, and let $\lambda\ge0$. Define $Z(\lambda)=\int e^{-\lambda U}\,d\gamma_C$ and $N_P(\lambda)=\int P e^{-\lambda U}\,d\gamma_C$ for every real polynomial $P$.

Then $0<Z(\lambda)\le1$, and $\mu_\lambda:=Z(\lambda)^{-1}e^{-\lambda U}\gamma_C$ is a Borel probability measure. Every polynomial insertion is integrable under $\mu_\lambda$. For each integer $r\ge0$,

$$Z^{(r)}(\lambda)=(-1)^r\int U^r e^{-\lambda U}\,d\gamma_C,\qquad N_P^{(r)}(\lambda)=(-1)^r\int P U^r e^{-\lambda U}\,d\gamma_C$$

for $\lambda>0$, with continuous right derivatives of every finite order at $\lambda=0$. No continuum field measure is asserted.

Under the hypotheses of [[thm-taylor-schlomilch-roche-remainder]], there are points $\xi_L,\xi_C$ between $a$ and $x$ such that
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_L)}{\iota((n+1)!)}(x-a)^{n+1}$$
and
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_C)}{\iota(n!)}(x-\xi_C)^n(x-a).$$

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

derivations.claim: By [F5], $f(x)=\exp(-x)$ is $C^{M+1}$ and $|f^{(M+1)}(\xi)|=\exp(-\xi)$. Apply [F4] at $x=\lambda U(q)\ge0$; [F6] gives $\exp(-\xi)\le1$. Thus pointwise $$\left|\exp(-\lambda U(q))-\sum_{j=0}^M\frac{(-\lambda U(q))^j}{j!}\right|\le\frac{\lambda^{M+1}U(q)^{M+1}}{(M+1)!}.$$ The case $\lambda U(q)=0$ has zero remainder.

Let $Z_M(\lambda)=\sum_{j=0}^M z_j\lambda^j$ and $A_M(\lambda)=\sum_{j=0}^M a_j(P)\lambda^j$. By the recurrence defining $b_j(P)$, every coefficient through degree $M$ in $A_M(\lambda)-\left(\sum_{j=0}^M b_j(P)\lambda^j\right)Z_M(\lambda)$ is zero, because $z_0=1$. The remaining polynomial terms have degree at least $M+1$, so their absolute value is bounded by a finite constant times $\lambda^{M+1}$ on $0\le\lambda\le1$.

Integrate the inequality in step 1.1 against $\gamma_C$ to obtain the stated partition-function expansion and bound. Multiply the same pointwise inequality by $|P(q)|$ and integrate to obtain the numerator expansion and bound. Every right-hand expectation is finite by [F2].

On $0\le\lambda\le1$, the polynomial $B_M(\lambda)=\sum_{j=0}^M b_j(P)\lambda^j$ is bounded. Using the remainder bounds in step 2.1 and the polynomial identity in step 1.2 therefore gives $|N_P(\lambda)-B_M(\lambda)Z(\lambda)|\le K_M\lambda^{M+1}$ for some finite $K_M$. As $\lambda\downarrow0$, $\exp(-\lambda U(q))\to1$ pointwise and $0<\exp(-\lambda U(q))\le1$ by [F6], so [F3] gives $Z(\lambda)\to Z(0)=1$. Choose $\delta>0$ such that $Z(\lambda)\ge1/2$ for $0\le\lambda<\delta$. Dividing by $Z(\lambda)$ yields $|\langle P\rangle_\lambda-B_M(\lambda)|\le2K_M\lambda^{M+1}$ there. Finally, [F2] writes every coefficient moment as a finite covariance-pairing sum; no limit in $M$ was taken.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $N\ge1$ be finite and let $C$ be a real symmetric positive-semidefinite $N\times N$ matrix; positive-semidefinite means $u^{\mathsf T}Cu\ge0$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^N$. The centered multivariate normal Borel probability law with covariance $C$ is $\gamma_C:=N_N(0,C)$ as defined by [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: every linear projection $q\mapsto u^{\mathsf T}q$ has scalar normal law $N(0,u^{\mathsf T}Cu)$, and the law exists even when $C$ is singular. Here $N(0,\sigma^2)$ is the law specified in [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], with density $e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ for the standard case.

Let $U:\mathbb R^N\to[0,\infty)$ be a real homogeneous quartic polynomial, meaning $U$ is a polynomial and $U(sq)=s^4U(q)$ for all $s\in\mathbb R$ and $q\in\mathbb R^N$. For a coupling $\lambda\ge0$, define the partition integral and its weighted measure by

$$Z_{C,U}(\lambda):=\int_{\mathbb R^N}e^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q),\qquad \nu_{C,U,\lambda}(A):=\int_Ae^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q)$$

for Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R^N$. Whenever $0<Z_{C,U}(\lambda)<\infty$, the **finite Euclidean interacting measure** is the Borel probability measure

$$d\mu_{C,U,\lambda}(q):=Z_{C,U}(\lambda)^{-1}e^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q).$$

For a polynomial $P:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R$ with finite integral, write $\langle P\rangle_{C,U,\lambda}:=\int P\,d\mu_{C,U,\lambda}$. The exact supplier [[thm-qft-finite-euclidean-polynomial-measure]] proves that $Z_{C,U}(\lambda)$ is positive and finite and that every polynomial insertion is integrable. This is a Borel measure on finite-dimensional $\mathbb R^N$; it is not a measure on distributions on continuum Euclidean spacetime and does not by itself assert reflection positivity or reconstruction of a continuum field.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Let $k$ be a nonnegative integer, and suppose $\mathbb E|X|^k<\infty$, with $|X|^0=1$. Then $\varphi_X\in C^k(\mathbb R)$ and $$\varphi_X^{(j)}(t)=\mathbb E[(iX)^j e^{itX}],\qquad 0\le j\le k.$$ No converse is asserted.

Let $1\le p,q,r\le\infty$ satisfy

$$\frac1r=\frac1p+\frac1q,$$

with the convention $1/\infty=0$. If $f$ and $g$ lie in the corresponding
measurable-function spaces ($\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ or $L^\infty(\mu)$ according to
whether the exponent is finite or infinite), then $fg$ lies in the
corresponding space for $r$ and

$$\|fg\|_r\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Let $I$ and $J$ be intervals, possibly open at finite or infinite singular ends, and let $\phi:I\to J$ be a monotone differentiable surjection. Assume $\phi'$ is locally Riemann integrable and the proper change-of-variable hypotheses hold on every compact truncation. If $f$ is locally Riemann integrable on $J$, then
$$\int_J f(x)\,dx\quad\text{and}\quad\int_I f(\phi(t))|\phi'(t)|\,dt$$
converge simultaneously and, when convergent, are equal. At several singular ends this assertion is applied separately to the corresponding ends; orientation is retained for decreasing parametrizations.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

derivations.claim: Let $Z\sim N(0,1)$. For an integer $k\ge0$, choose an integer $r$ with $2r\ge k$. On $|x|\ge1$, [F7] gives $e^{x^2/4}\ge (x^2/4)^r/r!$, so $|x|^ke^{-x^2/2}\le 4^rr!e^{-x^2/4}$. The right side is integrable by [F6], and the integrand is bounded on $[-1,1]$. Since [F2] represents any scalar $N(0,v)$ as $\sqrt v Z$ with $\sqrt v$ supplied by [F8], every scalar normal has finite absolute moments of every integer order, including the degenerate $v=0$ case.

For fixed $k\ge1$, define $T_k(u_1,\ldots,u_k):=\mathbb E\prod_{j=1}^k(u_j^{\mathsf T}Q)$. Each projection has a finite $k$th absolute moment by step 1.1 and [F1]. Applying [F5] successively shows the product is integrable. Linearity of each scalar projection and of the integral makes $T_k$ a symmetric $k$-linear form. The law exists under the stated Choice hypothesis [A1]. Since every polynomial is a finite linear combination of coordinate monomials, the triangle inequality also gives every polynomial a finite absolute moment.

On the diagonal, $T_k(u,\ldots,u)=\mathbb E[(u^{\mathsf T}Q)^k]$. Put $v=u^{\mathsf T}Cu\ge0$. By [F1], $u^{\mathsf T}Q\sim N(0,v)$, so [F3] gives its characteristic function $e^{-vt^2/2}$. At zero, [F4] gives $\varphi^{(k)}(0)=i^k\mathbb E[(u^{\mathsf T}Q)^k]$; extracting the $t^k$ coefficient of $e^{-vt^2/2}$ and dividing by $i^k$ yields zero for odd $k$, and for $k=2m$ gives $$T_{2m}(u,\ldots,u)=\frac{(2m)!}{2^m m!}v^m=(2m-1)!!\,(u^{\mathsf T}Cu)^m.$$ The identity also holds for $v=0$, when the projected law is the point mass at zero.

For even $k=2m$, define $W_{2m}(u_1,\ldots,u_{2m})$ by the pairing sum in the Statement; for odd $k$, define $W_k=0$. This is a symmetric $k$-linear form. On the diagonal, every pairing contributes $(u^{\mathsf T}Cu)^m$, and there are $(2m-1)!!$ pairings: pair index $1$ with one of $2m-1$ indices and repeat on the remaining $2m-2$. Hence $W_k(u,\ldots,u)=T_k(u,\ldots,u)$ by step 3.1, also for odd $k$.

For $k\ge1$, two symmetric $k$-linear forms agreeing on every diagonal agree everywhere. Indeed, for their difference $A$, expand $$\sum_{\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}^k}\left(\prod_{j=1}^k\varepsilon_j\right)A\!\left(\sum_i\varepsilon_i u_i,\ldots,\sum_i\varepsilon_i u_i\right).$$ In the multilinear expansion, the sum over signs cancels every term unless each label $1,\ldots,k$ occurs an odd number of times among the $k$ slots. Thus every surviving term uses each label once; symmetry makes all $k!$ such terms equal to $A(u_1,\ldots,u_k)$, and the sign sum is $2^k k!A(u_1,\ldots,u_k)$. Since the diagonal of $A=T_k-W_k$ vanishes by step 4.1, this sum is zero and $T_k=W_k$. For $k=0$, the empty product has expectation one and $\operatorname{Pair}(0)$ contains just the empty pairing, whose empty product is one, so the formula also holds.

citations.quote:
Let $d\ge1$, $X=\mathbb R^d$, and $n\ge1$. Write
$\mathcal D(X^n)=C_c^\infty(X^n;\mathbb C)$ for the complex test-function
space of smooth compactly supported functions
([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]), with its LF topology
([[def-test-function-topology]]). The convergence criterion used below is
that convergent test sequences have one common compact support and converge
uniformly with every derivative
([[thm-sequential-convergence-in-test-function-space]]). Here $C^\infty$
means every coordinate derivative exists and is continuous
([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]). All integrals are
compact Riemann integrals: each integrand is continuous with compact support,
so restrict it to a compact rectangle and apply
[[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]]. Let
$\mathcal D_{\mathrm{sym}}(X^n)$ be the subspace of kernels invariant under
every permutation of their $n$ $X$-variables. Fields are real smooth
configurations $\phi\in C^\infty(X;\mathbb R)$. For an integer $N\ge0$
and a finite family
$f_0\in\mathbb C$, $f_n\in\mathcal D_{\mathrm{sym}}(X^n)$ for
$1\le n\le N$, define
$$ F_f(\phi)=f_0+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\int_{X^n}f_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\prod_{j=1}^{n}\phi(x_j)\,dx_1\cdots dx_n. $$
The pairing is complex-bilinear, with no conjugation on the kernel or field.
An element of $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)$ is this finite symmetric
coefficient family, evaluated on fields by $F_f$. Pointwise sums, scalar
multiples, and products again have finite symmetric compactly supported
coefficient families: for products, expand the two finite sums and
symmetrize each tensor product $f_m\otimes g_n$. Thus these elements form
an algebra; the product-integral identity follows from Riemann Fubini on a
rectangle containing the compact supports
([[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]]).

For $k=0$, set $F_f^{(0)}(\phi)=F_f(\phi)$. For $1\le k\le N$,
the $k$-th functional derivative kernel assigned to this coefficient
family is
$$ F_f^{(k)}(\phi)(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=\sum_{n=k}^{N}\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}\int_{X^{n-k}}f_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\prod_{j=k+1}^{n}\phi(x_j)\,dx_{k+1}\cdots dx_n. $$
For $k>N$ it is zero. Each displayed kernel is smooth, symmetric and compactly supported in its $k$ remaining variables: compactness follows by projection of the finite union of coefficient-kernel supports, and derivatives pass through the finite-compact integrals by [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign-on-a-compact-rectangle]].
In the term $n=k$, the empty integral and empty product mean simply
$f_k(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$.

The scope is exactly smooth compact coefficient kernels. A local functional
whose higher derivative kernels are distributions on a thin diagonal is not
included merely because its field expression is polynomial.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a **distribution** is a continuous complex-linear map $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$, with the test-function topology of [[def-test-function-topology]]. Their vector space is denoted $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. Write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$; the pairing is linear in both arguments, with no conjugation.

Continuity means continuity for that topology: for each $\varepsilon>0$ the set $\{|u(\varphi)|<\varepsilon\}$ contains a zero-neighborhood. By linearity this suffices at every point. Sums and scalar multiples remain continuous and linear, so the indicated collection is a complex vector space. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its test space is zero and its distribution space is zero as well. The finite-order estimate and the sequential criterion are established separately; neither substitutes for continuity in this definition.

Let $X=\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, and let $W\in\mathcal D'(X\times X)$ be
any continuous complex bidistribution. For a real formal parameter $\eta$
and $F,G\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)$, define
$$ F\star_W G=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\eta^k}{k!}\left\langle W^{\otimes k},F^{(k)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(k)}(\phi)\right\rangle . $$
The pairing is over $k$ independent pairs of variables; $W^{\otimes k}$
is formed by iterated distributional tensor products, not by multiplying
distributions at coincident points. The sum is finite because the inputs are
polynomial. It defines an element of
$\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)[\eta]$, and $\star_W$ is associative.
If $W$ is Hermitian in the sense
$\overline{\langle W,\overline g\otimes\overline f\rangle}
=\langle W,f\otimes g\rangle$, then
$(F\star_W G)^*=G^*\star_W F^*$, where $F^*(\phi)=\overline{F(\phi)}$.
For $\ell_f(\phi)=\int_X f(x)\phi(x)\,dx$,
$$ [\ell_f,\ell_g]_{\star_W}=\eta\bigl(W(f,g)-W(g,f)\bigr), \qquad W(f,g):=\langle W,f\otimes g\rangle . $$

derivations.claim: Substituting the derivatives in [F1] into [F3], terms with $k\ge3$ vanish, so the only contributions are $k=0,1,2$.
The $k=0$ term is $\ell_f^2\ell_g^2$. The $k=1$ term is $\eta\langle W,(2\ell_f f)\otimes(2\ell_g g)\rangle =4\eta W(f,g)\ell_f\ell_g$.

The $k=2$ term is $\frac{\eta^2}{2}\langle W^{\otimes2},(2f\otimes f)\otimes (2g\otimes g)\rangle=2\eta^2W(f,g)^2$, because the two independent pairings each equal $W(f,g)$. Adding the three contributions proves the displayed formula.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 includes a zero input; every displayed contraction then vanishes.
Steps 2.1 and 3.1 show that if W(f,g)=0 only the ordinary k=0 product remains.

boundaries.reason: The example has two fixed quadratic inputs; no cardinality-one parameter case is stated.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 shows all k≥3 contractions vanish, and steps 2.1 and 3.1 compute the remaining finite orders.

Example of Explicit regular quadratic Wick star product: Let $f,g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)$, let $\ell_f(\phi)=\int f(x)\phi(x)\,dx$, and let $W$ be any continuous bidistribution. For the regular quadratic functionals $F(\phi)=\ell_f(\phi)^2$ and $G(\phi)=\ell_g(\phi)^2$, the finite contraction formula is $$ F\star_W G =\ell_f^2\ell_g^2+4\eta W(f,g)\ell_f\ell_g+2\eta^2W(f,g)^2. $$ The formula is exact in the formal parameter $\eta$. The displayed finite algebraic/test-contraction computation uses supplied objects rather than choosing elements of a family of nonempty sets; no nonempty-family selection is a separate conclusion.

Example of Explicit regular quadratic Wick star product: Let $f,g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)$, let $\ell_f(\phi)=\int f(x)\phi(x)\,dx$, and let $W$ be any continuous bidistribution. For the regular quadratic functionals $F(\phi)=\ell_f(\phi)^2$ and $G(\phi)=\ell_g(\phi)^2$, the finite contraction formula is $$ F\star_W G =\ell_f^2\ell_g^2+4\eta W(f,g)\ell_f\ell_g+2\eta^2W(f,g)^2. $$ The formula is exact in the formal parameter $\eta$. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, with $n\ge1$. A complex-valued function is smooth if its real and imaginary parts are $C^k$ for every finite $k$, in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Coordinate derivatives act on these two parts separately. We write $\partial^\alpha$ for the multi-index convention there, and $\partial^0\varphi=\varphi$.

The **test-function space** is $\mathcal D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$: its members are smooth functions whose support, the closure in $\Omega$ of their nonzero set, is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Equivalently, the zero extension to $\mathbb R^n$ is smooth with compact support contained in $\Omega$: compactness gives a neighborhood of every boundary point disjoint from the support, where that extension vanishes. Functions are actual functions, not equivalence classes.

Pointwise addition and scalar multiplication make this a complex vector space; the support of a sum lies in the union of the two compact supports. The zero function has empty support. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ there is just the empty function, which is the zero vector. The topology is specified in subsequent definitions. Distribution pairings throughout this page are complex bilinear, with no conjugation on test functions. One may restrict all constructions to real scalars.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. For the fixed-support spaces of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]], let $\mathcal P$ be the set of all seminorms $q:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $q|_{\mathcal D_K}$ is continuous for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. A seminorm means $q(av)=|a|q(v)$ and $q(v+w)\le q(v)+q(w)$.

The **test-function topology** is the topology generated by translated finite intersections of sets $\{\varphi:q(\varphi)<\varepsilon\}$, where $q\in\mathcal P$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Equivalently it is the finest locally convex topology making every inclusion $\mathcal D_K\hookrightarrow\mathcal D(\Omega)$ continuous; the universal-property lemma below proves this equivalence and the topology assertions. This is the locally convex inductive-limit or **LF topology**, not the unrestricted final topology of arbitrary spaces.

For precision, a locally convex topology here is a vector topology generated by a family of seminorms, and boundedness means absorption by every zero-neighborhood: for each such neighborhood $U$ there is $t>0$ with $B\subseteq tU$. Finite intersections may be empty, giving the whole space. When $\Omega$ is empty there is only the zero vector and its unique topology. No convergence criterion for sequences is used in the definition; that criterion will be a theorem.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a **distribution** is a continuous complex-linear map $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$, with the test-function topology of [[def-test-function-topology]]. Their vector space is denoted $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. Write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$; the pairing is linear in both arguments, with no conjugation.

Continuity means continuity for that topology: for each $\varepsilon>0$ the set $\{|u(\varphi)|<\varepsilon\}$ contains a zero-neighborhood. By linearity this suffices at every point. Sums and scalar multiples remain continuous and linear, so the indicated collection is a complex vector space. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its test space is zero and its distribution space is zero as well. The finite-order estimate and the sequential criterion are established separately; neither substitutes for continuity in this definition.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

For $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$, say $u$ **vanishes on** an open $V\subseteq\Omega$ if its restriction to $V$ is zero. Let $Z$ be the union of all such open sets. Locality in [[thm-distributions-form-a-sheaf]] shows that $u|_Z=0$, since these sets cover $Z$ and all its restrictions are zero. Thus $Z$ is the largest vanishing open set. The **support** is the relatively closed set $\operatorname{supp}u=\Omega\setminus Z$.

In particular $\operatorname{supp}u=\varnothing$ if and only if $u=0$: emptiness gives $Z=\Omega$ and vanishing there, while the zero distribution vanishes everywhere. If a test $\varphi$ vanishes on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}u$, its compact support is contained in $Z$, so $u(\varphi)=0$ by restriction. Consequently two tests agreeing on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}u$ have equal pairings with $u$, by applying this fact to their difference.

**Compactly supported** means that $\operatorname{supp}u$ is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Relative closedness in an arbitrary open domain is not by itself compactness or closedness in the ambient Euclidean space. On the empty domain support is empty. The union and locality argument require no selection of vanishing neighborhoods and no choice axiom.

derivations.claim: Define $d_X:X\to X\times X$ by $d_X(x)=(x,x)$. For $\Psi\in\mathcal D(X\times X)$, the diagonal restriction $x\mapsto\Psi(d_X(x))$ has first derivatives $\partial_{x_j}\Psi(x,x)+\partial_{y_j}\Psi(x,x)$ by [F2]. Iterating this formula on the smooth partial derivatives of $\Psi$ shows the restriction has continuous derivatives of every order, so it is smooth. Its support is contained in the first-coordinate projection of $\operatorname{supp}\Psi$, which is compact as a continuous image of a compact set. Choose a compact rectangle containing that projection; [F3] makes the displayed integral well defined.

The assignment is complex-linear. Fix a nonempty compact $K\subseteq X\times X$ and a compact rectangle $R\subseteq X$ containing its first-coordinate projection. For every $\Psi$ supported in $K$, $$ |\langle\delta_{\Delta_X},\Psi\rangle| \le \operatorname{vol}(R)\sup_{(x,y)\in K}|\Psi(x,y)|. $$ Thus the seminorm $q(\Psi)=|\langle\delta_{\Delta_X},\Psi\rangle|$ is continuous on every fixed-support test space. By the LF topology definition in [F1], such seminorms are continuous on $\mathcal D(X\times X)$. Therefore $\delta_{\Delta_X}\in\mathcal D'(X\times X)$.

If an open set $U\subseteq X\times X$ is disjoint from $\Delta_X$, then every test supported in $U$ vanishes at every $(x,x)$. Its pairing with $\delta_{\Delta_X}$ is zero, so [F5] gives $\operatorname{supp}\delta_{\Delta_X}\subseteq\Delta_X$.

Fix $(x_0,x_0)\in\Delta_X$ and any open neighborhood $U$ of this point. There is a ball $B$ about $x_0$ with $\overline B\times\overline B\subseteq U$. By [F4] choose $h\in\mathcal D(X)$ with $h\ge0$, $h(x_0)=1$, and support in $B$. The product test $\Psi(x,y)=h(x)h(y)$ is supported in $U$, and $\langle\delta_{\Delta_X},\Psi\rangle=\int_X h(x)^2\,d^4x>0$, since continuity makes $h$ positive on a ball about $x_0$. Thus $\delta_{\Delta_X}$ does not vanish on any neighborhood of $(x_0,x_0)$, so $(x_0,x_0)\in\operatorname{supp}\delta_{\Delta_X}$ by [F5]. Since the point was arbitrary, $\Delta_X\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\delta_{\Delta_X}$. Together with step 3.1 this gives equality.

For every $\Psi$, the diagonal restrictions of $\Psi(x,y)$ and $\Psi(y,x)$ coincide, so the distribution is symmetric. The diagonal has empty interior: every product neighborhood of a point $(x,x)$ contains $(x,y)$ with $y\ne x$. If a smooth function supported on the diagonal were nonzero at a point, continuity would make it nonzero on an open neighborhood, contradicting empty interior. Therefore every such smooth function is zero.
