Let $d\ge1$, $X=\mathbb R^d$, and $n\ge1$. Write
$\mathcal D(X^n)=C_c^\infty(X^n;\mathbb C)$ for the complex test-function
space of smooth compactly supported functions
([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]), with its LF topology
([[def-test-function-topology]]). The convergence criterion used below is
that convergent test sequences have one common compact support and converge
uniformly with every derivative
([[thm-sequential-convergence-in-test-function-space]]). Here $C^\infty$
means every coordinate derivative exists and is continuous
([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]). All integrals are
compact Riemann integrals: each integrand is continuous with compact support,
so restrict it to a compact rectangle and apply
[[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]]. Let
$\mathcal D_{\mathrm{sym}}(X^n)$ be the subspace of kernels invariant under
every permutation of their $n$ $X$-variables. Fields are real smooth
configurations $\phi\in C^\infty(X;\mathbb R)$. For an integer $N\ge0$
and a finite family
$f_0\in\mathbb C$, $f_n\in\mathcal D_{\mathrm{sym}}(X^n)$ for
$1\le n\le N$, define
$$ F_f(\phi)=f_0+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\int_{X^n}f_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\prod_{j=1}^{n}\phi(x_j)\,dx_1\cdots dx_n. $$
The pairing is complex-bilinear, with no conjugation on the kernel or field.
An element of $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)$ is this finite symmetric
coefficient family, evaluated on fields by $F_f$. Pointwise sums, scalar
multiples, and products again have finite symmetric compactly supported
coefficient families: for products, expand the two finite sums and
symmetrize each tensor product $f_m\otimes g_n$. Thus these elements form
an algebra; the product-integral identity follows from Riemann Fubini on a
rectangle containing the compact supports
([[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]]).

For $k=0$, set $F_f^{(0)}(\phi)=F_f(\phi)$. For $1\le k\le N$,
the $k$-th functional derivative kernel assigned to this coefficient
family is
$$ F_f^{(k)}(\phi)(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=\sum_{n=k}^{N}\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}\int_{X^{n-k}}f_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\prod_{j=k+1}^{n}\phi(x_j)\,dx_{k+1}\cdots dx_n. $$
For $k>N$ it is zero. Each displayed kernel is smooth, symmetric and compactly supported in its $k$ remaining variables: compactness follows by projection of the finite union of coefficient-kernel supports, and derivatives pass through the finite-compact integrals by [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign-on-a-compact-rectangle]].
In the term $n=k$, the empty integral and empty product mean simply
$f_k(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$.

The scope is exactly smooth compact coefficient kernels. A local functional
whose higher derivative kernels are distributions on a thin diagonal is not
included merely because its field expression is polynomial.

Let $d,n\ge1$, $X=\mathbb R^d$, and give
$\mathcal D(X^n)=C_c^\infty(X^n;\mathbb C)$ its LF test-function topology.
The finite linear span of elementary product tests
$$ (x_1,\ldots,x_n)\longmapsto\prod_{j=1}^{n}g_j(x_j),\qquad g_j\in\mathcal D(X), $$
is dense. More precisely, for each $\Phi\in\mathcal D(X^n)$, there is a
sequence of such finite sums whose supports lie in one fixed compact product
and whose derivatives of every multi-index converge uniformly to those of
$\Phi$. Symmetrized finite sums are dense in
$\mathcal D_{\mathrm{sym}}(X^n)$. Consequently the symmetric-kernel
representation in [[def-qft-regular-polynomial-functional-algebra]] is
unique: if a finite symmetric-kernel polynomial vanishes on every real smooth
field, every coefficient kernel vanishes.

For $u\in\mathcal D'(U)$ and $v\in\mathcal D'(V)$ the tensor candidate is a distribution on $U\times V$, uniquely determined by $(u\otimes v)(\varphi\otimes\psi)=u(\varphi)v(\psi)$. Its two iterated pairing orders agree, and $\operatorname{supp}(u\otimes v)=\operatorname{supp}u\times\operatorname{supp}v$. Three-factor pairings associate. Moreover $\partial_x^\alpha(u\otimes v)=(\partial^\alpha u)\otimes v$ and $\partial_y^\beta(u\otimes v)=u\otimes(\partial^\beta v)$. All claims hold in ZF.

Let $r,n\ge1$ be integers, let $X\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ and $Y\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $u\in\mathcal D'(Y)$, and let $F\in C^\infty(X\times Y;\mathbb C)$. Suppose that for each compact $H\subseteq X$ there is compact $K\subseteq Y$ with $\operatorname{supp}_y F(x,\cdot)\subseteq K$ for every $x\in H$. Then $a(x)=u(F(x,\cdot))$ is smooth and $\partial_x^\alpha a(x)=u(\partial_x^\alpha F(x,\cdot))$.

Assume Countable Choice for the following integral clause. For every compact measurable $E\subseteq X$, the function $G(y)=\int_E F(x,y)\,dx$ is a test in $\mathcal D(Y)$, its $y$ derivatives pass under the integral, and $u(G)=\int_E u(F(x,\cdot))\,dx$. Integrals here are Lebesgue integrals. The smoothness and differentiation claims hold in ZF; Countable Choice supplies Lebesgue measure for the integral clause. Neither clause uses tensor products or distributional mollification.

Let $X=\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, and let $W\in\mathcal D'(X\times X)$ be
any continuous complex bidistribution. For a real formal parameter $\eta$
and $F,G\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)$, define
$$ F\star_W G=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\eta^k}{k!}\left\langle W^{\otimes k},F^{(k)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(k)}(\phi)\right\rangle . $$
The pairing is over $k$ independent pairs of variables; $W^{\otimes k}$
is formed by iterated distributional tensor products, not by multiplying
distributions at coincident points. The sum is finite because the inputs are
polynomial. It defines an element of
$\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)[\eta]$, and $\star_W$ is associative.
If $W$ is Hermitian in the sense
$\overline{\langle W,\overline g\otimes\overline f\rangle}
=\langle W,f\otimes g\rangle$, then
$(F\star_W G)^*=G^*\star_W F^*$, where $F^*(\phi)=\overline{F(\phi)}$.
For $\ell_f(\phi)=\int_X f(x)\phi(x)\,dx$,
$$ [\ell_f,\ell_g]_{\star_W}=\eta\bigl(W(f,g)-W(g,f)\bigr), \qquad W(f,g):=\langle W,f\otimes g\rangle . $$

derivations.claim: For a homogeneous coefficient of degree $m$, one application of $\Gamma_K$ contracts two derivative variables against $K$, leaving a smooth compact kernel by [F1]–[F3]. It lowers the polynomial degree by two; therefore $\Gamma_K^jF=0$ when $2j>\deg F$, so $\alpha_KF$ is a finite sum in $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)[\eta]$. The same finite argument defines $\alpha_{-K}$.

On the auxiliary formal generator $E_f(s,\phi)=\exp(s\ell_f(\phi))$, each second derivative contracts to $K(f,f)E_f$. Coefficientwise this gives $$ \alpha_KE_f(s)=\exp\!\left(\frac{\eta s^2}{2}K(f,f)\right)E_f(s). $$ The exponential is formal; each coefficient used below involves only finitely many derivatives.

On two auxiliary generators, the left side of the asserted identity has the scalar factor $$ \exp\!\left(\eta stW(f,g)+\frac{\eta}{2}K(sf+tg,sf+tg)\right). $$ The right side has factor $$ \exp\!\left(\frac{\eta s^2}{2}K(f,f)+\frac{\eta t^2}{2}K(g,g)+\eta st(W+K)(f,g)\right). $$ Symmetry and bilinearity of $K$ make these exponents equal.

Comparing coefficients of $s,t$ in step 3.1 first proves the identity for powers of linear functionals. Replacing $f$ by $\sum_j s_jf_j$ and comparing the coefficient of $s_1\cdots s_m$, and doing the same independently for $g$, proves it for every finite product of distinct linear functionals. Each fixed coefficient is continuous in its smooth compact kernels by [F2]–[F4]; the density in [F1] therefore extends the identity to all $F,G\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)$. For an input of degree $d$, the coefficient of $\Gamma_K^r$ in $\alpha_K\alpha_{-K}$ is multiplied by $\sum_{j=0}^r\binom rj(-1)^{r-j}=(1-1)^r$, which is zero for $r>0$ and one for $r=0$. The sums are finite because $\Gamma_K$ lowers degree by two, so $\alpha_K\alpha_{-K}=I$; the reverse composition is identical.

Statement of Regular normal-ordering change is an exact star isomorphism: Let $W\in\mathcal D'(X\times X)$, $X=\mathbb R^d$, and let $K\in\mathcal D'(X\times X)$ be symmetric under interchange of its variables. If $F$ and $G$ have degrees $m$ and $n$, then $F^{(k)}=0$ for $k>m$ and $G^{(k)}=0$ for $k>n$. Hence only $0\le k\le\min(m,n)$ contribute; the sum is finite, independent of a coefficient presentation by [F1], and belongs to $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)[\eta]$.

For $f\in\mathcal D(X)$, use the auxiliary formal generator $E_f(s,\phi)=\exp(s\ell_f(\phi))$; it is a generating series and is not asserted to be an element of $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)$. Its $k$-th derivative in $\phi$ is $s^k f^{\otimes k}E_f$. Substitution into the finite coefficient formula gives, coefficientwise in $s,t,\eta$, $$ E_f(s)\star_W E_g(t)=\exp\!\bigl(\eta st W(f,g)\bigr)E_{sf+tg}. $$

Applying step 2.2 twice, both bracketings of three generators equal $$ \exp\!\bigl(\eta(stW(f,g)+srW(f,h)+trW(g,h))\bigr)E_{sf+tg+rh}, $$ by bilinearity of $W$. Comparing coefficients of $s,t,r$ proves associativity for powers of linear functionals. For distinct tests in one input, replace $f$ by $\sum_{j=1}^m s_jf_j$ in the same coefficientwise identity; its coefficient of $s_1\cdots s_m$ is the symmetrized product $\ell_{f_1}\cdots\ell_{f_m}$. Make this substitution independently in each of the three inputs. Thus the associator vanishes for every symmetrized elementary tensor-product coefficient kernel and for their finite sums.

By [F1], symmetrized finite product-test kernels are dense in every coefficient test space. Each fixed coefficient of the associator is a finite sum of compositions of continuous tensor-distribution pairings from [F2] and smooth parameter pairings from [F3], hence is continuous in the coefficient kernels. Passing to the limits of the product-test approximants from the preceding coefficient comparison proves associativity for arbitrary $F,G,H\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)$.

For linear functionals only $k=0,1$ occur. The $k=0$ term cancels in the commutator, while the $k=1$ terms are $\eta W(f,g)$ and $\eta W(g,f)$; this gives the displayed commutator. If $W$ is Hermitian, conjugating each finite contraction reverses its two variable groups and gives $(F\star_W G)^*=G^*\star_W F^*$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field. Write

$$\mathcal B(X,Y) := \{T:X\to Y : T \text{ is a bounded linear operator}\}.$$

This is a subspace of the vector space $\mathcal L(X,Y)$ of
[[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]], with the same pointwise operations:

$$(S+T)(x) := Sx+Tx,\qquad (\lambda T)(x) := \lambda\,Tx.$$

If $X=Y$, write

$$\mathcal B(X) := \mathcal B(X,X).$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].
For every $z\in\mathbb C$, the series $\sum z^n/n!$ converges absolutely.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

derivations.claim: If $a=b$, every integral is zero, $U_0=I$, and $U_n=0$ for $n\ge1$; all evolution and unitarity claims follow, while no $c<d$ lies in $I$, so the separated-support clause has no instance. Assume henceforth $a<b$. Suppose $U_n(r,s)\psi$ is continuous in $r$. For fixed $r_0$, $$ \|V(r)U_n(r,s)\psi-V(r_0)U_n(r_0,s)\psi\| \le M\|U_n(r,s)\psi-U_n(r_0,s)\psi\| +\|(V(r)-V(r_0))U_n(r_0,s)\psi\|, $$ which tends to zero by strong continuity of $V$. Thus the recursive integrand is continuous. Its vector-valued Riemann integral exists: uniform continuity makes the tagged sums for the explicit equal-mesh partitions Cauchy; completeness of $\mathcal H$ gives their limit. Uniform continuity also bounds the difference between sums on any two sufficiently fine tagged partitions by a quantity tending to zero, so this limit is independent of the partitions and tags. The tagged-sum triangle inequality, followed by the scalar Riemann-sum limit from [F5], gives $\|\int f\|\le\int\|f\|$. The integral as a function of its upper endpoint is continuous, since its increment has norm at most the interval length times the supremum of the continuous integrand; this supremum is finite by [F1]. This proves strong continuity of $U_{n+1}(\cdot,s)\psi$ and closes the induction.

The identity operator has norm at most one, including when $\mathcal H=\{0\}$. The integral estimate then gives inductively $$ \|U_{n+1}(t,s)\| \le\int_{\min(s,t)}^{\max(s,t)}M\frac{M^n|r-s|^n}{n!}\,dr =\frac{M^{n+1}|t-s|^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}. $$ This proves the factorial bound for both orientations of the integral.

The bound in step 2.1 makes $\sum z^nU_n(t,s)$ absolutely and uniformly convergent in operator norm on $I^2$, with total norm at most $\sum_{n\ge0}(|z|M(b-a))^n/n!=e^{|z|M(b-a)}$ by [F4]. The recursion and this uniform bound permit termwise integration on each vector: the norm of the integral of a uniform tail is at most $(b-a)$ times its supremum norm, which tends to zero. This gives the displayed integral equation.

If $X(t,s)$ and $Y(t,s)$ are two strongly continuous solutions, then for fixed $\psi$, $D(t)=\|(X(t,s)-Y(t,s))\psi\|$ is bounded on $I$ by [F3] and is Riemann integrable by [F5]. It satisfies $D(t)\le |z|M\int_{\min(s,t)}^{\max(s,t)}D(r)\,dr$. Repeated substitution gives an $n$-fold integral over the ordered simplex between $s$ and $t$; induction using [F5] and the polynomial derivative rule [F6] evaluates its volume as $|t-s|^n/n!$, so $$ D(t)\le C_\psi\frac{(|z|M|t-s|)^n}{n!} $$ with $C_\psi=\sup_{r\in I}D(r)<\infty$. The right side tends to zero, so the solution is unique. To prove composition, split the equation for $U_z(t,s)$ at $r$: for $t\ge r$, it reads $U_z(t,s)=U_z(r,s)-iz\int_r^tV(q)U_z(q,s)\,dq$. Multiplying the equation for $U_z(t,r)$ on the right by $U_z(r,s)$ shows $U_z(t,r)U_z(r,s)$ solves this same initial-value equation and has the same value at $t=r$. The uniqueness estimate just proved, with initial time $r$, gives equality; the reversed orientation proves it for $t<r$.

For a continuous vector-valued integrand, the average over a signed interval of length $h$ converges in norm to its value at the base point: the error is bounded by the supremum of its variation on that interval. Taking difference quotients in the integral equation therefore gives $\partial_tU_z(t,s)\psi=-izV(t)U_z(t,s)\psi$. If $u(t)=U_z(t,s)\psi$, then $$ \frac{\|u(t+h)\|^2-\|u(t)\|^2}{h} =2\operatorname{Re}\left\langle u(t),\frac{u(t+h)-u(t)}h\right\rangle +\frac{\|u(t+h)-u(t)\|^2}{h}. $$ The second term tends to zero and the first tends to $2\operatorname{Re}\langle u(t),-izV(t)u(t)\rangle=0$ for real $z$, because self-adjointness makes $\langle u,V(t)u\rangle$ real. Thus $U_z(t,s)$ is an isometry.

For fixed $t$, the reverse integral equation $$ R_t(s)=I_{\mathcal H}+iz\int_s^t V(r)R_t(r)\,dr $$ has a strongly continuous solution by the same recursive construction and uniform bounds established above. Signed difference quotients of its integral, bounded by the supremum variation of the continuous integrand, give $\partial_sR_t(s)=-izV(s)R_t(s)$. The composition law gives $U_z(t,s)=U_z(t,s+h)U_z(s+h,s)$ for every sufficiently small signed $h$. By the integral equation, $(I-U_z(s+h,s))/h\to izV(s)$ strongly as $h\to0$, while strong continuity gives $U_z(t,s+h)\psi\to U_z(t,s)\psi$ for each $\psi$. Subtracting $U_z(t,s)$ in the composition identity therefore yields $\partial_sU_z(t,s)\psi=izU_z(t,s)V(s)\psi$. For fixed $\psi$, add and subtract $U_z(t,s+h)R_t(s)\psi$ in the difference quotient of $U_z(t,s)R_t(s)\psi$. Strong differentiability of both factors and their local operator bounds show that the product derivative is the sum of the two derivatives. Combining this with the reverse equation for $R_t$ gives $\partial_s(U_z(t,s)R_t(s))=0$. Its value at $s=t$ is $I$, so $U_z(t,s)R_t(s)=I$. The isometry in step 4.2 is therefore surjective and hence unitary.

Let $Y(t)=U_z^{V_1}(t,a)U_z^{V_2}(t,a)$. For each $\psi$, $$ \frac{Y(t+h)\psi-Y(t)\psi}{h} =\frac{U_z^{V_1}(t+h,a)-U_z^{V_1}(t,a)}{h}U_z^{V_2}(t+h,a)\psi +U_z^{V_1}(t,a)\frac{U_z^{V_2}(t+h,a)-U_z^{V_2}(t,a)}{h}\psi. $$ Strong continuity, the local operator bounds, and the differential equations from step 4.2 make the right side converge to the product-rule derivative. Before the later support interval, $U_z^{V_1}(t,a)=I$; after the earlier support interval, $U_z^{V_2}(t,a)$ is constant. Thus on the earlier interval, the gap, and the later interval, this derivative is $\partial_tY=-iz(V_1(t)+V_2(t))Y$, and $Y(a)=I$. Integrating across the three regions and using continuity at their endpoints shows that $Y$ solves the integral equation for $V_1+V_2$. Uniqueness from step 4.1 yields the stated factorization at $b$. Both sides have operator-norm-convergent power series for every $z$. Their equality for all real $z$ forces equality of coefficients: if a first coefficient differed, divide the difference by its least power of $z$ and let real $z\to0$, contradicting the equality.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$, put $U=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and use the continuous complex-linear test-function pairing of [[def-distribution]]. For $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$ and $\rho>0$, define its dilation at the origin by

$$\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle:=\rho^{-n}\langle t,\varphi(\cdot/\rho)\rangle,\qquad \varphi\in\mathcal D(U).$$

Positive dilations preserve $U$, so the displayed pairing is defined for every test function in $\mathcal D(U)$. If $t$ is the regular distribution induced by a locally integrable function $g$, change of variables gives $\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle=\int_U g(\rho x)\varphi(x)\,dx$.

Convergence $s_\rho\to0$ in $\mathcal D'(U)$ as $\rho\downarrow0$ means $\langle s_\rho,\varphi\rangle\to0$ for every fixed $\varphi\in\mathcal D(U)$. The **scaling degree at the origin** is

This map is continuous. If $E\subseteq S^{n-1}$ is Borel, then

$$\{r\omega:\omega\in E,\ 0<r\le1\}=\Phi^{-1}((0,1]\times E)$$

$$\sigma(E):=n\,\lambda_n(\{r\omega : \omega \in E,\ 0<r\le 1\}).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box

For $0<\varepsilon<1/(4\sqrt n)$ the box $Q=\prod_{i=1}^n(x_{0,i}-\varepsilon,x_{0,i}+\varepsilon)$ lies in $K$, since $|x-x_0|<\sqrt n\varepsilon<1/4$ on $Q$. For every $\omega>\delta$, $\rho^\omega(G_\delta)_\rho=\rho^{\omega-\delta}G_\delta\to0$. For every $\omega<\delta$, the nonnegative annular test $\varphi$ from step 1.1 has positive pairing with $G_\delta$. Therefore $\rho^\omega\langle(G_\delta)_\rho,\varphi\rangle=\rho^{\omega-\delta}\langle G_\delta,\varphi\rangle$ does not tend to zero. Hence $\operatorname{sd}_0(G_\delta)=\delta$, and its restriction to $U$ is $t_\delta$.

Since $\delta<n$, the subcritical uniqueness clause [F8] applies to $t_\delta$ and the extension $G_\delta$ from step 1.1. Thus every extension of $t_\delta$ with scaling degree $\delta$ equals $G_\delta$.

At $\delta=n$, [F1] gives $\langle(t_n)_\rho,\varphi\rangle=\rho^{-n}\langle t_n,\varphi\rangle$. Thus every $\omega>n$ gives convergence to zero; for $\omega<n$, the nonnegative annular test from step 1.1 has positive pairing with $t_n$, so the rescaled pairing does not tend to zero. Hence $\operatorname{sd}_0(t_n)=n$. The polar integral is then $\sigma(S^{n-1})\int_0^1r^{-1}\,dr=+\infty$. Then there exists $T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ such that $T|_U=t$ and $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)=\delta$. The result applies to arbitrary distributions with finite real scaling degree; it assumes no smooth kernel or pointwise product representation.

For $a\in\Omega$ and $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$, $\operatorname{supp}u\subseteq\{a\}$ if and only if
$$u=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}c_\alpha\partial^\alpha\delta_a$$
for some finite $m\ge0$ and complex coefficients. The coefficients, with absent higher terms interpreted as zero, are unique. A nonzero such combination has support exactly $\{a\}$; the zero combination has empty support. This holds in ZF.

For $a\in\Omega$, the **Dirac distribution at $a$** is the complex-linear functional $\delta_a(\varphi)=\varphi(a)$ on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, with the bilinear convention of [[def-distribution]]. It is continuous: the seminorm $q(\varphi)=|\varphi(a)|$ restricts on each $\mathcal D_K$ to a seminorm bounded by $p_0$ (and is zero if $a\notin K$), so it is one of the admissible seminorms defining the test topology.

Its derivatives are those of [[def-distributional-derivative]]:
$$\langle\partial^\alpha\delta_a,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\partial^\alpha\varphi(a).$$
They are distributions by that definition; on each fixed-support stage the absolute value is at most $p_{|\alpha|}(\varphi)$. If $a\notin K$ all derivatives of the test vanish at $a$, so the bound has zero left side. For $\alpha=0$ this is $\delta_a$; a first derivative evaluates the negative first derivative of the test. No conjugation and no choice are involved. On the empty open set there is no permitted point $a$, rather than a new Dirac distribution. The sharp order of these distributions requires a test witness and is proved in the assigned example later.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

For $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$, say $u$ **vanishes on** an open $V\subseteq\Omega$ if its restriction to $V$ is zero. Let $Z$ be the union of all such open sets. Locality in [[thm-distributions-form-a-sheaf]] shows that $u|_Z=0$, since these sets cover $Z$ and all its restrictions are zero. Thus $Z$ is the largest vanishing open set. The **support** is the relatively closed set $\operatorname{supp}u=\Omega\setminus Z$.

In particular $\operatorname{supp}u=\varnothing$ if and only if $u=0$: emptiness gives $Z=\Omega$ and vanishing there, while the zero distribution vanishes everywhere. If a test $\varphi$ vanishes on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}u$, its compact support is contained in $Z$, so $u(\varphi)=0$ by restriction. Consequently two tests agreeing on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}u$ have equal pairings with $u$, by applying this fact to their difference.

**Compactly supported** means that $\operatorname{supp}u$ is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Relative closedness in an arbitrary open domain is not by itself compactness or closedness in the ambient Euclidean space. On the empty domain support is empty. The union and locality argument require no selection of vanishing neighborhoods and no choice axiom.

derivations.claim: By [F2], choose $T_0\in\mathcal E_\delta(t)$. For any $T\in\mathcal E_\delta(t)$ the difference $S=T-T_0$ vanishes on every test supported away from $0$, so $\operatorname{supp}S\subseteq\{0\}$ by [F6]. By [F3], $S=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}c_\alpha\partial^\alpha\delta_0$ for some finite $m$.

For $S\ne0$, let $m$ be the largest order with a nonzero coefficient, and choose $\alpha$ of order $m$ with $c_\alpha\ne0$. Choose $\eta\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$ equal to one near $0$ by [F5], and test with $\psi_\alpha(x)=\eta(x)x^\alpha/\alpha!$. The product rule gives $\partial^\beta\psi_\alpha(0)=0$ for all $|\beta|\le m$ except $\beta=\alpha$, where it equals $1$. Consequently $$\langle S_\rho,\psi_\alpha\rangle=(-1)^m c_\alpha\rho^{-n-m}.$$ For every test $\varphi$, [F4] likewise gives $\langle S_\rho,\varphi\rangle=\sum_\beta c_\beta(-1)^{|\beta|}\rho^{-n-|\beta|}\partial^\beta\varphi(0)$. The finite sum tends to zero after multiplication by $\rho^\omega$ for every $\omega>n+m$, while the chosen test prevents convergence to zero for $\omega<n+m$. Hence $\operatorname{sd}_0(S)=n+m$.

Since $T$ and $T_0$ both have degree $\delta$, for every $\omega>\delta$ both $\rho^\omega T_\rho$ and $\rho^\omega(T_0)_\rho$ tend to zero. Thus $\operatorname{sd}_0(S)\le\delta$. Step 2.1 implies that every nonzero coefficient in $S$ has order at most $\lfloor\delta-n\rfloor$; if $\delta<n$, no nonzero $S$ is possible.

Conversely, let $S$ be any finite sum of $\partial^\alpha\delta_0$ with $|\alpha|\le k$ when $\delta\ge n$. Step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{sd}_0(S)\le n+k\le\delta$, and $T_0+S$ still restricts to $t$. Hence $\operatorname{sd}_0(T_0+S)\le\delta$. Restriction to tests supported in $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ gives $\operatorname{sd}_0(T_0+S)\ge\operatorname{sd}_0(t)=\delta$, so equality holds. Uniqueness of the coefficients in [F3] identifies the displayed finite-dimensional affine space. For $\delta=n$, $k=0$, giving only $c\delta_0$.

The topology is generated by the seminorms $p_m$: neighborhoods at zero contain finite intersections of $p_m<\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon>0$. Derivatives are continuous on $K$, so these suprema are finite; for $K=\varnothing$ all suprema are defined as zero and $\mathcal D_K=\{0\}$. The term **fixed-support Fréchet space** refers to this topology and metric. Their agreement and completeness are established by the registered justifier [[lem-fixed-support-test-function-spaces-are-complete]], rather than included as unproved consequences of the name. If $K$ has empty interior, every test supported in $K$ is zero: a nonzero continuous value would have a neighborhood of nonzero values inside $K$.

For every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ with $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ open, the space $\mathcal D_K$ is Hausdorff, locally convex and complete for
$$d(f,g)=\sum_{m=0}^\infty2^{-m-1}\min(1,p_m(f-g)).$$
This metric induces exactly its derivative-seminorm topology. Multiplying the metric by two gives the equivalent convention with weights $2^{-m}$. These assertions require no choice axiom.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice ($\mathrm{DC}$). If a nonempty metric space $X$ is complete, then it is not the union of a sequence of closed sets each having empty interior. Equivalently, the intersection of countably many open dense subsets of $X$ is dense.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Let $X=\mathcal D_K$ with the metric of [F2]. It is nonempty because it contains $0$, and it is complete by [F3]. AC supplies DC by [F4]–[F6], so the Baire theorem [F7] applies. The proof of [F7] also chooses centers for its recursively constructed balls; that countable family of nonempty balls is covered by AC$_\omega$ from [F6] and [F8].

For fixed $\psi\in X$, set $L_\rho(\psi)=\rho^\omega\langle t_\rho,\psi\rangle$. The exponents $\eta$ for which $\rho^\eta t_\rho(\psi)\to0$ for every fixed test form an upward-closed set: if the limit holds at $\eta$, then for $\omega>\eta$ multiply by $\rho^{\omega-\eta}\le1$. Since its infimum is $\delta<\omega$, some such $\eta$ is below $\omega$, and consequently $L_\rho(\psi)\to0$ as $\rho\downarrow0$.

On any compact scale interval $[\epsilon,1]$ with $\epsilon>0$, the tests $\psi(\cdot/\rho)$ have support in one compact subset of $U$ and vary continuously in every derivative seminorm by the chain rule. Continuity of the distribution $t$ therefore makes $\rho\mapsto L_\rho(\psi)$ continuous there. Together with step 1.2 this proves $\sup_{0<\rho\le1}|L_\rho(\psi)|<\infty$ for every $\psi\in X$.

For each positive integer $N$, let $E_N=\{\psi\in X:\sup_{0<\rho\le1}|L_\rho(\psi)|\le N\}$. Each $E_N$ is closed because every $L_\rho$ is a continuous linear functional on $X$. Step 2.1 gives $X=\bigcup_{N\ge1}E_N$. By [F7], some $E_N$ has nonempty interior.

The topology of $X$ is generated by the increasing seminorms in [F2], so for some $\psi_0\in E_N$, $m\ge0$, and $\varepsilon>0$, the set $\psi_0+\{\zeta:p_m(\zeta)<\varepsilon\}$ lies in $E_N$. For every such $\zeta$, subtracting the two bounds for $\psi_0+\zeta$ and $\psi_0$ gives $|L_\rho(\zeta)|\le2N$ for all $\rho$. If $p_m(\psi)>0$, apply this to $\zeta=\varepsilon\psi/(2p_m(\psi))$; if $p_m(\psi)=0$, then $p_0(\psi)=0$ and hence $\psi=0$. Thus $|L_\rho(\psi)|\le(4N/\varepsilon)p_m(\psi)$ for every $\psi$ and every $0<\rho\le1$. Replacing $L_\rho$ by its definition proves the claimed uniform order estimate.

citations.quote:
Fix an integer $n\ge1$, put $U=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and use the continuous complex-linear test-function pairing of [[def-distribution]]. For $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$ and $\rho>0$, define its dilation at the origin by

$$\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle:=\rho^{-n}\langle t,\varphi(\cdot/\rho)\rangle,\qquad \varphi\in\mathcal D(U).$$

Positive dilations preserve $U$, so the displayed pairing is defined for every test function in $\mathcal D(U)$. If $t$ is the regular distribution induced by a locally integrable function $g$, change of variables gives $\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle=\int_U g(\rho x)\varphi(x)\,dx$.

Convergence $s_\rho\to0$ in $\mathcal D'(U)$ as $\rho\downarrow0$ means $\langle s_\rho,\varphi\rangle\to0$ for every fixed $\varphi\in\mathcal D(U)$. The **scaling degree at the origin** is

$$\operatorname{sd}_0(t):=\inf\{\omega\in\mathbb R:\rho^\omega t_\rho\to0\text{ in }\mathcal D'(U)\}.$$

The infimum of the empty set is $+\infty$; if every real $\omega$ belongs to the set, the infimum is $-\infty$. A finite scaling degree means a real value $\delta\in\mathbb R$. For a distribution $T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ use the same dilation formula on tests in $\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$. An **extension** of $t$ is a distribution $T$ on $\mathbb R^n$ whose restriction to $U$ equals $t$. The degree of divergence associated with a finite scaling degree $\delta$ in dimension $n$ is $\delta-n$. Exact homogeneity of scaling degree $\delta$ means $\rho^\delta T_\rho=T$ for every $\rho>0$.

The definitions use Euclidean dilations about the specified point only. They do not assert that a given distribution arises from a product of fields or that an extension is physically selected.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $U=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$ have finite real scaling degree $\delta$. For every compact $K\subset U$ and every real $\omega>\delta$, there are an integer $m\ge0$ and $C<\infty$ such that

$$|\langle t_\rho,\psi\rangle|\le C\rho^{-\omega}p_m(\psi)\qquad(0<\rho\le1,\ \psi\in\mathcal D_K),$$

where $\mathcal D_K$ and $p_m(\psi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in K}|\partial^\alpha\psi(x)|$ are the fixed-support test-function space and seminorms of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]]. The estimate is uniform over the entire moving-scale family, not merely over each fixed test separately.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, with $n\ge1$. A complex-valued function is smooth if its real and imaginary parts are $C^k$ for every finite $k$, in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Coordinate derivatives act on these two parts separately. We write $\partial^\alpha$ for the multi-index convention there, and $\partial^0\varphi=\varphi$.

The **test-function space** is $\mathcal D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$: its members are smooth functions whose support, the closure in $\Omega$ of their nonzero set, is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Equivalently, the zero extension to $\mathbb R^n$ is smooth with compact support contained in $\Omega$: compactness gives a neighborhood of every boundary point disjoint from the support, where that extension vanishes. Functions are actual functions, not equivalence classes.

Pointwise addition and scalar multiplication make this a complex vector space; the support of a sum lies in the union of the two compact supports. The zero function has empty support. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ there is just the empty function, which is the zero vector. The topology is specified in subsequent definitions. Distribution pairings throughout this page are complex bilinear, with no conjugation on test functions. One may restrict all constructions to real scalars.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. For the fixed-support spaces of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]], let $\mathcal P$ be the set of all seminorms $q:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $q|_{\mathcal D_K}$ is continuous for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. A seminorm means $q(av)=|a|q(v)$ and $q(v+w)\le q(v)+q(w)$.

The **test-function topology** is the topology generated by translated finite intersections of sets $\{\varphi:q(\varphi)<\varepsilon\}$, where $q\in\mathcal P$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Equivalently it is the finest locally convex topology making every inclusion $\mathcal D_K\hookrightarrow\mathcal D(\Omega)$ continuous; the universal-property lemma below proves this equivalence and the topology assertions. This is the locally convex inductive-limit or **LF topology**, not the unrestricted final topology of arbitrary spaces.

For precision, a locally convex topology here is a vector topology generated by a family of seminorms, and boundedness means absorption by every zero-neighborhood: for each such neighborhood $U$ there is $t>0$ with $B\subseteq tU$. Finite intersections may be empty, giving the whole space. When $\Omega$ is empty there is only the zero vector and its unique topology. No convergence criterion for sequences is used in the definition; that criterion will be a theorem.

In ZF the following linear maps are continuous for the LF test-function topologies: $\partial^\alpha:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathcal D(\Omega)$; multiplication by a fixed $a\in C^\infty(\Omega)$; translation $T_h\varphi(x)=\varphi(x-h)$ from $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ to $\mathcal D(\Omega+h)$; and composition $C_F\varphi=\varphi\circ F$ from $\mathcal D(V)$ to $\mathcal D(U)$ for a smooth diffeomorphism $F:U\to V$. Here smooth complex functions mean componentwise smooth real and imaginary parts. The translation and composition maps are topological isomorphisms. No joint continuity in varying $a$ or $h$ is asserted here.

For $a\in\Omega$, the **Dirac distribution at $a$** is the complex-linear functional $\delta_a(\varphi)=\varphi(a)$ on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, with the bilinear convention of [[def-distribution]]. It is continuous: the seminorm $q(\varphi)=|\varphi(a)|$ restricts on each $\mathcal D_K$ to a seminorm bounded by $p_0$ (and is zero if $a\notin K$), so it is one of the admissible seminorms defining the test topology.

Its derivatives are those of [[def-distributional-derivative]]:
$$\langle\partial^\alpha\delta_a,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\partial^\alpha\varphi(a).$$
They are distributions by that definition; on each fixed-support stage the absolute value is at most $p_{|\alpha|}(\varphi)$. If $a\notin K$ all derivatives of the test vanish at $a$, so the bound has zero left side. For $\alpha=0$ this is $\delta_a$; a first derivative evaluates the negative first derivative of the test. No conjugation and no choice are involved. On the empty open set there is no permitted point $a$, rather than a new Dirac distribution. The sharp order of these distributions requires a test witness and is proved in the assigned example later.

derivations.claim: Choose $\chi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$ equal to one near $0$ by [F3], and put $f(x)=\chi(x)-\chi(2x)$. Its support $K$ is compact and avoids $0$, so choose $0<a<b<\infty$ with $K\subset\{x:a\le|x|\le b\}$. If $\delta<n$, set $k=-1$ and $W\varphi=\varphi$. If $\delta\ge n$, let $k$ be the integer with $k\le\delta-n<k+1$, put $P_k\varphi(x)=\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}x^\alpha\partial^\alpha\varphi(0)/\alpha!$, and define $W\varphi=\varphi-\chi P_k\varphi$.

For $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$ define $$T(\varphi):=\langle t,(1-\chi)W\varphi\rangle+\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\langle t,f(2^j\cdot)W\varphi\rangle.$$ Each pairing is with a test supported in $U$: the first factor vanishes near $0$, and $f(2^j\cdot)$ is supported in $2^{-j}K$.

Choose $\omega$ with $\delta<\omega<n+k+1$; this interval is nonempty by the choice of $k$. Put $\lambda=2^{-j}$. By the dilation convention [F1], $$\langle t,f(\cdot/\lambda)W\varphi\rangle=\lambda^n\langle t_\lambda,f\,W\varphi(\lambda\cdot)\rangle.$$ The uniform estimate [F2] bounds this by $C\lambda^{n-\omega}p_m(f\,W\varphi(\lambda\cdot))$ for fixed $m,C$. When $k\ge0$ and $\lambda$ is small enough that $\chi=1$ on $\lambda K$, [F4] gives $p_m(f\,W\varphi(\lambda\cdot))\le C_\varphi\lambda^{k+1}$. Indeed, after each derivative of order $q\le m$, the Taylor remainder contributes order $\lambda^{k+1-q}$ if $q\le k$, and the chain-rule factor contributes $\lambda^q$; if $q>k$, the factor $\lambda^q$ is already at most $\lambda^{k+1}$ for $\lambda\le1$. The product rule with the fixed smooth $f$ preserves this bound. When $k=-1$, the same seminorm is bounded by $C_\varphi$. Thus the tail is bounded by a convergent geometric series with exponent $n+k+1-\omega>0$ (or $n-\omega>0$ when $k=-1$). The series in step 2.1 is absolutely convergent.

For tests supported in any fixed compact $C\subset\mathbb R^n$, the first term of step 2.1 is a continuous functional: its input is supported in a fixed compact subset of $U$, and the cutoff, multiplication, and finite jet maps are continuous by [F5]–[F8]. The geometric bound of step 3.1 controls the small-scale annular tail by one finite derivative seminorm on a compact containing $C$ and $0$; the finitely many larger scales are continuous by [F1] and [F7]. Hence $T$ is continuous on every fixed-support test space and is a distribution by [F6].

If $\varphi$ is supported away from $0$, all its jets at $0$ vanish, so $W\varphi=\varphi$. The partial sums telescope: $$\sum_{j=0}^{N}f(2^j x)=\chi(x)-\chi(2^{N+1}x).$$ For sufficiently large $N$, $\chi(2^{N+1}x)=0$ on the support of $\varphi$. Adding the first term of step 2.1 then gives $T(\varphi)=\langle t,\varphi\rangle$. Thus $T|_U=t$.

Fix $\Omega>\delta$ and choose $\omega$ with $\delta<\omega<\min(\Omega,n+k+1)$. Write $\varphi_\rho(x)=\rho^{-n}\varphi(x/\rho)$, so $T_\rho(\varphi)=T(\varphi_\rho)$. Choose $R$ with $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset B(0,R)$ and $C>R/a$, where $a$ is from step 1.1. Choose $\lambda_0>0$ so $\chi=1$ on $\lambda K$ for $0<\lambda\le\lambda_0$, and take $\rho$ small enough that $C\rho\le\lambda_0$ and $\operatorname{supp}\varphi_\rho$ lies where $\chi=1$. For a shell $\lambda K$ with $\lambda>C\rho$, its inner radius is at least $a\lambda>R\rho$, so $\varphi_\rho$ vanishes there. If $k=-1$, the first term in step 2.1 and all such coarse-shell terms are therefore zero. On the remaining shells $\lambda\le C\rho$, the chain rule and boundedness of $\lambda/\rho$ give $p_m(f\varphi_\rho(\lambda\cdot))\le C_\varphi\rho^{-n}$; their dyadic sum is $O(\rho^{-\omega})$ because $n-\omega>0$. If $k\ge0$, on each fine shell $\lambda\le C\rho$ the cutoff is one. For every derivative order $q\le m$, Taylor's formula for $\varphi-P_k\varphi$ when $q\le k$, and the chain-rule factor $(\lambda/\rho)^q$ when $q>k$, give $p_m(f\,W\varphi_\rho(\lambda\cdot))\le C_\varphi\rho^{-n-k-1}\lambda^{k+1}$; the fixed upper bound $\lambda/\rho\le C$ absorbs the finitely many higher derivative orders. Hence these shells contribute at most $$C_\varphi\rho^{-n-k-1}\sum_{\substack{\lambda=2^{-j},\ j\ge0\\\lambda\le C\rho}}\lambda^{n+k+1-\omega}=O(\rho^{-\omega}),$$ because $n+k+1-\omega>0$ and the dyadic sum is bounded by a constant times $\rho^{n+k+1-\omega}$. On the intermediate coarse shells $C\rho<\lambda\le\lambda_0$, only the subtracted Taylor polynomial remains. Its degree-$j$ term, $0\le j\le k$, contributes at most $C_\varphi\rho^{-n-j}\lambda^{n+j-\omega}$. Since $\omega>\delta\ge n+k\ge n+j$, the exponent $n+j-\omega$ is negative; summing dyadically from the smallest such $\lambda\asymp\rho$ up to $\lambda_0$ gives $O(\rho^{-\omega})$. For the finitely many outer shells $\lambda_0<\lambda\le1$ and the first term of step 2.1, continuity of $t$ on their fixed compact supports bounds the jet contributions by $O(\rho^{-n-k})=O(\rho^{-\omega})$, since $\omega>\delta\ge n+k$. Thus in both the fine and coarse regions $|T_\rho(\varphi)|\le C_\varphi\rho^{-\omega}$ for small $\rho$. Therefore $|T_\rho(\varphi)|\le C_\varphi\rho^{-\omega}$ for small $\rho$ in both cases, so $\rho^\Omega T_\rho(\varphi)\to0$. This proves $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)\le\delta$.

If an exponent $\Omega<\delta$ made $\rho^\Omega T_\rho\to0$, restricting to tests supported in $U$ and using step 5.1 would give $\rho^\Omega t_\rho\to0$, contrary to $\operatorname{sd}_0(t)=\delta$. Hence $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)\ge\delta$. Together with step 5.2, $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)=\delta$.

Let $n\ge1$, $U=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and let $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$ have finite real scaling degree $\delta=\operatorname{sd}_0(t)$. Fix an integer $n\ge1$, put $U=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and use the continuous complex-linear test-function pairing of [[def-distribution]]. For $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$ and $\rho>0$, define its dilation at the origin by

$$\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle:=\rho^{-n}\langle t,\varphi(\cdot/\rho)\rangle,\qquad \varphi\in\mathcal D(U).$$

Positive dilations preserve $U$, so the displayed pairing is defined for every test function in $\mathcal D(U)$. If $t$ is the regular distribution induced by a locally integrable function $g$, change of variables gives $\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle=\int_U g(\rho x)\varphi(x)\,dx$.

Convergence $s_\rho\to0$ in $\mathcal D'(U)$ as $\rho\downarrow0$ means $\langle s_\rho,\varphi\rangle\to0$ for every fixed $\varphi\in\mathcal D(U)$. The **scaling degree at the origin** is

$$\operatorname{sd}_0(t):=\inf\{\omega\in\mathbb R:\rho^\omega t_\rho\to0\text{ in }\mathcal D'(U)\}.$$

The infimum of the empty set is $+\infty$; if every real $\omega$ belongs to the set, the infimum is $-\infty$. A finite scaling degree means a real value $\delta\in\mathbb R$. For a distribution $T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ use the same dilation formula on tests in $\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$. An **extension** of $t$ is a distribution $T$ on $\mathbb R^n$ whose restriction to $U$ equals $t$. The degree of divergence associated with a finite scaling degree $\delta$ in dimension $n$ is $\delta-n$. Exact homogeneity of scaling degree $\delta$ means $\rho^\delta T_\rho=T$ for every $\rho>0$.

The definitions use Euclidean dilations about the specified point only. They do not assert that a given distribution arises from a product of fields or that an extension is physically selected.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, write $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ when $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is Lebesgue measurable and $\int_K|f|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. This extends [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]: equivalently, require integrability on every ball whose closure is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Such balls finitely cover each compact $K$, and conversely their closures are compact; on all of $\mathbb R^n$, any ball lies in a larger compact closed ball.

For a test $\varphi$ as in [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], define the **regular functional**

$$\langle u_f,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx.$$

This is well-defined since $|\int f\varphi|\le\sup_K|\varphi|\int_K|f|$ for $K=\operatorname{supp}\varphi$. It is complex-linear in $f$ and in $\varphi$ and depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $f$. For an empty support the integral is zero. The subsequent embedding theorem establishes continuity, so that this is a distribution, and injectivity modulo almost-everywhere equality. That theorem states the Countable Choice cost of its injectivity proof; no choice is needed to define the displayed pairing.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. In particular local $L^1$ convergence implies strong distribution convergence. The continuity estimate itself is choice-free; Countable Choice is used in the cited $L^1$ approximate-identity theorem proving injectivity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix $n \ge 1$
and write
$$S^{n-1}:=\{\omega \in \mathbb R^n : |\omega|=1\}.$$
Let
$$\Phi:\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\longrightarrow(0,\infty)\times S^{n-1},\qquad \Phi(x)=(|x|,x/|x|).$$
This map is continuous. If $E\subseteq S^{n-1}$ is Borel, then
$(0,1]\times E$ is Borel and
$$\{r\omega:\omega\in E,\ 0<r\le1\}=\Phi^{-1}((0,1]\times E)$$
is Borel in $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ by
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]], hence Borel in
$\mathbb R^n$ by [[thm-borel-sigma-algebra-of-a-subspace-is-the-trace]]. It is
therefore Lebesgue measurable by [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]].
Define
$$\sigma(E):=n\,\lambda_n(\{r\omega : \omega \in E,\ 0<r\le 1\}).$$

The next theorem proves that this is a Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ and that it
is exactly the surface measure needed for polar coordinates.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $U=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and let $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$ have finite real scaling degree $\delta=\operatorname{sd}_0(t)$. Then there exists $T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ such that $T|_U=t$ and $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)=\delta$. The result applies to arbitrary distributions with finite real scaling degree; it assumes no smooth kernel or pointwise product representation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $t\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\})$ have finite real scaling degree $\delta$, and let $\mathcal E_\delta(t)$ be the set of its extensions in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ having scaling degree exactly $\delta$. This set is nonempty by [[thm-qft-finite-scaling-degree-extension]]. If $\delta<n$, then $\mathcal E_\delta(t)$ has exactly one member. If $\delta\ge n$, let $k$ be the unique nonnegative integer with $k\le\delta-n<k+1$ (the floor of $\delta-n$). Then, for any $T_0\in\mathcal E_\delta(t)$,

$$\mathcal E_\delta(t)=T_0+\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{\partial^\alpha\delta_0:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$

Here a **point-local counterterm** means a distribution whose support, as defined in [[def-support-of-a-distribution]], is contained in $\{0\}$. Thus the same-degree freedom is finite dimensional, with precisely the displayed delta derivatives as its basis; at the threshold $\delta=n$, only a multiple of $\delta_0$ is allowed.

For $a\in\Omega$, the **Dirac distribution at $a$** is the complex-linear functional $\delta_a(\varphi)=\varphi(a)$ on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, with the bilinear convention of [[def-distribution]]. It is continuous: the seminorm $q(\varphi)=|\varphi(a)|$ restricts on each $\mathcal D_K$ to a seminorm bounded by $p_0$ (and is zero if $a\notin K$), so it is one of the admissible seminorms defining the test topology.

Its derivatives are those of [[def-distributional-derivative]]:
$$\langle\partial^\alpha\delta_a,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\partial^\alpha\varphi(a).$$
They are distributions by that definition; on each fixed-support stage the absolute value is at most $p_{|\alpha|}(\varphi)$. If $a\notin K$ all derivatives of the test vanish at $a$, so the bound has zero left side. For $\alpha=0$ this is $\delta_a$; a first derivative evaluates the negative first derivative of the test. No conjugation and no choice are involved. On the empty open set there is no permitted point $a$, rather than a new Dirac distribution. The sharp order of these distributions requires a test witness and is proved in the assigned example later.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. For the fixed-support spaces of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]], let $\mathcal P$ be the set of all seminorms $q:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $q|_{\mathcal D_K}$ is continuous for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. A seminorm means $q(av)=|a|q(v)$ and $q(v+w)\le q(v)+q(w)$.

The **test-function topology** is the topology generated by translated finite intersections of sets $\{\varphi:q(\varphi)<\varepsilon\}$, where $q\in\mathcal P$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Equivalently it is the finest locally convex topology making every inclusion $\mathcal D_K\hookrightarrow\mathcal D(\Omega)$ continuous; the universal-property lemma below proves this equivalence and the topology assertions. This is the locally convex inductive-limit or **LF topology**, not the unrestricted final topology of arbitrary spaces.

For precision, a locally convex topology here is a vector topology generated by a family of seminorms, and boundedness means absorption by every zero-neighborhood: for each such neighborhood $U$ there is $t>0$ with $B\subseteq tU$. Finite intersections may be empty, giving the whole space. When $\Omega$ is empty there is only the zero vector and its unique topology. No convergence criterion for sequences is used in the definition; that criterion will be a theorem.

Let $H_N:=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, with vectors identified up to almost

It is well defined because each derivative of $u$ and the product $Vu$ are

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) as in
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]];
it supplies the stated Hilbert-space construction and is not a physical
measurement assumption. Fix one finite nonempty label set $J$ with
$N:=|J|\ge1$, an enumeration of
$J$ by $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and dimensionless real coordinates
$q=(q_1,\ldots,q_N)\in\mathbb R^N$. The labels may represent sites of a
fixed finite spatial lattice or a fixed finite set of modes; any graph,
geometry, and couplings are additional fixed regulator data. The coordinate
space, Hilbert space, and polynomial differential expression are those of
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]:
$H_N=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, with inner product linear in its first
variable, $D_0=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$, and

$$h_0u=-\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\partial_j^2u+V(q)u,\qquad u\in D_0,$$

where $a_j>0$ and $V$ is a real polynomial. Require fixed constants $c>0$ and
$C_0\ge0$ such that

$$V(q)\ge c|q|^2-C_0\qquad(q\in\mathbb R^N).$$

For this physical model, take $q_j$, $a_j$, $c$, $C_0$, and the coefficients
of $V$ to be dimensionless. Adopt a positive energy scale $E_*$ in joules as
primitive finite-regulator data, and use $\hbar$ in joule-seconds under
[[def-qft-framework-units]]. When the mathematical supplier
[[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]] constructs its specified
self-adjoint form realization $h$ of $h_0$, the model Hamiltonian is
$H_{\rm phys}:=E_*h$ on that supplied domain. This postulate adopts the
finite-regulator polynomial data; it does not assert that the initial
differential expression is self-adjoint or choose an operator domain by
itself.

The finite label set and polynomial are held fixed. A finite spatial regulator
is not thereby Lorentz invariant, and this model asserts no continuum or
infinite-volume limit, no convergence of a perturbation series, and no
reported observation. Its parameters are selected model inputs, not measured
values.

Adopt the following physical reading only for an explicitly selected model
whose mathematical data have actually been constructed. Let $\mathscr H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $\rho_t$ be the model's density operator at
a time $t$ at which a measurement is made, and let
$\{M_{a,r}:r=1,\ldots,q_a\}_{a=1}^m$ be a supplied normalized finite bounded
Kraus instrument on $\mathscr H$ in the exact sense of
[[def-qft-finite-bounded-kraus-instrument]]. Assume the Axiom of Countable
Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ when using the normalization result of
[[lem-qft-finite-instrument-normalization]]. Its hypotheses include that
$\rho_t$ is a density operator and that the instrument really satisfies
$\sum_{a,r}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}=I_{\mathscr H}$; the supplier's result is a draft
with a complete conditional proof, not an independent approval or an
apparatus-realization theorem.

Put

$$E_a:=\sum_rM_{a,r}^*M_{a,r},\qquad
\mathcal J_a(X):=\sum_rM_{a,r}XM_{a,r}^*.$$

As the **Born interpretation postulate** for this selected model, read

$$p_a(t):=\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal J_a(\rho_t))
=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_tE_a)$$

as the model probability for outcome $a$. The mathematical supplier proves
$p_a(t)\in[0,1]$ and $\sum_{a=1}^mp_a(t)=1$ under the hypotheses just
listed. When $p_a(t)>0$, adopt
$\mathcal J_a(\rho_t)/p_a(t)$ as the model's conditional state after outcome
$a$; at zero probability no normalized update is assigned. These are
model-level probability assignments, not observations.

If the selected construction supplies a self-adjoint observable in the sense
of [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]] and its
spectral projection-valued measure as in
[[def-projection-valued-measure]], a declared finite Borel partition may be
used only after its projections have been constructed and verified as a
finite projective instrument. In that case the projections are the single
Kraus operators for their outcomes. A supplied bounded effect is read as an
outcome effect only as part of a supplied normalized instrument; this item
does not construct square roots, a spectral measure, or an instrument from an
arbitrary formal observable.

If a model has actually constructed a self-adjoint Hamiltonian $\widehat H$
and its unitary evolution, adopt the Schrödinger convention
$U(t)=\exp(-it\widehat H/\hbar)$ and
$\rho_t=U(t)\rho_0U(t)^*$ when that construction establishes that $\rho_t$
is a density operator. In the Heisenberg representation use
$O_H(t)=U(t)^*O\,U(t)$. This postulate neither constructs the Hamiltonian,
unitary group, state, field representation, nor their domains.

The model declaration identifies the selected species, field normalization,
regulator, preparation and measurement data using
[[def-qft-framework-units]]. It does not assert that every classical action
has a quantization, that every formal state is positive, or that any cutoff
can be removed. In particular it supplies no interacting continuum
four-dimensional QED Hilbert space, scattering operator, asymptotic
completeness, LSZ limit, or nonperturbative convergence. A formal coefficient
is not an exact probability without an additional controlled approximation
map and a constructed model. Agreement with reported data would test the
selected approximation and empirical inputs; it would not prove this
postulate or the model. No reported data are asserted here.

Assume Countable Choice. Use the finite data and notation of
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]: $N\ge1$,
$H_N=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, $D_0=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
and $W=V+C_0+1\ge1+c|q|^2$. For $u,v\in D_0$ define
$$a(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int_{\mathbb R^N}(\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv}\,dq+\int_{\mathbb R^N}(W+1)u\overline v\,dq,$$
and $\|u\|_Q:=a(u,u)^{1/2}$. Let $Q$ be the completion of this inner-product
space, constructed as equivalence classes of $\|\cdot\|_Q$-Cauchy sequences.
Then $Q$ is a complex Hilbert space and the map sending a Cauchy class to its
$L^2$ limit is a continuous injective linear map $Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ with
dense image. Each $u\in Q$ has weak derivatives $\partial_j u\in L^2$ and a
weighted function $\sqrt{W+1}\,u\in L^2$, and
$$\|u\|_Q^2=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2.$$
Here $g_j=\partial_j u$ means explicitly that
$\int u\,\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$ for every
$\varphi\in D_0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $N\ge1$, $a_1,\ldots,a_N>0$ and $c>0$. Let
$Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ be the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$
for the form inner product
$$a_{\mathrm{osc}}(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int (\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv} +\int (c|q|^2+2)u\overline v.$$
This is the space $Q$ of
[[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]] for $V(q)=c|q|^2$ and $C_0=0$.
For $\mathbf n=(n_1,\ldots,n_N)\in\mathbb N_0^N$, there is a smooth product
Hermite function $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ such that
$$\langle\psi_{\mathbf n},\psi_{\mathbf m}\rangle_{L^2}=\delta_{\mathbf n\mathbf m},\qquad \overline{\operatorname{span}}\{\psi_{\mathbf n}\}=L^2(\mathbb R^N),$$
and
$$\left(-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2+c|q|^2\right)\psi_{\mathbf n} =\epsilon_{\mathbf n}\psi_{\mathbf n},\qquad \epsilon_{\mathbf n}:=\sum_{j=1}^N(2n_j+1)\sqrt{a_jc}.$$
For the ground multi-index $\mathbf0$, the smooth representative is
$$\psi_{\mathbf0}(q)=\prod_{j=1}^N(b_j/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-b_jq_j^2/2}, \qquad b_j:=\sqrt{c/a_j}.$$
Each $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ belongs to $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and every $u\in
Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ satisfies the exact form expansion
$$\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+ c\||q|u\|_2^2 =\sum_{\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^N}\epsilon_{\mathbf n} |\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2.$$
All parameters are positive real mathematical parameters; this lemma makes no
physical identification.

Assume Countable Choice and use $Q$, $q_h$, and the operator $h$ from
[[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]]. Let $\lambda_1$ be the least
eigenvalue of $h$. Then
$$\inf\{q_h(u):u\in Q,\ \|u\|_2=1\}=\lambda_1.$$
The infimum is attained by every normalized vector in the lowest eigenspace;
no simplicity or nondegeneracy is assumed.

Assume Countable Choice and the data of
[[lem-qft-polynomial-positive-compact-resolvent]]. Its variational operator $R$
is compact, self-adjoint, positive, and injective on the infinite-dimensional
complex Hilbert space $H_N$. Let $(\mu_n)_{n\ge1}$ be its positive eigenvalues
in nonincreasing order, with multiplicity, and choose corresponding
orthonormal eigenvectors $(\psi_n)_{n\ge1}$. Put
$E_n:=\mu_n^{-1}-1$ and define
$$D(S):=\left\{u=\sum_{n\ge1}c_n\psi_n\in H_N:\sum_{n\ge1}E_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad Su:=\sum_{n\ge1}E_nc_n\psi_n.$$
The series for $u$ converges in $H_N$ by the Hilbert-space expansion theorem.
Then $S$ is self-adjoint and satisfies $\langle Su,u\rangle\ge\|u\|_2^2$
for every $u\in D(S)$; also $(S+I)^{-1}=R$ is compact. For every
$u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
$$Su=-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2u+Wu.$$
Consequently $h:=S-(C_0+1)I$, on the same domain, is a self-adjoint realization
of the differential expression in
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]] and satisfies
$\langle hu,u\rangle\ge-C_0\|u\|_2^2$ for every $u\in D(h)$.
It has compact resolvent, meaning that for some $z\in\mathbb C$ the map
$h-zI:D(h)\to H_N$ is bijective with bounded inverse on $H_N$, and that
inverse is compact; here $z=-(C_0+2)$ and $(h+(C_0+2)I)^{-1}=R$. Put
$\lambda_n:=E_n-C_0-1$, the eigenvalues of $h$; equivalently,
$$D(h)=\left\{u=\sum_nc_n\psi_n:\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
For every $u\in Q$,
$$a(u,u)=\sum_{n\ge1}(E_n+1)|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2,\qquad q_h(u):=a(u,u)-(C_0+2)\|u\|_2^2 =\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2.$$
The lowest eigenvalue is attained and has finite multiplicity. This selects a
form realization; it does not assert that the differential expression on
$C_c^\infty$ is essentially self-adjoint or that it has no other self-adjoint
extensions.

derivations.claim:
Since $V_\lambda(q)=r^2q^2/2+\lambda q^4\ge (r^2/2)q^2$, the
coercivity hypotheses of [F1] and [F4] hold with $c=r^2/2$ and $C_0=0$.
Countable Choice [A1] therefore gives the form domains of [F1] and the
self-adjoint compact-resolvent form realizations with attained least
eigenvalues from [F4], for both $q_\lambda$ and $q_0$.

On $C_c^\infty$, the shifted form norms obey
$\|u\|_{Q_0}^2\le\|u\|_{Q_\lambda}^2$ because their difference is
$\lambda\int q^4|u|^2dq\ge0$. Hence the identity extends continuously
$Q_\lambda\to Q_0$, and the two continuous injections into $L^2$ identify
the same representative. On the core,
$q_\lambda(u)=q_0(u)+\lambda\int q^4|u|^2dq\ge q_0(u)$; approximating any
$u\in Q_\lambda$ by core elements and using continuity of both forms passes
this inequality to $u$. For a normalized $u$, [F3] gives
$q_0(u)\ge\epsilon_g(0)$, so taking the infimum on $Q_\lambda$ yields
$\epsilon_g(\lambda)\ge\epsilon_g(0)$.

Let $g_b(q)=(b/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-bq^2/2}$ with $b=r/\sqrt{2a}$, the
normalized ground function in [F2] for $c=r^2/2$. Choose the smooth cutoff
$\chi_R(q)=\chi(q/R)$ from [F2], with $\chi=1$ on $[-1,1]$,
$\chi=0$ outside $[-2,2]$, and $|\chi_R'|\le C/R$. Then
$u_R=\chi_Rg_b\in C_c^\infty$. For $S>R$, $u_R-u_S$ is supported where
$|q|\ge R$, and
$\|(u_R-u_S)'\|_2\le\|1_{|q|\ge R}g_b'\|_2
+C(R^{-1}+S^{-1})\|1_{|q|\ge R}g_b\|_2\to0$.
The weighted part of its $Q_\lambda$ norm is bounded in square by
$\int_{|q|\ge R}(r^2q^2/2+\lambda q^4+2)|g_b(q)|^2dq\to0$.
These tails vanish because each polynomial times $e^{-bq^2}$ is integrable:
for large $|q|$, its product with $|q|^2$ is bounded. Thus $(u_R)$ is
$Q_\lambda$-Cauchy. Its $L^2$ limit is $g_b$, so injectivity in [F1] gives
$g_b\in Q_\lambda$.

From $g_b'=-bqg_b$ and $\|g_b\|_2=1$, integrate the derivatives of
$q e^{-bq^2}$ and $q^3e^{-bq^2}$ over $\mathbb R$. Their boundary terms
vanish by Gaussian decay, giving
$\int q^2|g_b|^2dq=1/(2b)$ and
$\int q^4|g_b|^2dq=3/(4b^2)$. Hence
$q_\lambda(g_b)=ab/2+r^2/(4b)+3\lambda/(4b^2)$. At
$b=r/\sqrt{2a}$, the first two terms equal
$\epsilon_g(0)=r\sqrt{a/2}$ by [F2], and the last term is
$3a\lambda/(2r^2)$.

Since $g_b\in Q_\lambda$ is normalized, [F3] gives
$\epsilon_g(\lambda)\le q_\lambda(g_b)$. Combining this with step 2.1 and
step 3.1 yields
$0\le\epsilon_g(\lambda)-\epsilon_g(0)\le3a\lambda/(2r^2)$.

Multiplication by $E_*>0$ preserves both inequalities and gives the
stated joule-valued bound. By [A3], this is a selected-model energy
prediction and not a reported measurement.
